HOPE

Movement of Hope

Celebrations and retreats

INTRODUCTION

After the Covenant, the biblical theme proposed as a subject of study and prayer for the journey of growth in faith and in the charism of the members of the MOVEMENT is that of HOPE, a theme closely linked to that of the Covenant because of the signs that the Lord himself wished to give (¹)

First of all, we say that the “Hope” of the members of our Movement is founded on the hope lived by St. Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate, who points out to us in Mary—who sings the Magnificat—the perfect model of our Spirituality of “waiting and gift,” of “Covenant and Hope.”

As we studied the theme of the Covenant throughout the whole Bible, we were able to see that it unfolds, on the one hand, as a progressive journey of faith and, on the other, as an inner tension toward the future. It is a journey that runs from the wonderful reality of God’s faithfulness to his “covenant of love,” offered from the very beginning to the people of Israel:

“…I am the Lord your God…

You shall be my people and I will be your God…,”

to the definitive, final and eternal fulfillment of that same Covenant, when the Church—the Bride of the Lamb—calls out with burning desire to her Bridegroom:

“Maranatha, come, Lord Jesus” (Rev 22:20).

At the center and at the conclusion of this journey stands Mary, the daughter of St. Anne, a historical and at the same time symbolic figure of the Covenant between God and his people. She is the perfect model of the “already”—welcomed by faith and lived in love—and of the “not yet” of Hope, which she has already attained and toward which we are all journeying, until the times are fulfilled and he comes in glory to unite us definitively to himself.

The hope of the members of the Movement is therefore founded on the hope of Mary, the “woman of Hope, she who brought to full expression the longing of the Poor of Yahweh, shining as a model for all who entrust themselves wholeheartedly to the promises of God…” (²).

Mary, conceived immaculate in the womb of Anne, holds within herself all the hope of the patriarchs and the prophets, all the expectation of the people of Israel, the longing and burning desire to see the face of God expressed in the psalms, the spirituality of the just ones of the Old Testament, among whom Joachim and Anne, her mother, stand out together with Mary herself.

“…in me all the righteous deeds and all the ancient law found their fulfillment; in me the groans, the sighs, the tears and the prayers of all the Just of the Old Testament came to rest” (Rule of 1869).

Heir and fulfillment, then, of the promises God made to his people, Mary is also the anticipation of the expectation of all peoples; she is the announcement of universal salvation; she is the mystical dawn of salvation for every human being, the womb of blessing through which divine motherhood entered the world forever; she is the true ark of the Covenant, who receives within herself the Word of God—conceived virginally—and spiritually brings him to birth in all hearts until the end of time. Mary’s “Yes” expresses the hope of the Church. Mary is the mother of all historically, but she is also our mother in a charismatic way. Her hope must mark the very fabric of the lives of the members of the Movement; it must express humanity’s lively desire for the definitive coming of Christ, who came once in history, comes every day and waits to meet us. It must be able to express the eagerness and commitment of each one to acknowledge the primacy of God over everything; the search, first of all, for what gives glory to him and makes him known; the witness to his truth, his justice and his Kingdom in the world; the loving and watchful care to live in communion with him and to know how to seek him, discover him and meet him within the fabric of our days and daily events (cf. Statutes nos. 18-23).

Following the example of Mary and of St. Anne, her mother, the members of the Movement are called to live and bear witness to hope, open to the faithfulness and love of God, with poverty of heart, unshakable trust in the One for whom “nothing is impossible,” detachment from things for a concrete sharing of goods “of nature and of grace,” joy in awaiting the Kingdom and longing for eternal and perfect communion with God: the object of the love we await, the center of our Hope.

Hope, openness to God’s future

The whole history of salvation is therefore woven together and marked by faith, which means openness to the fulfillment of God’s “impossibles.”

— The God of Abraham made a numerous posterity “possible” for a sterile old man!

— The God of Israel created a “holy people” out of a helpless mass of desperate slaves!

The God of David was able to keep a promise of faithfulness to a divided and corrupt monarchy!

— The God of a “Remnant” of Israel made another “exodus” shine forth, giving life again to a people who were paying in exile the consequences of their own infidelities and adulteries!

— The God of the “poor” stopped the “curse” that weighed on all humanity (the consequences of original sin) by giving the “immaculate conception” of Mary in the womb of St. Anne!

— The God of the “virgin” was able to bring into the world… divine motherhood!

— Finally, in the fullness of time, the most awaited of the divine “impossibles”: Jesus, the divine Lamb, sacrificed in atonement for the sin of the world, is exalted at the right hand of God, lifting humanity to the heights of heaven.

God, then, makes possible the expectation of a future that would be absurd if it did not rest on the faithfulness and truth of his divine “Word.”

The religious experience of our fathers in faith therefore bears witness to this attitude of hope, by which we lean on God, whom we feel and call upon as Father, rock, help, shield, defense, benefactor…

We believe in his promise and we await the future as the time of the full realization of the gift of stability, of support, and above all of liberation and communion.

The memorial of the “exodus,” recalled in the celebration of Passover, evokes and confirms for us today as well that the history of salvation is guided by the God of the exodus, the God of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, …Anne, Joachim, Mary, Joseph. He is the God who asks us to learn to trust in him, who calls us to “go out” from our riches and our slaveries, to live in the dimension of hope, awaiting the full fulfillment of his promises: the possession of him.

May this series of celebrations help each one to deepen the theme of HOPE in the spiritual and charismatic line that is proper to us, bringing to maturity an existential and ecclesial response that must set us apart as a “gift” and a “leaven” of life in the Church, in the footsteps of Mother Rosa.

DIRECTIONS

We will celebrate the “Word” as in the sheets on the “covenant.”

In these you will notice more biblical quotations, and psalms added for “further reflection.”

The celebrations may seem too… dense, but everything can serve to shed better light on the gift of “hope” that God gives us, above all so that the brothers and sisters may find moments of personal reflection even at home.

The “retreats” that follow every five or six celebrations help to deepen the monthly journey of the “Word.” The brothers and sisters are therefore invited to follow the order indicated.

The journey of hope through the Old Testament finds its outcome and fulfillment in the New. So, once we get there… after some necessary paths have been indicated, the themes that interest them most will be left to the research and discovery of the individual groups: for “inscrutable,” indeed, are the “riches of Christ”!

CELEBRATION 1

GOD REVEALS HIMSELF AS A LOVER OF LIFE

Introduction to the celebration

God’s promise to humanity (Gen 3:14-21) associates Mary with the Messiah, who becomes the object of the hope of all humanity. The Patriarchs, the Prophets, the Judges, the Kings and the poor, the “faithful remnant,” awaited her; among them we look with special affection to Anne and Joachim, who deserved to have, for all generations, Mary as their daughter, the Mother of the One who is the answer to the “hope of the nations.”

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Genesis 1

Reflection on the Word

Opening the first page of the Bible, we immediately find the divine initiative: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” But that is not all: “The earth was without form or shape, with darkness over the abyss.”

And again the initiative of God: his Spirit hovered so that light might appear… and the firmament and the fruitful earth… and the sun and the moon and then living beings: creatures of every kind and finally the human being.

And from that sovereign will, every reality knows its own goodness. Every creature receives life from the One who alone is good and the source of life.

This free will of God, who creates everything that exists and calls it into being for a good purpose, is what grounds hope.

That “blessing” of God will make the animals fruitful and allow them to multiply on the earth (1:22).

And the human being too, the crown of creation, is “very good” (1:31). For, unlike the other creatures, the human being will bear in himself the divine image and likeness. For the human being too that blessing will hold: to grow, to multiply, to be fruitful, to have dominion over the earth; in short, to be a bearer of life, a witness of this splendor of God, inaccessible yet now made manifest: the human being is called to share in the divine life.

Even after the tragedy of sin and the entrance of death into the world (Wis 1:12-15; 2:23-24), hope appeals to that divine will which continues to be faithful to the original command: “Let us make man in our image.”

Despite the experience of death, no curse for the human being! Indeed, a promise will be sealed in his heart: enmity between the “accursed one,” author and lord of death, and the woman, “mother of all the living” (Gen 3:14-21).

The ground will be cursed, and the human being, in order to be saved, will have to walk upon it as a pilgrim, protected only by providential “tunics” (Gen 3:21).

From the depths of any abyss of death, the human being, by virtue of that promise, will therefore be able to… “cry out” (Ps 130:1).

Even far from the Spirit of God, having fled from his presence, he can be seized and guided once more by the divine hand (Ps 139:7-10).

After reading Psalm 130:

– In what “word” does the psalmist hope?

– What does he expect from the Lord?

– What kind of “redemption” is there with the Lord?

As you meditate on the page of creation, what certainty do you discover in it?

Compare yourself with what Wisdom says (1:12-15; 2:23-24) and Psalm 139:13-14:

– Why the tragedy of death?

– Why the envy of the “devil”?

– What is the “mystery” of our life?

– Who are we really?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“Always clinging to my Good, I kept repeating: Oh! my sins deserve worse, even hell itself; and I will gladly go there to feel those pains, provided that you lead me, and I am near you and close to you: you alone are my paradise! And I wept much for having offended him. With the permission of obedience I increased my penances as much as I could…” (M 1.1, p. 2f).

(from The Spiritual Physiognomy of Rosa Gattorno, p. 53).

CELEBRATION 2

THE PROMISE OF LIFE THROUGH SACRED HISTORY

Introduction to the celebration

Trust in the fulfillment of the promise, which runs through the whole history of salvation, reaches its peak in the one whose “Seed” engages in battle against the evil one. Her hope in Yahweh, founded on the certainty that struggles and tribulations would not nullify the fulfillment of the divine promise, allowed the Word to enter this world as a light that scatters the darkness, and as the life of every human being.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reflection on the Word

The promise of life runs through the whole of sacred history.

Even before the Patriarchs it is already evident… (Gen 3:21)

For Adam and Eve there are those “tunics of skin”: that fruitfulness, though painful, is not taken away! (Gen 3:16).

The cry of the blood of innocent Abel from the depths of the earth awaits an answer (Gen 4:10), while Cain is given a sign that will keep him from being killed (Gen 4:15).

With Noah (see Covenant sheets, celebrations 4, 5 and 6) life will be renewed for all humanity…

God keeps seeking the human being, keeps nourishing hope. His will is faithful to that original call: “Let there be light!”

And the light “was good.”

That light enlightens every human being: it is given as a gift!

Reading: John 1:1-18

In the beginning God created…

In the beginning was the Word…

The inaccessible light reveals itself…

The silence of nothingness is broken by the eternal Word… And the Word, divine life, creates life…

The Word became… Jesus!

He is the fulfillment of every promise of “something very good.”

Jesus is the answer to every groan, to every cry that rose up from that pilgrimage through darkness and tribulation.

Jesus must be welcomed so that the hope for life may find rest in the human heart.

To deepen prayer

Read Psalm 27: “The Lord is my light and my salvation.”

The journey through sorrow, abandonment and death need not frighten us if we keep that original “word”: the earth is good and the human being remains the “wonder” of creation, because the Word of God continues to remain among us. “Hope,” then, take heart: the light still exists in the land of the living. “The call of God is irrevocable”: Paul said this of the history and destiny of Israel (Rom 11:29). Even that “people” who did not welcome him… can hope. Let thanks be given, then, to God, who has freed us from death through Jesus (cf. Rom 7:24-25).

Jesus is the light that enlightens every human being because he is the Word who creates, redeems and sanctifies (cf. 1 Cor 1:30).

Reflecting on these passages of Scripture, try to renew your act of faith in Jesus Christ:

– Do you believe that he is the Lord of the universe, of history, of invisible and visible realities, head of the Church, visible image of the invisible God, divine life itself appearing in human form?…

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

Rosa receives as a gift the certainty that in weakness the strength of the presence and intercession of the Mother of Christ triumphs:

“… new tribulations came upon me that tore me apart, so strong were they … but dear Mother Mary did not delay in coming to comfort me, appearing to me together with the dear Child, my Beloved.

Oh, what comfort. But the evil serpent… kept bringing ever new torments…” (M 1.1, p. 55).

The work that God accomplished in Mary by associating her with the saving mystery of the Son has permanent value.

The effectiveness of the Mother’s mission, for every time and every person who lets himself be guided docilely by her, is for Rosa an experience that generates full adherence to the Economy of God, who sends the Son to bring it to completion: “Behold, a Son comes into the world, the ‘offspring of the woman,’ who will defeat the evil of sin at its roots: ‘he will crush the serpent’s head.’

Mary, Mother of the Word, is placed at the center of that enmity, of that struggle which accompanies the history of humanity on earth and the very history of salvation” (RM 1).

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 141)

CELEBRATION 3

THE HOPE OF THE PATRIARCHS

Introduction to the celebration

It is clear that the hope of the Patriarchs is founded on faith in the God of the Covenant and of the Promises.

Mary will sing of this hope in her canticle of exultation, when she realizes that the Lord had chosen her as the New Eve: “… He has helped Israel his servant, remembering his mercy, according to his promise to our fathers, to Abraham and to his descendants forever.”

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reflection on the Word

Reading: Genesis 12

The journey of the Patriarchs will be bound to this divine promise: “In you shall all the families of the earth find blessing” (Gen 12:3).

The hope of the Patriarchs will therefore rest on that “word.” Abraham had already had this experience: “hoping against hope” (Rom 4:18) he could keep walking, giving glory to God, that is, believing that God could accomplish what was humanly impossible. But: “I am God the Almighty… and I will make you exceedingly numerous” (Gen 17:1-2).

The promise had to produce in the heart of the old patriarch a truly exceptional openness to the future. Looking at that present of sterility and old age, one cannot doubt that grace had truly mysterious ways of becoming effective in the life of Abraham (Gen 18:14); this will give confidence, for example, to the prayer of supplication (Gen 22:8). Abraham now knows, from experience, that God provides: he provides for life.

So will Isaac learn (Gen 26:2-5) and Jacob (Gen 28:13-15).

Jacob himself, in his trial, will lean on that promise of blessing, which is precisely effective, in this case, to save him from solitude and from death (Gen 32:23-31 and 35:10-11).

God will provide for Egypt (Gen 41:16.25.36) by sending it, at the right moment, the… “charismatic” Joseph. He too will understand that the God of his father has plans of peace and salvation, even in the midst of tribulations (Gen 41:50-52) and not only for the “good”; his kindly providence extends to the ungrateful and the wicked (Luke 6:35) (Gen 45:5-8).

And on this experience the book of Genesis will close (Gen 50:19-20).

The journey of the Patriarchs will therefore begin with this invitation: to hope in life (Gen 12:1-2)!

It will end with this certainty: God makes use even of evil for good: an echo of the first original command (Gen 1:28). There is a blessing that calls for fruitfulness: “multiply… fill the earth… have dominion!”

Despite the dark parenthesis of sin, that promise will persist: Eve is “the mother of all the living” (Gen 3:20) and the offspring of the woman will crush the head of the deceiving murderer (Gen 3:15; cf. John 8:44).

– After reading and meditating on the biblical texts mentioned above, can you sincerely say that your hope is truly rooted in the promises of God?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“Come, take courage! Soon you will see that the Lord will console you; but an ounce of patience and two of faith in God, and you will have everything, I assure you. But peace, and little overthinking; day by day embrace the cross that the Lord sends us; remember that new days bring new crosses” (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: Aug. 12, 1870).

It will not always become easy to be joyful in the anguish that oppresses us; then at least resignation is needed, not the passive kind that makes a virtue of necessity, but the kind that consists in a courageous conformity to the will of God.

(from Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 161)

CELEBRATION 4

THE HOPE OF ABRAHAM

Introduction to the celebration

Abraham’s hope gains strength from the experience of the Covenant, which in part anticipates what he awaits: communion with God, experienced as Creator, Savior, Redeemer and forgiving Mercy, who takes upon himself the frailty of his people. This same hope will later animate the hope of the Holy Parents of Most Holy Mary and, naturally, the hope of Mary herself.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Genesis 18:16-33

Reflection on the Word

We have seen where the Patriarchs drew strength on their journey: their hearts were attentive to keeping that divine blessing of good… And in that “promise” they persevered: hoping, then, in the faithfulness of God and never in their own abilities.

This hope enabled Abraham to make truly unheard-of requests: he is now addressed by God (Gen 18:17-19), he knows God’s feelings, which he knows to be those of a lover of life (Gen 18:23-25); it matters little that Abraham is nothing: dust and ashes; he now holds in his heart the gift of that Living God: an oath that promises fruitfulness. So he can… dare to speak (Gen 18:27)!

And that request is accepted, welcomed: “Very well… I will forgive… I will not destroy.” God lets himself be overcome by the “friend” he has chosen.

– Do you not believe that precisely this hoping in the promise of blessing made it possible to open a fruitful dialogue between God and the Patriarchs?

– Do you not think that the foundation of every prayer should be precisely the hope of being welcomed by God?

– And does hoping to be welcomed by God not have to presuppose an awareness of our own spiritual… “insubstantiality” (“dust and ashes,” Abraham confessed)?

– Can you find similarities in the attitudes of Abraham and of Mary at Cana? (John 2:1-9)

– Does the introduction to the “Our Father” that the Church celebrates in the Eucharistic liturgy not still seem to you similar to that “daring” of Abraham?

For personal reflection: Psalm 65

Praise rises spontaneously to God when we admire his wonders, his beauty, his holiness (see also Psalm 66). “To you all flesh will come,” because God listens to the inmost prayer of every human being. And every human being, when he learns to recognize his own limits, needs to feel welcomed by someone who regards him as “near,” who feeds him with his graces…

Abraham, the friend of God, the one “called near,” does it not seem to you the necessary experience of every human being who wants to be saved?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

Just as the decision of God about Sodom and Gomorrah is made known to Abraham (cf. Gen 18:16ff), so Rosa contemplates God’s judgment on Rome and Paris so that she may take part in it with prayers, offerings and penances.

Significant and programmatic is the illumination about the trial that the Father permits for sinners, which leads her to offer herself as a victim for them and to plead insistently with Jesus himself to suspend his punishments upon the cities of Rome and Paris. Her description of it underlines the different elements of the economy of salvation.

“Another day he showed me how His Majesty was angry and that there was nothing that could calm him. Mary was praying and I was terrified at the sight of the greatest destruction of two cities, one by fire and the other by war. One, Paris, was fire, and Rome was war! The slaughter was horrible, my God, have mercy, and I offered myself as a victim so that everything might (be poured out) upon me and he might be calmed.

How much I suffered I cannot describe; I was so grieved that I could not make myself come alive. Everything served me as sorrow, always before my eyes my God, in a severe and angry attitude!…” (M 1.1, pp. 51-52).

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 66)

CELEBRATION 5

THE PATRIARCHS OPEN TO GOD’S NEWNESS

Introduction to the celebration

The expectation of the Patriarchs was characterized by openness to the newness of God, who revealed himself and acted progressively according to his Promises. They walked with God and were aware of his infinite transcendence and of his unpredictable breaking into history. St. Anne, heir of the hope of Abraham, will then bear witness, on the threshold of the New Testament, to this heroic trust of her ancestors.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Wisdom 10:1-14

Reflection on the Word

The Patriarchs experienced the Living God, who took care of their… sterility, their fears, their weaknesses; they walked guided by this new light that shone in their lives: their minds and their wills received constant help to understand more and more how that “mysterious” God wished to reveal himself as the One, the Almighty, the Savior.

Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph have taught us to hope in this God of theirs, who always drew them out of dramatic situations, who accompanied them, defended them, exalted them at the right moment, “delivered them from their sufferings,” “led them along straight paths.”

A God who “went down” into their prisons, who did not abandon them in their chains!

For personal reflection: Psalm 71

The Patriarchs proclaim to you the power of this God of theirs.

They tell our generation too of his wonders. They trusted: “… you will give me life again” … “… you will again comfort me.”

Because they experienced the goodness of God, they can say: “You, Lord, are my hope… may I never be put to shame”; their sense of being freed and saved makes them proclaim: “I will multiply your praises… I cannot measure your salvation… so I do not cease to hope.”

– As you meditate on the life of the Patriarchs, underline their attitudes in the face of God’s saving interventions, how they were strengthened in their trust in God and how they hoped. Try to write down these observations of yours: they will be the subject of a communal sharing, to be held in groups at a celebration in the homes or at the next monthly retreat.

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“… I always find myself in the presence of God… There are times when I feel certain words coming out of my mouth to answer in the affairs of his Work, and so I never think about what I must say, because my love speaks for me… Words come out that are certainly not mine, but his, who acts and speaks in me. I would say that it is a rest for me, because in him I stay and taste his delights.” (M 1.1, p. 149f).

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 37)

RETREAT 1

GOD’S REST

Introduction to the celebration

It is God who creates hope in the human heart and illuminates a history that would make no sense if it did not become “history of salvation”: that is, a testimony to all… the impossibles of God, created by him so that the human being may find his rest. This rest God has always safeguarded for the human being. After the disobedience that could have led to definitive death, he announces to him the promise that he will not take back what he has given. The promise, precisely, reveals the coming of the Messiah Redeemer, born of a Woman to win victory over the enemy who will continue to fight against her. The Bible places at the beginning of its narrative a hope in the human heart.

Lauds

Reading: Psalm 1

Reflection on the Word

“Blessed is the one who does not follow the counsel of the wicked.”

The Patriarchs are teachers of hope: they saw and bore witness that God loves the world, that he did not remain indifferent to the sterility and death of the human being. That God is the author of life and that all his ways lead to life. This is exactly what we must learn: to reflect and meditate on the wonders of the Living God and to flee the wicked, who by their life and their “counsel” declare: “God does not exist.”

To meditate, instead, is to “remember” the works of God: Pss 77:13; 105:2.5; 106:4.7.21; 107:22; 111:4; 102:13; 135:13; 143:5. “Even in my rest I remember you”: Ps 63:7. Especially in times of… trial: Ps 77:3-7.

These “remembered” works must be “proclaimed”: Ps 92:2-3.13-16; 118:17; they encourage and give hope: Ps 108:14.

It is therefore the constant, faithful and convinced “delighting” in the Law of the Lord that “holds” in our heart and memory the great “deeds” of the God of Abraham, of Isaac, of Jacob, which help us to transcend ourselves, to come out of our incapacities and sadnesses. They push us toward confidence, toward that… daring which is proper to Christian hope. And hope… “will give everything in its time.” For hope… all his works will succeed!

Besides all the psalms cited, “meditate” on Psalm 136: a great “litany” of thanksgiving.

CELEBRATION 6

THE CHILDREN OF JACOB, PEOPLE OF HOPE

Introduction to the celebration

After the Patriarchs, Yahweh forms with the descendants of Jacob a people who must learn to hope, purifying themselves of everything that directs them toward the pursuit of purely earthly goals. Yahweh will become their liberator in the struggle against Pharaoh, but Israel must train itself to hope against hope. St. Anne contemplated such hope to the point that it became the supporting spiritual axis of her spiritual life.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Exodus 1

Reflection on the Word

Exodus, too, presents itself at once as the book that proclaims the power of the Living God. His promises, in fact, are being fulfilled: “the Israelites were fertile and prolific; they became so populous and strong that the land was filled with them” (Exod 1:7).

But this life does not grow without drama! The new pharaoh did not know Joseph; he did not see in this people growing in his midst a sign of blessing… Quite the opposite… Fear leads him to plans of extermination: “let us prevent them from multiplying” (Exod 1:10). Life, then, will struggle against death, and the Exodus will forever mark the journey of hope for all who, trusting in God, will come out of the darkness and the anguish of death to reach the light and the possession of life!

– The midwives fear God: in what does this consist, in your opinion? Where does it have its roots, according to this passage of Exodus?

– How are they blessed by God?

– Does your life seem to you a witness to the Living God? Or do you too resign yourself to a mentality of fear and death?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

Within the horizon of the words of Jesus, addressed to all disciples of every age, there emerge those spoken for her alone while she is absorbed in the presence of the Crucified One:

“They will devote themselves to the growth of our holy faith; to the care of the sick…; they will receive… in their houses girls at risk and they will teach Christian doctrine.”

It is a mission carried out with a portion of the Church (daughters and sons) that she receives as a gift from her Savior. The whole Church, in fact, was born of the total gift of Christ, anticipated in the Eucharist and accomplished on the cross.

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 130)

CELEBRATION 7

GOD PREPARES SALVATION FOR THE CHILDREN OF JACOB

Introduction to the celebration

The living and effective presence of the Lord animates the hope of the children of Jacob. In him they find answer and help. They meet God’s personal concern and a response of love that prepares their salvation and liberation. Perseverance in hope will make them sharers, through an adherence that is not easy, in the intervention of God, who chooses them as his people. He expresses a personal possession, because he loves them and because he is faithful to the oath made to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. With Israel, God prepares a holy people, bringing about and anticipating a small privileged part of humanity which, in the fullness of time, will welcome the Messiah in the person of Mary.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

God observes the misery of the human being and… “comes down” to set free. As he saw the “sterility” of Abraham and “came down” to bless him. Here again is the foundation of hope: God intervenes when the human being groans and suffers.

Reading: Exodus 3

Reflection on the Word

God reveals the NAME: “I am who I am…” I am the ONE WHO EXISTS… the One who is LIFE ITSELF, the source of everything that exists. In short: “I alone give life and bring into existence the things that are not.” Thus the God of Abraham, of Isaac, of Jacob makes himself a liberating presence for Israel in Egypt. He acts, therefore, in the history of human beings and nations, to give meaning and a future. Removing humiliation, pain, death.

Reflecting on Exod 2:23:

– God is faithful to the covenant with Abraham (Exod 2:23-25): he welcomed that “cry,” even though it was silent (see the Covenant catechesis, 17th celebration). Now he hears the lament of those descendants. Above all he is sensitive to the lament of the “little ones” (Gen 21:17)… Where, in your opinion, is God turning his gaze today? Whom do you think he is taking care of?

– Would you like to be chosen, as Moses was, to become an instrument of liberation for your brothers and sisters?

– How, in your opinion, did God prepare Moses for this mission?

For further reflection: Psalm 102

God’s years have no end (Ps 102:28): he continues to be the Eternal One, the “I AM,” who wants to show mercy to the wretched and the despised of today… “A new people will praise the Lord” (Ps 102:19).

– Do you sense that you are part of this people of the poor whom God wants to redeem?

– In which part of the psalm do you find yourself?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

Under the direct action of God, who will guide her with jealous love, the Words of her Crucified Beloved will accompany her until they become fully clear.

Her fears, perplexities and doubts are no obstacle for God, who has found in her, up to this point, a response of radical love to Christ. He now demands the same availability for the Work that is to arise in the Church with her. Here is how she describes this demand of her God:

“… those that I had put away…, began to disturb me, because an inner Voice kept tormenting me, telling me that I had to show them, that it was His work, but I drove it away and, to put it better, I did not understand what He wanted. One evening: what do you want, my dear Crucified One? why must I show this writing, which is to be of use? He answered me: ‘For the Work that I want, it will be great!’ My God! I began to think and understood nothing: where is it to be, who is to do this work? I felt so confused that I put the thought aside and began to pray, clinging to my dear Crucified One, and a Voice that was certainly His, my Beloved’s, said to me: ‘I want this Work from you!’ (M 2, pp. 10-11).

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 60)

CELEBRATION 8

ISRAEL’S HOPE IS PUT TO THE TEST

Introduction to the celebration

Israel’s hope is put to the test. The prevailing of Pharaoh’s oppressive power makes faith waver in the God who had rescued them from famine and fed them for centuries in the land of Egypt. The God of Abraham and of Jacob now appears weak, powerless, looking on idly at the pain that the powerful inflict on the weak. God’s voluntary lowering of himself, however, will culminate in an unforeseeable and surprising triumph that will last through the centuries and that Mary of Nazareth will proclaim in her hymn of exultation: “He has shown might with his arm, dispersed the arrogant of mind and heart, has thrown down the rulers from their thrones but lifted up the lowly” (Luke 1:51-52).

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Exodus 5

Reflection on the Word

There is a command (like the one Jesus will often give to demons) to the “enslaving powers” to let go… so that a feast to the Lord may be celebrated in the desert.

Every human being, even a slave, is visited by this feast in honor of the Lord. He prepares it there, in the desert… where it seems impossible.

Then the “battle” begins. Between freedom and constraint. Between “going out” to life and “staying,” for fear of the unknown…

The closer God draws, the more intense the reaction of evil appears: how painful!

– Does it not seem to you that the third commandment reminds us of God’s will to give us a feast, while the will of the world nails us to a continual “overwork” (worries, ambitions, insecurities, fears)?

– How do you interpret certain liberations that an atheistic world offers? Certain aspects of modern progress? Certain conquests of technology?

Remember Pharaoh’s reaction to the announcement of “celebrating” the feast of the Lord: “They are lazy. Let more work be laid upon these men!”

– The Scriptures recall the works of God that lead the human being to joy and praise. Whoever “does not know God” reveals his oppressive and destructive intentions: are you convinced of this?

Do you have this discernment in your life, to understand truly what leads you to peace? And not to affliction?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“I wept: I told my eternal Father to send me Providence: he appeared to me so beautiful that I remained in ecstasy, and he told me very clearly that he would take care of whatever would be needed for his work.” (M 1.1, p. 172)

(from Spiritual Physiognomy, pp. 201-202)

CELEBRATION 9

GOD’S FAITHFULNESS AND THE PEOPLE’S FRAILTY

Introduction to the celebration

The history of the children of Jacob is the supporting axis of the whole history of humanity, where the alternation of God’s faithfulness with the frailty of his people does not make God himself desist from the progressive fulfillment of his promises. Love and forgiveness are interwoven until they arrive at her who brings forth the object and the subject of a new hope: Jesus the Savior.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the reading

God’s saving intervention provokes tension, bewilderment, uncertainty, fear.

We have heard it in the reactions of Moses, of Pharaoh, of the scribes of the Israelites, of the people… Try to read, in these Gospel passages, the saving work of Jesus: Mark 9:14-29; Luke 8:26-39; John 15:18-27. Compare them with the attitude of Pharaoh and with that of Moses.

Reading: Mark 9:14-29; Luke 8:26-39; John 15:18-27

– Why do the demons cry out: “Do not torment us”?

– Why the pain, the suffering and the slavery, even in this generation?

– Do you understand that word of Jesus: “hatred without reason”?

– Do you need to be saved? Do you know your Exodus?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“One of the commanders of the large ships came up and wanted to know how the matter had gone, and told me to be careful not to do this or that again. I turned and said to him:

— I beg you to leave me! Your argument is hardly logical: in the Work of the Lord philosophy and calculation have no place; they are all empty lecterns.

— What kind of reasoning is this? — he said to me.

— As a poor slave, which I am, I never studied and I understand nothing. I have tried to study and to perfect myself in only one subject: the will of God, trying to do it blindly in perfect abandonment to him, like a faithful slave to her beloved Master” (TC p. 219f).

(In Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 20).

CELEBRATION 10

ISRAEL LEARNS THAT GOD PROVIDES

Introduction to the celebration

The God who had said to Abraham: “I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, so that you will be a blessing,” fulfills his promise even though Israel shows greed, arrogance and ingratitude during the time of purification. His provident intervention forms the basis of the people’s further hope. They will learn that their God will not abandon them, to the extent that they entrust themselves to him in total poverty. But Israel will reach this perfect hope in Mary, who will be able to say of herself: “… he has looked upon the lowliness of his servant; behold, from now on all ages will call me blessed.”

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Exodus 16

Reflection on the Word

The journey through the desert becomes difficult.

Pharaoh has been defeated… but not the people’s laziness, their ties to the old slavery, which nevertheless bring out God’s kindness and magnanimity.

His patient firmness continues to educate and feed a people who are greedy and arrogant, forgetful of the benefits received and slow to enjoy that feast to which the holiness of God wants to lead them.

The glory of the living God will gradually be revealed in that desert, which is more moral than physical.

That daily bread becomes the sign of God’s faithfulness to that people of exasperating unbelief and absurd ingratitude.

Yet Israel must place its hope in that bread, in order to be saved from everything that demeans the human being and would condemn him to despair.

– What do you mean by: “seeing the glory of the Lord”?

(You can deepen your reflection by reading the notes on Exod 24:16; John 1:14; Acts 6:15; 1 Cor 2:8).

– Why does God want to educate the people to… this ration of daily food?

– And why the importance of that “absolute rest” consecrated to the Lord?

– Where do you find reasons to hope, even today, from this divine pedagogy?

For further reflection: Psalm 106

Despite their stubbornness, “He took note of their distress” (106:44). When he heard their cry “he remembered his covenant with them, he took pity in his great love” (106:45).

– Can we too not found our hope on this “great love” of God?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“I went to receive Holy Communion. What I experienced, my Good,… I remained absorbed in him…, when I came to myself, I was so comforted, strong as a giant, I would have defied the whole world, persecutions…” (M 1.1, p. 9; 142).

From him, who chose to use as matter and symbol the elements that recall not only the primary nourishment of life but also the sharing of bread with the poor, Rosa learns to love those who are alone and suffering.

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 90)

RETREAT 2

GOD REVEALS THE FUTURE TO HUMANKIND

Introduction to the celebration

It is impossible for the human being to give himself a future or to build a happiness that goes beyond his earthly horizons, that does not fall within the possibilities of his own nature. Only God reveals this path to the human being: a history that projects itself into the future. Israel’s attitudes of unfaithfulness do not tire him; he makes himself Providence, remembering that he has promised the Messiah as restorer and victor, born of the new Eve.

His interventions awaken the hope that lay dormant in the heart of the people.

Lauds

Reading: Exodus 17

Reflection on the Word

Protests and murmurings are constant. Like that food that comes down from heaven. It is hard to lead that journey… It becomes difficult to ask for help from a God who nonetheless shows himself faithful, attentive and provident. But the more God shows himself generous and lavish in blessing… the more the enemies seem to rage.

Always new, always more powerful. “But is God truly with us?”

Even Moses’ plea would run dry if he were not helped.

Everything tires us, bores us. We would all end up dragged into a deadly “resignation” if God did not fight for us (Exod 10:2; 14:14)! It is true: the enemies are battle-hardened… they deceive… they set obstacles so that faith in the saving power of God may not grow… but then they are put to shame: Exod 7:22; 8:3; 8:14; 9:11; 9:30; 10:7; 11:3; 12:30.33. Indeed, those enemies will have to testify: “No one is as powerful as God”: Exod 9:14.16. Israel’s hope must be founded solely on the sovereign power of God: “the whole earth is his!” (Exod 9:29). The salvation of Israel is a divine work: Exod 14:13. Israel will see: Exod 14:31! Only this hope, sown in the heart, will finally heal: Exod 15:26. Jesus will be the “strong and beloved man” who will “wipe out entirely the memory” of the “adversary” from the scene of the world (Luke 11:21-23).

Reflect on:

Exod 6:6-9 and 7:4-5: underline the promises by which God commits himself to Israel (verbs in the future!) and note the situation in which the people find themselves…

After reading all the citations:

– How do you judge your journey of faith?

– What is your spiritual situation?

– Do you believe in those promises?

– What do you do, or what attitude do you find in yourself, to dispose yourself to become a “spectator” of God’s work?

CELEBRATION 11

MOSES’ HOPE FOUNDED ON PRAYER

Introduction to the celebration

Union with God in contemplation strengthens Moses’ hope. He becomes more and more completely his God’s and totally in solidarity with his people. As we reflect on the hope of Moses, we think that St. Anne too, meditating on and contemplating the same biblical events, nourished her hope in the fulfillment of the Lord’s promises.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Exodus 32:11-14

Reflection on the Word

“Moses cried out to the Lord for help” (Exod 17:4).

It is the constant of all spiritual guides: to call upon God’s help for themselves and for the people.

It was the path of Abraham (Rom 4:16-25): he always leaned on that promise of God, which alone could make him a “father.”

After the grave sin of idolatry committed by Israel, it will be necessary to call for help.

“Hoping against hope,” because forgiveness is… pure grace! (Exod 32:30-35).

Through the intercession of Moses, the people will be able to walk once more with their God (Exod 33:12-17).

We will thus be able to understand the meaning of priestly consecration: to “draw” divine favor.

The priest is chosen and placed there, before God, to plead with him in the name of the people (Exod 28:36-39).

This priesthood will appear fulfilled and in all its splendor in the paschal mystery of Jesus: Heb 4:14; 5:10; 7:22-28; 9:7-14; 10:19-25.

– How do you profess this hope of yours, without wavering, in the intercession of Jesus, the high priest?

– How much do you encourage your brothers and sisters in this charity: the invocation of the name of Jesus?

– Sincerely: are you among those who “desert” the meetings? Or rather among those who encourage us to keep walking, despite the hardships, trusting in the faithfulness of the One who has promised?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“Prayer is our only shield of defense” — “It is the key to graces” — “Do not forget to stay always in the presence of God the Father; remember the instructions that this wretched woman gave you” — “Ah! how happy it is to be united with the good God! But you, my dear, if you stay far from this most loving Bridegroom, what can you ever have? Nothing. Go, go and suck the honey of sweetness; he is its essence, so run to his fountain and drink, get drunk!…” (to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: Dec. 5, 1868; Sept. 18, 1869; Jan. 16, 1870; Nov. 14, 1873; to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino: Dec. 3, 1872).

In a special way she recommended attention and faithfulness to God’s inspirations, which requires the spirit of prayer that disposes one to listen to the divine calls. “Woe to the creature who has become deaf to the inspirations that God, in his mercy, gives her” (Letter to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: Dec. 21, 1868).

(from Spiritual Physiognomy, pp. 78-79)

CELEBRATION 12

THE HOPE ANNOUNCED BY THE PROPHETS

Introduction to the celebration

By recalling the “benefits of the Lord,” Israel’s hope opens to every new saving act of God and prepares for new expectations of the revelation of the glory of God, who leaves nothing undone to make Israel his son. The hope experienced in the long wandering of the desert, and the hope announced by the Prophets, animated the life of St. Anne, making her a lover of God, of his justice, of his glory, of the observance of the commandments as harmony and transparency of his Kingdom.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Isaiah 63:7-19

Reflection on the Word

We leave Exodus with this word of Isaiah: “let us remember the benefits of the Lord.” “All that he has done for us.” Everything was written for our instruction. We too are his people… for us too he remains savior… Even if we are still far from his ways, if our heart is hard, if our life remains little illumined by the “stirring of his tenderness,” and perhaps we are those “over whom he never ruled,” nevertheless he will tear open the heavens and come down again!

– What is your impression after the celebrations on Exodus?

– What difference do you notice between the God of the Patriarchs and the God of Israel?

– Do you too want to be treated according to the greatness of his mercy, or do you instead hope more in your merits, in your attempts to be found righteous?

For further reflection: Psalm 2

“Ask of me.” The invitation to hope lies in this divine statement: “You are my son!” You exist because you are wanted, loved, created as a son. Created from nothing through that Word begotten from eternity, you too can therefore “dare” to “ask”! You will have the nations for your inheritance… the ends of the earth for your possession! The powerful of the earth can do nothing: what pharaoh can rise up against God or oppose his work of salvation?

“The one enthroned in heaven laughs.”

After reading Psalm 2, reflect on these Scriptures that announce or recall divine fatherhood: Ps 89:27; Rom 8:29-37; Eph 1:3-5; 2:18; 3:12.14-15, which Christ has won back for us, having defeated all those powers that dominated us: Col 2:15. So do not be afraid!

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“I remained in ecstasy and could not say anything more; and everything is little and nothing that can be said to a God so merciful toward a poor ignorant creature. After a good while I turned to my Father St. Francis, to all the seraphim and cherubim: that they should sing hymns of thanks and thanksgiving for me to my God” (M 1.1, p. 12).

(from The Spiritual Physiognomy of Rosa Gattorno, p. 112)

CELEBRATION 13

ISRAEL’S HOPE, FOUNDED ON GOD’S MERCY

Introduction to the celebration

Israel’s expectation rests on the experience of God’s mercy. As we meditate on and share the message that the biblical texts offer us, let us join in the trust that Mary lived, growing like her in the certainty that the Lord will remember his mercy, just as she herself testified: “He has helped Israel his servant, remembering his mercy” (Luke 1:54).

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

You can find everywhere in the Scriptures the divine mercy that awaits you, so that you may learn to trust and to hope in his nearness and in his help when you call upon him.

Reading: Leviticus 19

You can notice at once the invitation to… holiness, because your God is holy! He is the living one and… he wants, he commands you, to be a living one too! Notice also his delicacy toward all those whom… you often forget: “do not reap flax at the edges of your field, nor gather what is left to glean… you shall leave them for the poor and for the stranger!”

“The poor you will always have with you”—says Jesus—Because always, our selfishness is the cause of all injustices, violence, discrimination, deceit, which lead to hatred and death. We will always have the poor: a consequence of our not wanting to be holy, as God is; that is, delicate and caring and attentive to giving life to… everyone.

We therefore always need to be measured against this “holiness,” in order to hope to “come out” from the dominion of despotic and cruel “pharaohs.”

– Do you want to be holy? That is, able to love as God loves?

– How much are you too a slave to certain injustices that prevent you from living together with your neighbor? For example: dislikes, resentments, grudges, touchiness, avarice…

– God’s attention is always turned to the one who groans, to the weak, to the needy. How distracted, indifferent and superficial are you, by contrast, regarding the needs of your neighbor?

To deepen prayer: Psalm 25

One turns to God often with the experience of the past: no one who has trusted in God’s “holiness” has been disappointed. The enemies are many and battle-hardened. There is a risk of betraying, of yielding to temptation: the poor one is alone and unhappy. “The flesh is weak”… desperate! An appeal is then made to divine faithfulness, to his love. At this moment, past sins also weigh heavily…

But even to sinners God’s “holiness” gives the right way, that of conversion: there is therefore hope. For everyone. The humble and the poor take refuge in him. Even if sin should grow great!… (Remember how in Gethsemane Jesus struggles with… the “great” sin! And Moses had already struggled, bearing the sin of the people). Sin generates turmoil, unease, throws us into anxiety, into fear: “Father, if it is possible!” And here is the plea: turn to me! Ease my anguish! See my misery.

The anguish becomes deadly: the enemies hate with violence. God’s holiness makes you hope: protect me, save me, God! In trial, only hope sheds light!

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“… I was so convinced of my nothingness… that it seemed to me I no longer had the courage to stand in the presence of my God…; the more intimate the union became, the more I discovered my nothingness…”;

“…I was afflicted because I had no one to whom to say a word. A Voice said to me: ‘Why do you say this? Do you not remember what I told you a short time before that dispute reached you from Rome? I am your Teacher, be calm.’ The peace of conscience that I enjoy in the midst of so many tribulations… is such that I see there is a most powerful Spirit who sustains me…” (M 3, p. 21; M 4.1, p. 4)

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 109)

CELEBRATION 14

THOSE WHO HOPE ENTER INTO GOD’S REST

Introduction to the celebration

The anguish of the people in the face of the new difficulties at Kadesh becomes fatal for Israel. The lack of faith and hope in their God, who had filled them with benefits, freed them from slavery and saved them from death, will force them to remain forty years in the desert. And for Moses it will be the reason that kept him from entering the promised land. Only the few who knew how to hope entered the place of God’s rest.

Let us be helped by the witness of those who persevered in trust in God, particularly by Mary, who personifies the perfect fidelity to God of all those who preceded her.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

Israel is near the promised land. God has shown himself faithful. He has freed that people from a terrible slavery, he has fed them in the desert. Now the fruits of that land are there: the scouts must testify: “It is truly a land flowing with milk and honey!” But then they end up “discrediting the land: ‘It is inhabited by strong people.’” And the people protest…

Reading: Numbers 13:25-33; 14:1-24

To discredit is the most insidious temptation: the one that destroys hope.

The original temptation that deceives and kills the divine life in the human being.

Was not the “tree of life” in the middle of the garden, together with every sort of tree pleasing to the eyes and good for food? (Gen 2:9).

If the human being had only persevered in trusting… But then that demonic “discrediting”: “Did God really say: You shall not eat from any of the trees in the garden?” (Gen 3:1).

That seduction so corrupts the human heart that it no longer reminds him of the divine promises. He himself forgets the truth and ends up distorting it: “… of the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden God said: You shall not eat it or even touch it, or else you will die” (Gen 3:3).

Could God, after promising immortality, change his mind and tell the human being that he is destined for death?

Can a promised land, hoped for and longed for, now become unreachable?

Discrediting God becomes the tragedy of the human being, the end of every journey, of every expectation.

“… the people cried aloud… the people wept all that night.”

Certainly it is anguish, despair. The folly of thinking: God is leading us to death. “What will become of our children? Let us choose a leader.” The absurdity: wanting to lead ourselves back to a slavery without end. It is accepting hell!

– How much do you too tend to discredit the divine promises?

– Concretely, do you believe and hope in that eternal life which Jesus has repeatedly announced and offered to us? It is our “promised” land. Or do you fear the difficulties and trials of reaching it?

– What temptations do you suffer from your surroundings that can put your faith in crisis?

– Sincerely, whom do you resemble: Joshua? Or do you despair as soon as there is a problem and “curse” God, that is, put his word in doubt?

To deepen prayer: Psalm 14

“The fool says in his heart: There is no God!” Here is the work of all those who are corrupt, who want to confuse the hope of the wretched, of the poor… All of them go astray and all devour the people of God, when they “discredit” his work. It is God who loves, who seeks what is lost, it is he who bends down from heaven over all the slaveries of this world: does anyone truly welcome him?

– After reflecting on this psalm, reread John 3.

– God so loved the world… and so loves the Son that he has put everything into his hands… Do you still doubt this? Do you still think you hold life in your own hands, so as to guide it as you wish and wherever you wish?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

Although she is in a different historical situation from the conditions of the pilgrim people, Rosa lives a religious experience of similar spiritual content, aimed at orienting her journey in God and that of all those who make up the Family that God has entrusted to her:

“… in the midst of so much tumult from an abyss of business, yet I am never deprived of union with my God; indeed for some time, since he provided me with that dear treasure that I always see at my side, and it is a cloud, something beautiful, a being is seen to be contained, because, as I said above, I already saw him…” (M 1.1, pp. 86-87).

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 114)

CELEBRATION 15

JOSHUA’S HOPE

Introduction to the celebration

Joshua’s hope deserves the wonderful reply of the Lord: “Arise, cross this Jordan… as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. Be strong and steadfast, for it is you who must lead this people back.” From contemplating these deeds of the Lord, the holy Anne and Joachim, as devout Israelites, learned to found their hope on God’s historical experience. Israel had, properly speaking, experience of his love and forgiveness. The Lord was the cause, the soul and the goal of its history. He was the God who had made Israel his own people.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Deut 1:19-46

Reflection on the Word

Only Caleb and Joshua will know the promised land and… take note: precisely those children whom Israel feared would become “plunder of war” (Num 14:31)! It is painful to despise the grace of God… but this seems to become a constant note in the journey of the chosen people! “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 26:14).

Despite the refusals, God will fulfill his promises. That land is a gift for that people. Deuteronomy will confirm: God wants the human being to be happy!

As he revealed himself to the Patriarchs, poor men, so he will continue to reveal himself “eagerly and constantly” to Israel: because he loves it (2 Chr 36:15).

– List in this passage the sins of David

– Do you recognize what God’s will is? Highlight the phrases that make it known to you

– Where would you rest your hope?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“A voice said to me:

— Live only in God and seek nothing else. Converse with him and seek no other comfort than in him. Let everything be enough for you in him…

— Yes, my Good, in you alone!” (M 4.3, p. 15).

(In Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 196)

RETREAT 3

WALKING IN STEP WITH GOD

Introduction to the celebration

Israel’s destiny is to walk in step with God, to reach the goal that God himself indicates. By following the divine footsteps, in fact, the human being learns to walk on new paths, to look toward new dwellings, to sense in his own existence the presence of a new reality, that of the Covenant, which is a communion of life that saves the human being from solitude, from the limits of matter, from the failure of a history that ends in death. The God of Abraham made a numerous posterity “possible” for a sterile old man. The God of Israel created a people out of a formless mass of desperate slaves and had Moses prophesy once again the coming of the Messiah, that Messiah born of a Woman for the definitive salvation of Israel and of humanity.

Lauds

Reading: Deuteronomy 8

Reflection on the Word

The foundation of hope for Israel is God’s love and his free election (Deut 4:37; 7:6-8.13-16; 10:15-22). It can be said that Deuteronomy is an invitation to reflect on all that God has done to create Israel’s happiness. In Deut 8 we see that God walks precisely with Israel, to reassure it of this (3:22; 20:1-12; 31:3-6). God has never withdrawn from the task of taking care of his people (2:7; 6:10-12). If the divine blessing can come down upon an enemy city, how much more those norms of life commanded by God: they become a providence that extends to all: the poor, workers, foreigners, orphans, widows. Israel must remember its… own origins, in order to become mercy for its fellow human beings (24:5-22). So God does not abandon his people, even if they should be scattered (4:1.40; 4:30-31; 5:33; 6:3.18.24; 30:9-16; 32:46-47), because even punishment is corrective, medicinal: always for life (25:2-3).

NB: God chose Israel in order to reveal himself: this theme of election pervades the whole Old Testament. After reading all the citations from Deuteronomy, you can pause to examine the note on Deut 6 and go on, if you wish, with the parallel texts of Jer 2:3 and Amos 3:2.

CELEBRATION 16

THE HOPE OF JOB

Introduction to the celebration

Job founds his hope on God’s faithfulness to his promises. He remains faithful to him in the harsh trial and continues to believe that God will reveal himself to his eyes, and so he will see him as he is in his reality and not as others have described him to him. By hoping, he comes to understand the ever more spiritual contents of his faithfulness, progressively overcoming the limits of the expectation of material goods. The infinite light of God, which guides Job’s conscience to overcome the limits of evil and death, is the same Light that, clothed in flesh in the womb of Mary, conquered the darkness of the world and defeated death by his death and resurrection.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Job 7

Reflection on the Word

Briefly, gleaning from the Pentateuch, you have been able to reflect on this will to save that God shows first with the Patriarchs, then with the whole people. Does it not seem to you that in this… struggle of God with the resistances of the human being, he wants to show us that he is instilling in the heart of humanity the hope of eternal life? Or at least awakening the longing for those “preternatural” gifts which he had already placed in human nature at the dawn of creation and which were then lost through sin? Can you really think that the whole happiness of the human being could be to build houses, to multiply his livestock or to increase his bank account? Can becoming holy because God is holy consist in this one concern: to abound in everything? If generations pass and God keeps working and giving life to new ones, why can the desire not arise that perhaps that length of years promised might become like that of God? Does God not continually declare himself to be the God of Abraham, of Isaac and of Jacob? So Jesus will reveal to the Sadducees, who still did not believe in the resurrection: God is a God of the living: those “departed,” that is, have not disappeared, but live (Luke 20:34-38). So too Paul will admonish the Christians of Corinth: “If for this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are the most pitiable people of all” (1 Cor 15:19).

Israel therefore cannot be content with a God who limits himself to making it happy for a few years: death remains a drama.

Why, then, so many wonders worked in its own history by the living God, if everything is then to be consumed in nothingness?

This anxiety and this question will haunt the “wise men” of Israel. They will give rise to reflection…

For example, the book of Job will ask itself why all the human tragedies that find no answer… The God of Abraham, of Isaac and of Jacob will keep humanity waiting for a “fulfillment” of revelation: “I know that his commandment is eternal life!” (John 12:50).

For personal reflection: Job 3-9.

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“May it always be as pleases my God. He has sent it to me: in everything fully resigned and tranquil, cheerful, as if this donkey carried nothing, which this morning did not want to stand straight at all, I always felt myself failing; but now I am a little better. May my Jesus do what pleases him: always happy to be able to suffer!”

Thinking of the many in the world who have to bear even more painful sufferings, she ends with one of her beautiful outpourings of love: “I would like to be able to absorb all the sufferings of the world, if it would please my sovereign Lord!”

(from Spiritual Physiognomy, pp. 166-167)

CELEBRATION 17

THE HOPE OF THE HUMBLE AND THE POOR

Introduction to the celebration

The Psalmist, identified with the experience of Israel, invites all the faithful to take refuge in the Lord, the salvation of every human being. But since the Lord so often delays in intervening, the humble and the poor turn to him, pleading with confidence that he not forget them, that he raise his hand on behalf of the oppressed. St. Anne teaches us this spirit of hope through spirituality: “Be firmly persuaded that when you are planted in this heavenly hope, you will always live like a little girl (or boy) in the arms of the Heavenly Father, so that you will never lack anything that is truly good for you, no harm will ever touch you, and this will be so even when at some moment it seems to you, and seems to others too, that everything is lost to you” (Rule 1869, ch. II).

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Psalm 9-10

Reflection on the Word

God does not abandon those who seek him. In the preaching of the Prophets too there is this continual appeal: return to the Lord! Why seek him? Why return?

There is only one reason: the Lord is king forever! His greatness becomes hope for the desire of the wretched.

God sits enthroned forever, and for this reason he can see the misery and affliction of the wretched, the work of that deadly enemy who made us fall headlong into death! This is why Israel must not forget!… That “remembering” of the divine interventions sets it on the way to hope: God will do justice, God will save, he will be a refuge for the oppressed and a secure shelter in distress. Only the wicked can deny God, can call his providence into doubt.

– Why, in your opinion, will the hope of the afflicted not be disappointed?

– What can the afflicted desire?

– Why does Jesus declare them blessed?

– What have been the situations of affliction in your life?

– In those situations, sincerely, did you hope in God?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

In the symbol of the right hand, infinitely transcending the symbol itself, which nevertheless announces his presence, the Father shows his Omnipotence to Rosa:

“… I remained in the presence of the Eternal Father; he stretched out his right hand to me; it was so resplendent that I cannot express it…” (M 1.1, p. 58).

CELEBRATION 18

GOD’S ABSENCE AND PRESENCE IN HUMAN LIFE

Introduction to the celebration

With the reflection on the book of Ecclesiastes we penetrate into the silence of God, into his pedagogy which, although it aims at the fullness of time in which a Woman will give birth to the One who will be the definitive explanation of everything that “happens under the sun,” works slowly and progressively. This way of acting generates distrust in those who do not know how to persevere in waiting. Not so the vision of the Book of Proverbs, in which God is contemplated as always present in the history and in the life of the human being who hopes in him, Creator and Providence.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

Before leaving the Pentateuch and continuing to advance along the historical path of salvation, it is perhaps still fitting to meditate, even if briefly, on two wisdom books. They should help us realize once again that true happiness for Israel could not be the mere material possession of a land, even one “flowing with milk and honey.” Let us take Ecclesiastes: the human being and all his activity have an undercurrent of pessimism and futility.

Pessimism about man (7:20), about woman (7:26), about society (8:9-11 and 9:3). Pleasure is vain (2:1), of what use is laughter? (2:2).

Progress… useless (4:4). Iniquity and injustice cause bitterness (3:16).

Even riches… a chasing after the wind (2:11)! Oppressions are constant (4:1-2).

There is no lasting remembrance: everything is forgotten (2:16). Wisdom itself becomes a painful occupation (1:13.18). Everything, in short, seems to sink into a desolate bitterness. If all things are wearisome (1:8), nothing is new under the sun (1:9) and everything seems to be “vanity.” Why would God have revealed himself as the God of the living? To give what in the end does not make the human being happy? Does that not seem absurd?

In the book of Proverbs, on the other hand… there seems to be a future: the just desire what is good (11:23), their root will not be moved, their house stands firm: they bear fruit, they do not sin; no harm will befall the just. They will be guides. The situation of the wicked is different: they do not stand firm, they deceive, they are merciless, full of evils; once overthrown they are no more… (12:3.5-7.10.12-13.21.26). If the heart of the proud is an abomination to the Lord and deserves punishment, surely the just will not receive death as the reward for his search for what is good.

Reading: Proverbs 1

If the human project is truly happiness, the answer can come only from the Lord… when the just, precisely, entrusts to him all his activity (Prov 16:1-5).

The human being cannot want a journey with a tragic ending. Is everything vanity? If his history has a future, it is God who directs its steps, and it is precisely the path of salvation that God reveals to the human being, so that in it he may transcend himself and in it remain firm (Prov 16:9 and 19:21).

The human being can understand his own destiny when he enters into the one that God reveals to him. This hope lifts up from every tragedy, from every fall, the one who possesses this kind of wisdom. The just one, therefore, knows how to trust in God. The wicked cannot have a future. Truly his hope perishes with misfortune: death (Prov 11:7 and 24:14-20).

– Are your plans oriented toward eternal life?

– Do you care, in all your actions, to please God, by keeping his commandments, directing your life along the ways he has revealed? (cf. 2 Cor 5:9-10)

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“Courage, my daughter! Why disturb yourself so?

Listen: in consolations there must also be some bitterness; otherwise I would fear that it was not the work of God.” (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni)

(In Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 160)

CELEBRATION 19

HOPE FOUNDED ON THE FAITH OF THE FATHERS

Introduction to the celebration

The religious message of the book of Joshua is steeped in the hope founded on the fathers’ faith in God and in his interventions. The memory of the past nourished their hope in a future that would reveal the same God of the Covenant. And God really answers, going before them in the conquest of the promised land. After crossing the Jordan, they celebrate the first Passover in Palestine and renew the Covenant, a figure of the definitive one that will be fulfilled by Jesus, Son of God and of Mary, Priest and Victim of Love for humanity.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Joshua 6:1-20

Reflection on the Word

The sixth book of the Bible tells the story of the conquest of the promised land.

One by one the peoples who lived in Palestine will be subdued by Israel. Joshua will be the man chosen by God, after Moses, to accomplish this plan: to lead into freedom a people lying in despair. The promise made to the Fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, is fulfilled. No rebellion, not even unbelief, will prevent God from showing this saving will of his. Those enemy powers that had frightened Israel and had forced it to doubt the power of God are now defeated. Indeed, those peoples who were supposed to destroy the children of Israel (Num 14:1-4) now flee in fear at the mere sound of Israel’s approach (Josh 2:9; 5:1; 10:1-2). God, who promised that land, will fight for Joshua, the faithful disciple of Moses who, together with Caleb, had listened to the voice of the Lord and is now a spectator of that gift handed over to the new generation of Israel (Josh 5:6-7). God will glorify Joshua (Josh 3:7; 4:14), as he had already glorified Moses (Exod 33:18-19; 4:5; 33:11; 34:29), because, like the fathers, these two leaders of Israel too trusted and opened their hearts to hope, awaiting from God what it was impossible for them not only to “ask” but even to “imagine” (Eph 3:20-21).

They will be brought into that land fighting, but they must not fear (Josh 1:5-6.9; 8:1; 10:8; 11:6): God chose Abraham from beyond the river, he multiplied his descendants in order to give him a land that Israel had not known (Josh 24:2-18) and that it now sees with its own eyes.

– Jericho is “tightly shut up” against the Israelites. What allowed them to see the walls of the city fall?

– How do you understand this phrase: “you shall pass over armed before your brothers and help them until the Lord grants rest to your brothers”? (Josh 1:14-15)

– Compare the armor that Paul describes to the Ephesians: 6:10-20 and the real battle that we too must fight. Compare Josh 3:5 and 5:6-7: how can God work wonders with you too?

– For you, what is the most important attitude, capable of “sanctifying” you?

– What teaching do you read in those “forty years in the desert” of the “old” Israel?

– What meaning does what is written in Josh 5:12 have for you?

– At this point in your life, can you sincerely say with Joshua what he says in 23:14?

“If nothing has been able until now to halt my steps for your good and for the greater glory of God, I assure you that, until the last breath of my life, I will always be the same and will not fail to come to your aid in any need of yours.”
