(in Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 279)

CELEBRATION 20

GOD’S COMPASSION OVERCOMES ISRAEL’S SIN

Introduction to the celebration

Israel goes through the experience of sin, of punishment, of repentance, until the Lord is moved to compassion. Once again he raises up a Savior, a Liberator, a Judge and a few unarmed men to show the “Power of his arm” in the victory over the Midianites. Jesus will later insist on the strength of the prayer of supplication, on this expression of trusting expectation of an answer from God: “Seek and you will find, knock and the door will be opened to you…” in order to arouse hope and trust in him in the heart of all human beings.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Judges 7

Reflection on the Word

ISRAEL FORGETS THAT IT IS CALLED TO LIFE (Judges)

“After the death of Joshua, the Israelites consulted the Lord” (Judg 1:1). So begins the book of Judges. It is important to consult the Lord, and more important still is the awareness that the… battle continues: “Who among us will go up first to fight?” The enemies are strong, and we know how much Israel feared them, so much that it preferred to return to slavery in Egypt rather than face them with God’s help. But this is the truth: that land is a figure, a sign, an anticipation of a reality that it is not within the human being’s power to give himself: the divine nature, eternal life, endless happiness lived in communion with the very source of being, with “He Who Is,” the infinite and immensely rich Being, with the One who is fullness without beginning and without end, is impossible for the human being! The human being, called to so much, risks bewilderment. How is it possible? The gift sets before us an end that cannot be compared to the limited life, full of uncertainties and hardships, that we are in some way forced to live: “Is not man’s life on earth a drudgery? Are not his days those of a hireling?” So Job laments (7:1; cf. also Rom 8:18). How is it possible, then, that there be so much glory, so much life, such abundant happiness? Why? What can the human being have done to deserve such a “land”? Accustomed to so much misery and such long groaning, how could Israel think it possible to have a land all for itself: free and rich, to be received almost without effort, there, already prepared, to make it happy? How is it possible?… But how was it possible that a sterile old man became the father of multitudes? And that a Virgin conceived and gave birth to God himself? In short, how is it possible that God draws so near to the human being as to become one with him? Why?…

All this was possible because God willed it and brought it about. Hope, therefore, does not disappoint if it dares to lift its eyes to such events.

Inconceivable for the human being.

In this episode too God glorifies his servant: Gideon will be the chosen instrument to save Israel. How is it possible that three hundred men without weapons could rout a people “as numerous as locusts,” with “camels” and “herds” beyond number, who for seven years had reduced Israel to hunger? (cf. Judg 6:1-6) The human being must learn to understand that God is not a man and that his paths are not those of the Most High!

– Do you think it is necessary to learn to “consult” the Lord?

– What does this mean concretely for you?

– What do you mean by “going out to fight”?

– Do you see any analogy between the episode of the fall of Jericho and that of the victory over Midian?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“I received a most beautiful lesson on how I must love my neighbor, and this concerns my children too. How I must conduct myself and the perfect equality with which I must treat all creatures and love them all in him and for him. To give to creatures what was given to me, in order to save them and lead them to love and serve him. Oh! incomprehensible Love of mine, what I felt!” (M 1.1, p. 108f).

(In Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 37)

RETREAT 4

THE OBJECT OF HOPE: TO POSSESS THE PROMISE

Introduction to the celebration

God projects the history of the human being beyond history, into a happiness that finds its fulfillment in the possession and enjoyment of God himself. The object of hope is precisely to possess this very promise of God. Since God enters into our world and our history, it is therefore possible for the human being to hope for the impossible. The God of the Remnant of Israel stopped the “curse” that weighed on all humanity, by giving the Immaculate Conception of Mary in the womb of St. Anne and by accomplishing the Incarnation of the Word through the divine motherhood of Mary. God worked the wonder because his faithfulness to the Promise met Mary’s decision to lose her own life in order to find it again in him.

Lauds

Introduction to the Word

We have seen how God “glorifies” his chosen ones: Moses, Joshua, Gideon… That is, he shows his saving power in the weakness of his creatures, who freely make themselves instruments of his will, when they are addressed by him and informed of a particular plan of mercy that will involve all humanity. Do you remember Abraham? “Go forth from your land… in you shall all the families of the earth find blessing” (Gen 12:1-3). And Moses? “Now go, I am sending you… Bring my people out of Egypt” (Exod 3:7-10). So it will continue with Joshua: “Come now, cross this Jordan… No one will be able to withstand you” (Josh 1:1-9). For similar saving purposes Gideon will be chosen: “Valiant and mighty man… go with this strength of yours and save Israel” (Judg 6:12-16). But we must not forget that from the beginning the human being had been called to make himself available so that the glory of the Almighty might appear in him: “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness, and let him have dominion…” He too, like Abraham, received the blessing: “Be fruitful and multiply… have dominion.” Like Israel, he was placed in a land of delights: “He put him in the garden of Eden, to cultivate and care for it” (Gen 1:26-28; 2:15). Sin, then, is wanting to prevent God from showing his life. How many times atheistic humanism has tragically exalted the toil, pain and death of the human being as a challenge to the benevolence and the “abundant” life offered by God!

Reading: John 12:20-36

Reflection on the Word

Jesus too, indeed above all he, awaits the hour of being “glorified,” in order to “draw” everyone to himself!

For this he came, to manifest the glory that the Father will give him. And the Father now must glorify that “name,” chosen by him from the beginning, from the conception: the name of Jesus, that is: “God-saves.” And with this announcement, with the gift of this “name,” the Father chose Mary. Was this creature available to make manifest, in her life, the… “God-saves”? The whole work of salvation finally brought to completion for all humanity? Mary “hated” her life as a woman in this world and… welcomed the gift of that son. That voice from heaven now confirms: “Many times I have manifested my glory, making Abraham fruitful, bringing my son Israel out of Egypt, bringing him back to his land from exile… but once again I will now lift him up from the humiliation of a meek lamb who bears upon himself the sin and death of the world.” For this, in fact, Jesus came, and he understands the fulfillment of this mission when the Greeks want to see him! The “pagans” knock at the door of his heart; human beings need light, truth, life. Here the hour has come! “Lamb of God, who take away our sins, who raise us from our falls, who destroy our deaths, who sow hope in our hearts, have mercy indeed! For this, in fact, the Father chose you, for this he will glorify you: for having announced to us and given us what is his commandment from the beginning: ETERNAL LIFE!” (John 12:49-50).

Compare the priestly prayer of Jesus: John 17 with Exod 2:23-25 and 3:7-9:

– What are our oppressions that God is concerned about?

– Do you understand that there is an evil into which God has truly come down in order to destroy it?

– What is it, then, today, thanks to Jesus, that “good and spacious land” promised to us long ago?

– Does it not seem to you that Jesus himself reveals here that “surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe” (Eph 1:19-20)?

– Observe in what way we are precious to the Father, to the Son, to the Holy Spirit himself (John 17:26). How the human being appears, from the revelation of this prayer of Jesus, an unheard-of receptacle of divine delight, already foreshadowed, moreover, in the Annunciation, with the divine motherhood of Mary!

– Can you then come to understand why Jesus desires to be glorified? How out of love he took upon himself and shared the death of sinful humanity and from that abyss of prostration implored divine mercy, so that there might finally appear, in all its splendor, what “fullness of joy” was granted to us by that divine event which is the Resurrection of Jesus?

CELEBRATION 21

GOD FIRST

Introduction to the celebration

Earthly goods often lead us away from heavenly goods. The story of Samson and Delilah shows how true this statement is. Knowing our frailty, Jesus says that no one can become his disciple unless he is ready to renounce all his earthly possessions. Only Mary, his Mother, was able to overcome in a perfect way the temptation to put creatures, or even his adversary, before the Lord.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the reading

If Jesus is the “leader and perfecter of faith” (Heb 12:2), all the more will he perfect hope in us. In that struggle of his against death and against the “evil one,” which he took upon himself alone for all of us, lies the secret of our being able to live without the deadly anguish of a future without meaning. We can truly go on trusting and hoping even in the face of the evidence of death, as Jesus precisely wants from his disciples (cf., for example, Mark 5:35-36). The sacrifice of Jesus therefore enlightens all human beings, even those who before him trusted in that divine promise: to continue to glorify Israel.

Who else could have moved Samson to that invocation and given him the certainty of victory over his enemies, after, as one chosen, he had known the humiliation of sin?

Reading: Judges 16:22-31

Reflection on the Word

Samson had revealed the secret of his strength to Delilah, who “pestered him every day” and he “was bored to death” (16:16). His “strength left him” (16:19). In this episode we must not think of the woman as the cause of sin. Jesus held women in too high esteem, and the Church has always taught the equal dignity of man and woman in the vocation to holiness. Rather, sin is “crouching” at the door of our heart (Gen 4:7) and we are all seduced by our own desire (Jas 1:14). For from our heart come all kinds of evil (Mark 7:21-23). So it was Samson who yielded to temptation. The sensible, the immediate, the pleasant, in the end seduced him. He betrayed grace, he forgot the gift of God. He did not know how to watch, to fight, to wait. He did not keep the “strength of God.” He… rested in his own way. Weakened, he ended up in the hands of his enemies.

Earthly goods lead us away from heavenly goods. For this Jesus will say that no one can become his disciple unless he is ready to renounce all his possessions (Luke 14:33). It is the sin of all times: that fruit near me is seductive, beautiful to look at, tasty, to gain an earthly wisdom that destroys hope (Gen 3:6). But in humiliation, in blindness, there arises in the human being that cry that makes hope grow again! It was sown in the heart of Adam: do you remember? It is what made Abraham walk; what made Israel wait. It is a cry that no seduction can extinguish in the human heart.

Jesus, for this reason, can take on the sin of the world: error, pain, death. The Father will glorify that Son who will abandon himself totally to him. That cry on the cross of the dying Jesus is the cry of all suffering humanity that awaits liberation. Samson will utter that cry: “Lord, remember me!” And hope takes vengeance on all oppressions, on all enemies, on every weariness, on every false rest; it trusts in that “strength” which can be given back!

– Compare the sin of Adam (Gen 3) and that of Samson. What “strength” had been given to Adam?

– List the consequences of sin.

– What is the “nakedness” of Adam? And of Samson?

– By what, in your opinion, is that prayer of Samson dictated?

– Have there been, or are there, moments in your life when, although humiliated, you went on hoping in God?

Personal research:

Eve, in the biblical account of creation, is probably a figure of our sensible nature: she was not in fact visited by any “word” (= strength) of God. God had spoken to Adam. Different is the “woman” who welcomes, when addressed by God, his “word.” Mary, as we have seen, is made fruitful by the “power” of God. Then Eve is “taken” from Adam, from his nature. She is intimate with the man, his bone, his flesh.

The “woman,” on the other hand, is created by God and brings forth life. Eve is deceived because she does not know the depths and riches of the “word” and loses herself in what is the interest of her attention: the sensible. This “weakness” and “narrowness” of horizons of hers will overstimulate and distract Adam, who… will yield. Eve will become for him a source of anxieties and a constant generator of passions, of desires, of… “deadly boredoms.” Compare what Jesus precisely says: Luke 12:22-32.

Different is the “woman” companion of the man, of whom Mary is a figure and therefore the Church: she who accompanies the man, comforts him, urges him to rise again, to hope; who has the power of intercession with God (compare what the Church proclaims of Mary in the “litanies” and in the third part of the “Hail Mary”). Who, above all through the gifts entrusted to her by Christ, has the other “power” of bringing forth children of God through “preaching” and the “sacraments.”

Try to gather how many times Paul, in his letters, alludes to… such an Eve, calling her “flesh.” That is, that sensible part of the human being: weak and disordered, which does not let itself be guided by the Word and the Spirit and which… could not even do so!

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“Your love, my Good, surpasses everything and is the support, the relief, the security of acting. It is the anchor that lies fast at the bottom of the sorrowful sea of our tribulations. Most lovable God, when in the midst of such sad suffering you leave us anchored to your love, it is enough to say to the sufferings: You are sweet, O my beloved! And the fear of having displeased you is followed by trust in your forgiveness, the assurance of soon having clarifications in the rest of our actions and, finally, the beatitude of your perfect union, which, by means of love, is always tasted, though in greater or lesser intimacy” (M 4.2, p. 89).

(In Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 139)

CELEBRATION 22

THE HOPE OF REBIRTH COMES FROM GOD

Introduction to the celebration

The hope of being reborn to life comes only from God. He raises up capable leaders, so that Israel may learn to fight in order to gain its identity as a people. The Lord will go before it in battle, but it must not remain idle. The fear of God will be its true strength in every relationship. Mary, the Mother of Jesus, recalls this merciful protection of God in her Magnificat: “His mercy is from age to age to those who fear him.”

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

Before leaving the book of Judges, it will be good to pause a little to help us reflect on this difficult but necessary journey of Israel, and to understand its difficulties and the maturing of its faith; to see also its resistances, so as to discern the ways of “grace”: above all that “compassion” of God which is the protagonist in the human being’s growth toward the knowledge of the whole truth. God’s “letting himself be moved” (Judg 2:18) by our groans is in fact the source of our rebirth. “From above,” in fact, we must be born, in order to see God (John 3:3). So Jesus will say to Nicodemus. The hope of being reborn to life comes only from God: “from above.” For God is not a man and his ways are not our ways. Only he has that “tender compassion” capable of accomplishing the impossible: to “regenerate” the dead (cf. Luke 1:78 in the note)!

Reading: Judges 3:1-6

Reflection on the Word

We see, then, a first divine mercy: the nations are spared in order to test Israel. That is, God does not destroy our enemies. Why? So that the new generations may learn war. That is, so that you may learn to fight. The enemies are there, God will fight for you, but you must not remain defenseless. You are free: you need to discover the mystery of iniquity; that this world is not the final one; that death, against which you fight and must fight, is not the work of God, nor a natural fact or, worse, a matter of chance!… Have you seen the episode of Samson?

According to Judg 2:10-19, the enemy nations of Israel have the task of punishing Israel’s unfaithfulness. Often you too do not accept the divine teachings. You neglect the “knowledge of God,” you let yourself go to “itching for novelty,” which is at bottom the search for pleasure, the taste for possessing, the surrender to idleness and to every form of excessive comfort. All this makes you a victim of the “material,” it hinders your journey of freedom. It leaves you in discontent, in turmoil, in boredom, in a deadly malaise. These “enemies” truly lead the human being to death. And yet… divine mercy: it raises up leaders capable of freeing us from these snares. Of shedding light on the perverse strategies of certain enemies. But you still… although tried, although you have experienced the hardness of sin and have received signs of kindness, announcements of forgiveness, invitations to conversion, you persist in your stubbornness. You resist grace. By your ingratitude you despise the gift of this divine “womb” that could welcome you and make you… “living.” It seems impossible: but as soon as the leaders disappear, Israel goes back to corruption. How many times have you too seriously considered the reality of this history?

In Exod 23:29 and Deut 7:22, divine pedagogy lets the enemy nations remain: they render a service to Israel: they destroy the wild beasts and keep the land from becoming a desert. Many of our own “passions” or not-good “desires” can also have a benevolent function in the spiritual journey: if destroyed at once, perhaps, they would keep the soul from knowing itself, from “fighting,” from acquiring the virtuous habit. See: Jesus too, in that parable of the weeds (Matt 13:24-30), commands us not to uproot the bad plant right away. It too has a task…

But the book of Wisdom (12:3-22) wants to read a greater mercy in that biblical episode of leaving the enemy nations without hurrying to drive them out. Even if the human being commits “abhorrent crimes” and “unholy rites,” God does not strike him “instantly with an inexorable order,” but always leaves “room for repentance,” because he “judges with clemency” and “governs with great leniency.” God was teaching Israel to love human beings! This will finally be the commandment of Jesus. “…I have other sheep that do not belong to this fold. These also I must lead” (John 10:16).

Paul will reveal: “Jesus is our peace, who made the two one, … breaking down the enmity” (Eph 2:14-16). As God was patient with the Canaanites and with the resistance of his own people, so Jesus, the good Shepherd, will lead into the fold of reconciliation Jews and Gentiles, disciples and pagans. Through the Cross he will destroy the hatred that makes human beings enemies and will proclaim forgiveness.

– Can you understand why Jesus commands his own to go out like “sheep in the midst of wolves”? (Matt 10:16).

– …And that “extraordinary” thing which he wants from his own: love for enemies? (Matt 5:43-48).

– …And why does he demand “mercy”? (Luke 6:35-38).

– Were you not also at one time (or perhaps still are) “rebellious,” an enemy of God, without mercy and always ready for judgment and condemnation? (cf. Eph 2:1-7).

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

God’s will, God’s pleasure, God’s good pleasure, God’s approval, are synonyms that also stand at the center of her pedagogy with the sisters:

“If you only knew what consolation I feel just in pronouncing this word — God’s pleasure — and even more, if the sweet thought of being, or of being able to become, pleasing to him comes alive in me! I feel completely beside myself, so that if I had to face the cruelest martyrdom, I would feel nothing…”

(Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 203)

CELEBRATION 23

GOD’S UNEARNED LOVE FOR HUMANITY

Introduction to the celebration

Israel’s unfaithfulness, if on the one hand it is a call to vigilance, on the other makes the Lord’s unearned generosity toward humanity stand out all the more. His displeasure is changed into mercy that returns to love by forgiving. He waits, in his turn, for the faithful response of a “small remnant” in order to fulfill the promise made to our first parents (Gen 3:15). Israel will wait until the fullness of time: when the Immaculate Conception of Mary will be accomplished in the womb of St. Anne, an event that introduces the Incarnation of the Word, the greatest wonder of his love for us.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: 1 Cor 10:1-13; Rom 2:1-11

It is a refrain, in the book of Judges that we are leaving: “the Israelites cried out to the Lord,” because they were oppressed by stronger enemies. And then… punctually, the divine intervention: “The Lord raised up a deliverer for them.” But again: “The Israelites again did what was evil.” The usual forgetfulness appears… Israel seems not to learn to walk behind its God. Ingratitude, unfaithfulness to its duties, the search for selfish securities, not listening to the word of its God, inevitably lead it into the hands of its enemies. This seems to be its destiny. Remember: how much effort it took to free it from Egypt? And then to lead it through that desert? And again: to bring it into what was, after all, its own land? So the history goes on… In the book of Kings a refrain similar to this one in Judges will make an impression: “He did what was evil in the eyes of the Lord.” With this lapidary verdict more than thirty kings will be addressed. We might be led to despise Israel. To be unable to bear such behavior. Perhaps we might grow tired of reflecting on such… deeds! To what purpose? Tedious and to no avail. Other stories might prove more interesting… Were these really written for our instruction?

For personal reflection: Judges 3:9.12.15; 4:1.3; 6:1.6.8; 8:33; 10:6.10.16; 13:1

– What impressions do you draw?

– In what can this attitude of Israel instruct you?

– Why does God give it to you today?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

With her there conversed the One who in the history of salvation appears as a reality both near and transcendent, the one divinity, who lets himself be glimpsed as the Triune God in the Old Testament: “the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters” (Gen 1:2); “See, I am sending an angel before you” (Exod 23:20); “so shall my word be that goes forth from my mouth” (Isa 55:11); and who reveals himself as such, in the fullness of time, in the Son and through the Son.

This same God was pleased to show Rosa his infinite love for the human being and his action aimed at saving him. His initiative gives her an inexhaustible dynamism that involves her totally:

“Great Mystery. Oh! if only I could obtain that you be made known to the whole world. You (if one may say so) are mad for the human being and he? Alas! A Voice says to me: Yes, I love him dearly, but I am not loved in return. In saying this to me, he came so near that I felt myself carried away. Oh! Sanctifying Spirit, Divine Essence, always ready to pour yourself into the ungrateful hearts of human beings, how precious a nectar breathes from a single drop that a human being might come to taste. Oh! incomparable sweetness. Oh! whoever comes to taste and possess this divine essence is surely one for whom all that is earthly serves only to nauseate; with the intellect opened by divine power, he communicates with his immortal being and, in this infinite sea of infinite greatness, he understands everything, delights and rejoices in love. Oh! how infinite you are in your power, sovereign, absolute, and then Father and beloved Bridegroom of hearts. Oh! fortress of loving souls and of whoever lives in you and for you” (M 1.2, p. 1ff).

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, pp. 34-35)

CELEBRATION 24

THE LORD IS THE ANSWER TO THE HOPE OF THE LITTLE ONES

Introduction to the celebration

The message of the book of Ruth introduces us into the universal plan of God’s Love. Salvation is not destined only for Israel, but for all peoples. The Lord is the answer to the hope of the weak and of those who trust in him. He chooses what is nothing in the eyes of this world to make it an instrument of his faithfulness to the promises. The “Offspring” of the “Woman” announced in Gen 3:15, who will defeat divisions, hatred and racial discrimination, has in her genealogy the marriage between a Hebrew man and a Moabite woman, a scandal for Hebrew nationalists, a sign of God’s infinite Love, who guides history toward the unity of peoples through the faithfulness of the humble and the poor.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the catechesis on Ruth

Before passing on to the books of Samuel and of Kings, the Scriptures give us this little book of Ruth. This woman, a foreigner besides, obliges us to a brief pause. Above all to serious reflection: a widow, she will follow her Hebrew mother-in-law, telling her: “Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.”

What did Ruth see in that people?

What do we not see?

Why is she attracted to that God whom she does not know?

And do we know the God of Abraham, of Isaac, of Jacob? Perhaps, as Paul warned us, we too quickly judge harshly or superficially, without understanding the patience and the richness of God’s goodness; or we believe ourselves secure in everything and confident in our own strength, without thinking what it means to be “overtaken by temptation.”

Catechesis on the book of Ruth

Ruth does not have a… brilliant story. She is a young Moabite woman who married a Hebrew emigrant. After ten years of marriage she is left a widow. She could “make a new life for herself”… Her own mother-in-law thanks her for the good she did to her son and blesses her: “May the Lord grant that you find a settled home in the house of a husband” (1:9). But Ruth is concerned about her mother-in-law’s fate and refuses to abandon her to the adventure of a solitary return to her homeland; the mother-in-law’s resistance is of no avail: “No, my daughter, I am too badly off to be of any help to you, because the hand of the Lord is stretched out against me” (1:13).

But Ruth is determined: she will accept a voluntary exile. She will go to the land of Israel, setting aside—for reasons of charity—“her father’s house and her people” (cf. Ps 45:11), thus truly becoming a “neighbor” (cf. Luke 10:36) to her mother-in-law: “Wherever you go I will go, wherever you lodge I will lodge; your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (1:16).

Ruth thus has before her a hard pilgrimage… a desert of solitude, of detachment, of sterility…

She hands herself over to an unhappy and embittered old woman: “Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the Lord do so to me, and more, if anything but death separates me from you!” (1:17).

And she will also be patient in the trials that await her in Israel. To live she will accept humble and tiring work, and not without… dangers: “Let me go to the fields and glean ears of grain after someone in whose sight I may find favor” (2:2). It has always been rare to find disinterested kindness! Let us contemplate this ancestress of the Messiah: … she will gather behind the reapers, in hard labor from morning till evening, with the only right… of the poor: to have something to eat, if the good heart of the owner of the field allows it!…

But “the foreigner” will find favor!

Her astonishment at the attention Boaz pays her lets us understand the gentle simplicity of the young woman… concerned only with the mission she has chosen (2:10.13).

She would have slowly worn herself out in obscurity until the death of the one she loved… But God “looks at the heart, not at appearances,” just as he will do with her great-grandson (1 Sam 16:7), and for that voluntary hiddenness, accepted solely out of love for a poor woman without protection, God—who “has not withdrawn his kindness from the living or the dead” (2:20)—will exalt her! He who “raises the lowly from the dust and lifts the poor from the ash heap to seat them with princes… gives the childless wife a home, as the joyful mother of children” (Ps 113:7).

Through this free divine election (cf. Rom 9) Ruth, a foreigner, will enter the predestined, blessed genealogy of the Messiah!

How wonderful God is in all his ways!

Who teaches Ruth in the depths of her heart, so that she is not scandalized by the God of Naomi, who seems to embitter the life of this faithful woman of his with such hard trials?

Ruth has no hesitation in worshiping the God of Naomi; what ever attracts her to this God?

What mysterious instinct reveals to her that precisely in that “throwing away her life” she can find the reason for her own living? (Luke 9:23-26).

Only God can have prepared this woman’s heart. No insistence turns her from her purpose. The other daughter-in-law, generous too, will in the end remain in Moab… Prudently, she will prefer a new plan of life… certainly not a bad one!

Here we see an application of that word of the Lord: “Two women will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and the other left” (Matt 24:41)… Ruth is chosen for a mission: guided by a secret inspiration, she will show what possibilities of loving the human heart has when, docile, it lets itself be led along a… truly “narrow” road, but one that leads to life! (cf. Matt 7:13-14).

“They shall all be taught by God,” and “everyone who has learned from him comes to me” (John 6:45), Jesus will say. Ruth did not see the Father, but she must have sensed, deep within herself, his attraction, in order to accept what humanly cannot attract… the “last place”! (cf. Luke 14:10). Naomi was truly “poor,” but Ruth will serve her, trusting in another reward (Luke 14:12-14). For it is written: “Whoever comes to me will never hunger, and whoever comes to me I will not reject, because I came down from heaven to do the will of the one who sent me” (John 6:35-38).

Ruth was not a daughter of Abraham, and yet she enters into the “promise” made to Abraham. Moreover: Ishmael was a son of Abraham but was excluded from the promise. God chooses whom he wills! And John the Baptist will be so peremptory as to seem almost mocking toward Jewish “religious” racism: “Sons of Abraham? I tell you, God can raise up sons of Abraham from these stones!” Rather: to be chosen is one thing and to respond is another: there must be cooperation between human freedom and divine freedom: Ruth responds, Ruth does not refuse the divine attraction.

Personal reading of the catechesis on Bathsheba (Appendix no. 1)

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“O my Love! use once more this wretched instrument of yours to revive the faith and the conversion of sinners!” — “All souls, come! Ah! love Jesus, do not offend him!… I would have run through all the streets crying out that they should love Jesus. I threw myself face down on the ground and asked the eternal Father with all my strength to let me die a martyr to save the souls he redeemed. Am I not your instrument?” (Year 1867: M 1.1, pp. 60, 119).

(in Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 257)

CELEBRATION 25

THE HOPE OF THE WOMEN OF THE BIBLE

Introduction to the celebration

We can consider Ruth a figure of other women of the Bible, who were a delight to God because of their virtue, which made them trust in him and hope against hope in the trials of life. The tradition of the Church has handed down to us an image of Anne, mother of Mary Immaculate, who stands in the line of the humble and gentle women of the Bible, who cooperated in the saving plan by their faithful life, open to the Promises of God and above all completely abandoned to his divine will.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

Important and… providential, this pause. Above all the remembrance of this “foreigner” welcomed as an ancestress of King David, now that we are about to enter the history of the kings… Before we begin to get to know a series of men and events that will not please the heart of God, Ruth is given to us! Why?

Another light from God to instruct us.

A woman who is determined to… walk, first of all. She has bound her life to her mission. If her mission is to serve the least… she is less than they! So she considers herself. Nothing, therefore, disturbs her. She is concretely aware of being less than a slave (Ruth 2:13). She spares no effort and certainly does nothing to win favors. She does not go hunting for human “glory” and… only to please her mother-in-law will she give herself to the elderly Boaz. Her patient and loving care for old Naomi will allow her to cooperate in the history that God is mysteriously weaving with her. It is only fidelity in keeping that last place that will not allow her to be discouraged!

And God exalts her!

Reading: 1 Cor 1:26-31

– Sincerely, what do you boast about?

– What in your life do you really consider important?

– What mission have you chosen for yourself?

– Do you believe that God is pleased with what you do? Or rather: do you care about being pleasing to God?

– Ruth was faithful to that last place, obscure and without glory… Do you really agree with Paul that God often chooses, for his works, incredibly weak and poor instruments?

– Do you want to be chosen by God?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

From the description that Rosa left of the presence of St. Anne in her life, the values that she develops by living in communion with her shine through:

“The calumnies were terrible (in reference to these), Mother St. Anne consoled me, saying to me: ‘My daughter, who has been more calumniated than I? While I had to carry the most precious fruit of the Eternal Father, and this gave me strength and patience to bear everything’” (M 1.1, p. 126).

This confidence is enough for Rosa to learn to bear everything, loving and forgiving, after the example of the Holy Mother. Jesus himself, in infused contemplation, lets her know some aspects of the life of St. Anne:

“…I stayed there listening to what my Good was teaching me, and it was about St. Anne and what I had to say. So sublime was his speaking that, on coming back to myself, I did not understand many things and could not grasp their meaning. Ah! my All-Beloved did not delay in teaching me… to open my mind to knowledge and to the capacity to discern. Then I went over everything I had heard, word by word, and I saw very well what he wanted me to do…” (M 4.1, p. 82f).

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, pp. 154-155)

CELEBRATION 26

POVERTY AND PRAYER OBTAIN GOD’S ANSWER

Introduction to the celebration

The sorrowful accents of Hannah, wife of Elkanah, reveal the drama of her sterility. In her case too, as it was for Sarah, Rebekah and Rachel, the Bible highlights the providential intervention of God, who makes them fruitful. This is so that it may be well understood that the continuity of the history of salvation is given by the acknowledgment of the extreme limit of human smallness, transformed into a prayer full of hope, which obtains God’s surprising answer. It is God’s pedagogy, which reaches its peak when, breaking into history, he accomplishes with the Virgin Mary an event that has no precedent and that will not be repeated in the future.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

It is again providential that the historical books that follow Ruth open with a female figure: Hannah. She is not a widow like Ruth; on the contrary, she is much loved by her husband. But, like Ruth, she is tried by a humiliating story.

Hannah is sterile. But she presents herself to the Lord and raises her prayer to him. Weeping bitterly, she shows God this misery of hers. Just as Samson, from the depths of his blindness and his chains, will raise a cry to God: “Remember me, give me strength!”, so Hannah, in the excess of her sorrow and bitterness, pours out her heart before the Lord: “Lord of hosts, remember me, do not forget your handmaid.” The Lord will visit her (1 Sam 2:21).

Reading: 1 Samuel 1

Reflection on the Word

God visits the poor, he lifts up the humble. If only Israel would understand. If only all of us would reflect. Yet these two women, Ruth and Hannah, are placed here, perhaps, to give meaning to all the history that will follow. Our humanity is sterile: it does not possess life. It is a foreigner or a pilgrim, because it still has no homeland, it does not know the face of God. These bitter realities should lead us before God and make us ask that he visit us, make us fruitful, make us his own. We should plead with the saints, like Ruth: “May your God be ours!” and let ourselves be guided, without murmuring: “May your homeland become ours too!” We should weep over our sterility like Hannah: “Lord of hosts, have pity on us! Convert us to yourself. You alone have the words of eternal life!”

For further reflection: Psalm 22

Jesus will be able to proclaim the Name of God to his brothers and sisters: a Name that is mercy, forgiveness, resurrection, life! Because God has freed the one who trusted… And Christ knows that God does not despise the affliction of the poor. For this he can enter into death, take on the sin of the world. Israel has never been disappointed when, in anguish or in any trial, it has hoped in God! What God has done in the Son is wonderful: for this the poor will be blessed and will be satisfied. This divine work must be told to the new generation!

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

The Holy Spirit of the promises (cf. Gal 3:14; Eph 1:13), who prepared the time of the Messiah by announcing him through the mouth of the prophets so that he might be awaited and welcomed at the moment of his manifestation, keeps Rosa’s hope alive by showing her the Work of God in its future fulfillment:

“In the distance I see many great things for our Institute. A Light let me see the grand panorama of the order in the future; I will say that the divine ordering was so beautiful and so intertwined that I remained in ecstasy and rejoiced, while I also saw in it a river of many sufferings. At that sight they did not frighten me at all…” (M 3, p. 17).

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 108)

RETREAT 5

GOD PRESENTS THE WAY OF SALVATION

Introduction to the celebration

The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob presents to us the way of salvation. It is an itinerary of trust in him, who calls us not to hesitate, but to wait for him to bring salvation to completion.

In Hannah, Ruth and Most Holy Mary the Bible points out to us female figures faithful to the directions of their God.

Undoubtedly Mary stands out among them, who, because of her radical hope in the God of Israel, her personal history, and her poverty of heart lived in humility and gentleness, was chosen by God as Mother of the Messiah, Jesus the Savior.

Lauds

Reading: Luke 1:26-38

Reflection on the Word

It seems that at every crisis of Israel, but I would say of humanity, God makes himself present with his “compassion.” Was it not so for Abraham?

It is the epic of the Exodus: was it not God who “bent down” over that Israelite slavery, having welcomed the groaning and the oppression of the people?

Will it not again be God who rebuilds Jerusalem, after a series of unfaithful kings has already brought Israel to defeat? And in the “fullness of time,” that is, in the fulfillment of the promises, we will again find two women: Mary and Elizabeth. The one watchful and so intent on that God whom she knows to be so compassionate toward every generation that she decides not to want to know anything else in her life (Luke 1:34). She awaits only that… fullness of grace (Luke 1:28)! And Elizabeth, whose prayers will be heard (Luke 1:13), will be visited by that divine kindness which alone takes away all shame (Luke 1:25). On the threshold of this new era, God again confounds the powerful (Luke 1:52) and chooses the “little ones”: Mary and Elizabeth, also an image of a humanity that longs to be visited by the One who alone can do great things (Luke 1:49), helping the human being in his misery and his hunger!

Do you not find some similarity with Ruth and Hannah? The first determined to leave everything: land, family, future… because she is drawn by that God who cannot disappoint. And Hannah? Insistent, in her sterility, in pouring out her trusting bitterness to that God of hers who lifts the poor from the dust (1 Sam 2:8)?

Read the prayer of Hannah: 1 Sam 2:1-10, comparing it with Mary’s “Magnificat”: Luke 1:46-55. Compare also the two announcements: to Zechariah: Luke 1:5-20 and to Mary: Luke 1:26-38. These four women: Ruth, Hannah, Mary, Elizabeth, even though in different eras, bear witness to the presence of God in their lives and above all in the history of the world.

– Could you briefly gather the spiritual characteristics of their personalities?

– You know well how, from their personal encounter with the Living God, they came away with a particular blessing.

– Can you testify that you have had some “encounter” with God?

– That you have experienced a particular “blessing” of his in your life?

CELEBRATION 27

A WOMAN CAPABLE OF HOPE GIVES BIRTH TO SAMUEL

Introduction to the celebration

The vocation of Samuel as judge of Israel leads us to contemplate the God who animates the history of the human being from within and who chose a sterile woman capable of hope to give birth to the greatest judge of Israel. As we meditate on the proposed readings, let us exult in our spirit with the hymn that the Bible places on the lips of Hannah, mother of Samuel, which is the prototype of the Magnificat: “My heart exults in the Lord, my head is lifted high through my God.”

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: 1 Samuel 3

Reflection on the Word

The historical books of Samuel and Kings will bring to light yet another unfaithfulness of Israel. Here too, that attitude of stubbornness and ingratitude on the part of the whole people continues, which we briefly observed in the book of Judges. But against this background of moral misery, one reality must console us: God does not abandon Israel! God does not tire! God is faithful. He has bound himself by oath to be the God of Abraham, of Isaac, of Jacob. He keeps the pact, we would say. Despite the spiritual decline of the priesthood (Eli is weak: 1 Sam 2:29-30; his sons are “wicked men”: 1 Sam 2:12-14), by visiting Hannah, God will grant Israel the greatest of the judges: Samuel.

– For each of us there are these repeated “calls” of God. Do you agree?

– We are all called to “welcome” this gift: “not letting a single one of the divine words go to waste.” True?

– For each one, the consoling expectation of further divine visits: “afterward the Lord appeared again to Samuel.” This will also be the experience testified to by Paul: Acts 16:9; 18:9-10; 20:23; 23:11; 26:16. What do you say?

– Reflecting on Eph 4:1-6, can you understand what the “vocation received” is?

– And how hope lies precisely in this “vocation”: “One God and Father of all… present in all.”

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

The Father reveals himself through his mission in time: in creation, in the word of the Prophets, in the Incarnation of the Word in the womb of Mary, in the life of the Son and his work, in the proclamation and work of the Apostles after the glorification of Jesus, he fully manifests the fullness of the Trinitarian mystery and continues his work in the mission of the Church…

Her “time”—the stretch of history entrusted to her, to Rosa—was a time of God and of his witness, but also a time marked by various needs and by trials that did not spare her, a time of vigilance and trusting expectation.

On every page of her Memoirs the presence of God in her life and mission is attested:

“… but He who governs and works in this very work of his knows well how to take away and to give as he pleases… the mental illuminations became much clearer and more alive for me, so that, to my amazement, I feel such sublime words coming out of my mouth, and I find everything easy: preaching, explaining and resolving whatever is asked of me…” (M 3, p. 1).

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 110)

CELEBRATION 28

SAMUEL’S HOPE IS NOT DISAPPOINTED

Introduction to the celebration

Samuel’s hope is not disappointed. God is pleased to dwell in the midst of the people, through the visible sign of the Ark, and to work terrible wonders in the presence of Israel’s enemies, so that all may understand his omnipotence. His Presence will shine out fully when he takes up his dwelling in Mary of Nazareth, holy ark of the Son, whose presence will be the definitive consolation for all who lived waiting for his coming.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

“Samuel’s word came to all Israel as the word of the Lord,” and Israel could enjoy the kindly guidance of Samuel, who patiently directed the people’s heart to the service of the one and only God, “Father of all and present in all.”

Reading: 1 Samuel 7

Reflection on the Word

We often find Israel “raising cries of lament.” By now we have grown used to it.

But always because of its sin of unfaithfulness. And yet Samuel’s voice keeps sowing hope: “God will set you free! Return to him!” And however powerful and oppressive the enemies may be, that intercession of Samuel is nevertheless effective. God knows how to defend and how to… defend himself. He clearly shows that he is a fearsome “presence” (if you wish to read that episode of the Ark in the hands of the Philistines: 1 Sam 5 and 6).

– How much does the unceasing intercession of Jesus Christ the Lord reassure you, who at the right hand of the Father intercedes for all of us (Heb 7:24-25)?

– Do you too not live too much in anxiety, or worried, often to the point of exasperation, about those “enemies” of yours, ignoring what is recalled to you, for example, in Heb 4:14-16?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“… I remained absorbed, rapt in my Good, and he filled me with strength; as soon as I felt myself carried away, I heard something torn from me on the side of the heart, I do not know what; in him I immediately found myself, and it seemed to me that I had flown into the Tabernacle” (M 1.2, p. 33).

So Rosa learns to fix her dwelling in him, in the Tabernacle, tent of the new chosen people, the Church, in the dwelling of God’s permanent presence among human beings:

“… I heard something torn from me, on the side of the heart.”

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 98)

CELEBRATION 29

GOD’S POVERTY AND THE PEOPLE’S HOPE

Introduction to the celebration

Trust in God has disappeared in Israel, but Samuel tirelessly affirms that God is the sovereign of the people and that only the Prophet can mediate him. A new intervention of God frees Samuel from affliction and enlightens him about the decisions to be made.

The Almighty clothes himself in poverty and respect for consciences in order to obtain even the smallest response of faith and hope from his people.

Only when this God gives the sign of his infinite love through Jesus Crucified and Mary beneath the Cross will humanity be converted to his message of love, which still today opens the hearts of the poor to hope.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

Israel asks for a king. Although it has experienced how the other peoples became “traps” on its journey of liberation, it asks Samuel to give it a king. “As is the case with all the peoples.” Although it has to testify that every time it cried out to the Lord, he always rescued it from anguish… nevertheless it “does not listen to Samuel.” It is useless: Israel wants to be “like all the peoples”! It forgets that it was chosen to become a “special” people: like that Living God who wants it to share in his life… No. Israel chooses to be like the pagan peoples: without life, without hope, without a future, without a history of salvation. This is what Samuel calls: “the great sin.”

Reading: 1 Samuel 8 and 12

Reflection on the Word

…And again God’s patience: “Listen to the voice of the people, Samuel: they have not rejected you, but they have rejected Me, so that I should not be king over them!” “Today they have rejected Me, who save them from all their evils and all their anguish” (cf. 1 Sam 10:19). “Listen to their request too… let a king reign over them.” But the king they choose will demand much!…

And yet: again the gentleness of God: “Do not be afraid: you have done all this evil, but at least from now on do not turn away from the Lord, but serve him…”

“From now on”… When? When Israel, when all of us, “will no longer turn away from God to follow empty things that cannot profit or save”? But history goes on with… the facts. The monarchy will lead Israel to disaster.

Personal reflection: read 1 Samuel from chapter 9 to chapter 31.

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“This horizon seems to me very dark for us, but the right hand of our eternal Father can in an instant dispel everything, and the Daughters of St. Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, can enjoy the most beautiful light in all of Catholicism and carry it to shine in the most idolatrous countries, and there plant the banner of St. Anne!” (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: June 2, 1871).

CELEBRATION 30

THE DESIRE TO START AGAIN DOES NOT ESCAPE GOD

Introduction to the celebration

King Saul, anointed by Samuel to represent the sovereignty of God in the midst of the people and on behalf of the people, does not persevere in the sacred mission signified by the rite of anointing. It is true that all sacred history highlights God’s freedom in his choices, but it is just as clear that the continuing of a chosen one in grace depends on his faithfulness, on his direct dependence on the Lord, from whom he must await inspirations in order to govern wisely. Only Jesus was and will be the authentic King of the Universe, since he learned to obey his Most Holy Mother Mary, to give himself totally to the will of the Father, and for this he was raised up by him as King of the Universe.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the catechesis

Saul is the first king. The beginnings seem auspicious. But he will be rejected for his disobedience. He will not follow Samuel’s counsels. He will prefer compromise… he will want to please everyone… to satisfy his vanity.

Catechesis on Saul

David, having entered the army, stays at Saul’s court as a singer. It will be his songs, accompanied by the lyre, that calm the king’s “superhuman evil spirits.” Saul is disapproved of by God, but David, the chosen one who pleases God not for appearances… he precisely is called to… quiet Saul’s anxieties, fears and inner turmoil (1 Sam 16:14-23). The long and bitter period of that absurd persecution against David will reveal Saul’s inner imbalance; that mad murderous jealousy of his will bring out David’s calm, charity and respect, and will let us glimpse the patient presence of God who… in the new chosen one, bears with the cruel eccentricities of the other… tirelessly offering him opportunities for “second thoughts.”

And yet:

was Saul not loved by God as David was?

No one is more handsome than he (1 Sam 9:2)…

chosen to be the… “first” king of Israel

anointed leader to have powers of liberation (1 Sam 10:1)…

he too humbly amazed at this predilection of Heaven (1 Sam 9:21-24)…

He was rejected for his disobedience to directives of decisive importance, for his inconstant spirit in pursuing the mission that was the only reason for his election… for not having persevered in listening to God…

How many tears he cost those who loved him tenderly (1 Sam 15:10-11 and 16:1)!

How many signs of mercy did he not go on receiving from God himself, though disapproved of?

Was David’s presence, in that period of anguish… not a sign of God’s merciful patience? Through the discreet and calming service generously rendered to him by David, did Saul not have the opportunity of a… return to God? Why did Saul not learn to practice critical reflection? What a mistake to give free rein to his disordered instincts! If he had had more… courage in facing himself… inwardly?

Unfortunately he fled from responsibility, from God, from himself.

Certainly, from Samuel he had received a terrible rebuke: “The Lord has torn the Kingdom of Israel from you and has given it to another better than you!” (1 Sam 15:28).

But what would have happened if he had… truly repented?

“A broken and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise!” (Ps 51:19).

The people of Israel too have suffered a rebuke no less dramatic (Luke 13:34-35 and Luke 19:41-44), but they know a prophecy of hope (Rom 11:11-15), because God is faithful… his gifts and his “call” are irrevocable (Rom 11:28-29)!

And how many signs in Saul’s life, of this tireless divine faithfulness?

… divine justice condemns him and divine mercy draws him: he, instead, flees.

When he asks Samuel not to dishonor him before the elders of the people, the old prophet agrees. Could that gesture (even if dictated by the charity of not publicly disowning a “consecrated one”) not have been an opening, an invitation to hope… to try once more to… put himself humbly into God’s hands?

It is true: God has no need to correct his judgment (1 Sam 15:29). But it remains equally true that to him alone is it granted… the impossible (Matt 19:25-26).

If you, Saul, knew that you were loved, why did you not hope in God even against all human hope?

Story of Saul, of Judas Iscariot, of so many Christians!

If you had pleaded more… waited more?

Let us think for a moment of the two parables that Jesus taught on the effectiveness… of prayer (Luke 18:1-14): it is absurd to think that a poor widow could be heard by an unjust judge!

Just as absurd as it may seem that a hardened sinner should find welcome with God…

But will God not do justice to “his chosen ones” who cry out to him day and night?

If you too, Saul, had been chosen, why did you lack… that cry?…

David will sin as you did, more than you perhaps…, but he will acknowledge it, he will humble himself… he will want to fall into the hands of mercy!… (2 Sam 24:10.14).

Saul, why did you ask so little for this mercy for yourself?

Did you not sense in that rebuke of God a glimmer of hope? And what if the Lord wanted to test you, no longer addressing his word to you? You, instead, are preoccupied with these words of Samuel: “God has torn the Kingdom from you to give it to one better than you.”

But consider:

“Better than you”… so you, Saul, in God’s eyes, are still good! David is better, certainly, but you are not bad. The women of Israel will sing: “David has slain his ten thousands” (1 Sam 18:7), but to you, Saul, they will still acknowledge that “you have slain your thousands”!

Why, then, let yourself be robbed by the evil spirit of jealousy or envy or presumption or vainglory?

Who seduced you? “Who told you that you were naked?” (Gen 3:11)… so as to throw you into that murderous madness? (1 Sam 18:17-19.21-25.28-29; 19:1.14-15; 20:30-31). You wanted to drag your son Jonathan along too…

But how can you fight against God?

If you yourself are afraid of David, because you see that God is with him, how do you hope to take away what God has already decided to give?

One would be tempted to advise you what Gamaliel proposed to the Sanhedrin (Acts 5:34-42).

But a “superhuman spirit” dominates you!

You come to take it out on the Benjaminites, feeling yourself the victim of a conspiracy (1 Sam 22:7-8)… You will kill all the priests of Nob by the hand of an Edomite, refusing to listen to the reasonableness of their testimony (1 Sam 22:13-19).

Blind to the point of not stopping before the “consecrated ones,” to order their extermination! What you did not do in application of the laws of war accepted by the pre-Christian environment (for reasons of political opportunism or greed, perhaps disguising yourself as pious, perhaps hypocritically scandalized at divine severity)… you do at the fierce instigation of quite another… “spirit” (1 Sam 15:1-3.9-11).

And yet for you, O Saul, all is not yet lost!

In that deep and mysterious restlessness of your heart, so tortured by your passions, moments of lucidity will still be granted to you: you will listen to your son (1 Sam 19:4-6); God himself will intervene directly, preventing your murderous intentions (1 Sam 19:23-24). Repentant of your error, you will weep and call the persecuted David your son when he sets before you the evidence of the respect he has kept for your life. You came to confess your guilt and to propose entrusting your descendants precisely to his word… as future king! The light is still granted to you, then! You seem to stop pursuing him: the goodness of the one whom you now consider a son… has appeased you (1 Sam 24:17-23). Once again, as in the past with his songs, his voice has driven away the demons!

But darkness prevails! (1 Sam 26:2-3).

David, however, will give you the gift of life for the second time… he will call you back from the darkness, leading you back to reason, to the evidence of the facts… and you seem to have understood (1 Sam 26:17-25).

David’s ability to bear so many difficulties, hardships, fears, solitudes… keeping intact in his heart so much devotion for the “anointed of the Lord” and defending this sentiment against everything and everyone… will it keep Saul from being lost for good? …

That obstinate testimony of his… of faithfulness seems to win the agitated heart of Saul: “I have sinned… my life today has been precious in your eyes… I have been very, very mistaken.” Saul seems to come to his senses (1 Sam 27:4). He will indeed be terrified by the true enemies of all time: the Philistines (1 Sam 28:5); but in those straits Saul will bring a light: “David loves me! For him, at least, my life is precious! I wanted to kill him… he saves my person. God has rejected me… but his new chosen one honors me… he will not forget me.” In his drama, his only comfort will be precisely the memory of that night, on the hill of Hachilah. And when, full of fear, he dares to consult the Lord again… he will have no answer… but in so much silence there is still a glimmer of light! God by his silence punishes… but he will allow the reckless evocation of the occult to announce the imminence of death (1 Sam 28:19).

Could Saul have been saved?

It is not lawful for us to venture into the secret judgments of God. The human heart is an abyss (Ps 64:7)… who can fathom it?

Not even the forces of hell, much as they would like to, can come to possess the secrets of the human heart, even of a sinner! They are given power to seduce, to tempt, to deceive… But no one, except God, can sovereignly penetrate the heart of the free creature to know every desire, every wish… He alone has the power to confirm the will to perdition of a human being who has become wicked (Matt 10:28).

St. Peter, in the light of Easter, lets us glimpse a hope of salvation even for those… incorrigible spirits who, at the time of the flood, had refused to believe in the goodness of God, shown in the patience of Noah. Was Jesus a messenger of salvation for them too (1 Pet 3:18-20)?

It cannot be said that Saul was more unbelieving than they, or more obstinate… The last moments of his life make us doubt that this unhappy king was touched by the magnanimous patience that God continued to show him in David: “I have sinned… I will no longer do you harm, David!… I have acted foolishly… I have been very, very mistaken!…” (1 Sam 26:21).

St. Paul, commenting on Psalm 68 in the letter to the Ephesians (4:7-10), affirms that the One who descended to earth, Christ Jesus, has now ascended in triumph to heaven, taking with him human beings… as captives and filling all earthly realities with his grace.

Now, if God “gives the desolate a home and abandons only the rebellious to a parched land…” (Ps 68:7), the apostolic revelation, which possesses the fullness of the Spirit, announces that with the manifestation of the limitless love of the meek Lamb… even the “rebellious” can hope to “dwell with the Lord” (Ps 68:19), if they return to “piety.”

For all sinners, for all those who find themselves in slavery to their passions (how many stirred the heart of this first and unhappy king?), we can pray Psalm 38. It is the prayer of the sinner. Of one who has experienced his own incapacities: “nothing is left intact”… Foolishness, that is, having held holiness and the fear of God in little account, has led him to misery: “my wounds are foul.” And yet there is a groan, an attempt, a desire to start again that cannot escape the God of mercy: “You will answer… You will say a word… In you I hope, Lord!”

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“What am I to say? Only that this happens because of me: here are my sins! Courage, let us trust in God: he, as his own Work, will provide for everything” — “Ah! yes, let me say it: this Work, the blows it takes are all the fruit of my wickedness. If it so pleases God, let us adore his divine Majesty” (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: Aug. 6, 1870; Nov. 16, 1871).

This same awareness of being herself the real obstacle to the progress of God’s Work made her think more than once of resigning and leaving to another the responsibility of the general government.

(from Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 263)

CELEBRATION 31

THE HUMBLE ONE HOPES IN THE LORD

Introduction to the celebration

David represents Israel’s trust in the power of its God. He approached Goliath in the name of the Lord: “You come to me with sword, spear and javelin, I come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts.” The victory over Goliath was a decisive event in establishing himself as a possible leader of his people. Trust in God rather than in one’s own strength is a biblical constant proper to those who, with a poor heart, expect everything from the Lord. As long as David remained faithful to this capacity of his to expect everything from the Lord, he prospered. This capacity for abandonment typical of a poor heart, and the predilection of God that it draws upon itself, are attested in the Magnificat by Mary, daughter of St. Anne: “… my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, for he has looked upon the lowliness of his servant.”

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: 1 Samuel 16

Reflection on the Word

In place of Saul, David is consecrated king of Israel: the youngest of the sons of Jesse, who is out tending the flock.

“Man looks at appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart!”

God looks at David and reserves him for himself. More than a vocation, it is a divine election made known to David through the prophet Samuel. This election marks an important stage in the history of the covenant, in the history of salvation: after the promises made to Abraham, to Moses, to the Judges… God now gives Israel a “king-shepherd,” capable of governing the people with wisdom and justice. With David, Israel will have a “Savior,” entrusted with the task of resisting the Philistine Goliath—defeated by him not with human strength, but only with a few pebbles, perhaps solely by faith in God—and of beginning a new line of descendants, a blessed dynasty, capable of embodying historically the authority of God and the national unity of the people, and of being a bearer of messianic hope.

Jesus several times accepted the title “Son of David.” So the Canaanite woman and the two blind men of Jericho called him, so the crowd acclaimed him at the solemn entry into Jerusalem, and he himself declared that he was the fulfillment of the promises made to David. In this sense, for the Spirituality of the Movement, the prophecy of Isaiah takes on a quite particular meaning: “A shoot shall sprout from the stump of Jesse…”

Personal or small-group reading of the catechesis on David (in Appendix no. 2)

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

No less tender and trusting was her devotion to the Holy Spirit, “joy of hearts,” in which he has the mission of reviving divine love and consuming every earthly affection (M 1.1, p. 39). In 1872, when she found herself so alone, without the guidance of a director, she felt secure under that of her “governing Spirit”:

“What a consolation it is for me, who am so abandoned by every human help, to have my dear Spirit, who guides me in everything, directs me and sustains me so well, even in the days of such a painful state. He works and leads everything with excellence. I find nothing but misery and shame and confusion.”

(M 3, pp. 9, 11f)

(from Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 200)

RETREAT 6

GOD MAKES WAITING FOR THE FUTURE POSSIBLE

Introduction to the celebration

In the awareness of his own means and abilities, the human being, proud of his own history, risks presuming so much as to turn his gaze toward other promises that are not those of God. God makes the expectation of a future possible because it rests on his own faithfulness. But, since he respects human freedom, he waits for someone’s availability in order to reveal to all the progressive realization of his plan of salvation. To the Prophet Nathan he entrusts the message addressed to David: “…the Lord will make a house for you. When your days are fulfilled… I will raise up your offspring after you, who will come forth from your body… Your house and your kingdom will endure forever.” The descendant of David is Mary, from whom Jesus was born.

Lauds

Reading: 2 Samuel 7

Reflection on the Word

The beginnings of the monarchy are difficult. Besides, Samuel had prophesied it: rejecting God is no joke, and certainly the claims of a man, even a king, cannot be compared with those of a God who has always sought to give life and above all to form bonds of benevolence, showing himself lavish with tenderness and attention toward that people of his who truly at one time… had not been a people. But now Israel has insisted on living in the manner of the “world” and will suffer… the same disordered passions that lead the world, precisely, to death. We have seen the jealous madness of Saul, his inconstancy, his wanting to win the sympathy of the people, and finally that frightening loneliness of agony and his inglorious death.

David too, although carefully and attentively prepared with abundant graces from his youth, could not avoid dramatic missteps. He too, chosen to be a shepherd and guide after God’s own heart, yielded to violence, to the thirst for possession, behaving in the manner of the kings of the other nations.

We have seen how the consequences of sin lead to unheard-of sufferings, to social disasters, to humiliating renunciations.

However much the human being may want to build his own security: a gratifying posterity, using for this purpose, even if in good faith, his own religious sentiment, in the end it is always God who guarantees the ultimate truth of the human being. It is God, in fact, who answers that anxious search for good and promises: “I will make you great, I will secure your descendants, I will make you stable forever!”

You can notice how, amid the difficulties of these first two kings, the fears and obstinacy of the people, the bitterness of Samuel who suffers for the contempt and ingratitude shown to God, God himself appears… “serene and tranquil,” not at all offended or indignant; indeed this prophecy is the confirmation that God wants to go on being the God of this people.

– The Revelation of the New Testament is: “God is love” (1 John 4:8-10). In the hymn to charity of St. Paul, can you begin to recognize the true attitudes of love?

– That is, to understand, as John again says, that God loved us first? (1 Cor 13)

– If God is love, can Israel then truly hope, despite its wrong choices? Why?

CELEBRATION 32

GOD’S FAITHFULNESS LASTS FOREVER

Introduction to the celebration

The biblical statement: “God’s faithfulness lasts forever” came true for David, even though he had sinned. Chosen while he was following the flock, to become the leader of Israel. God never abandoned him to himself and promised him: “your house and your kingdom will endure forever before me, and your throne will be made firm forever.” The descendant spoken of is the Messiah, mediator between God and human beings. The perspective is future. Past and future always intersect at a point that reveals the One who, associated with his Mother, reveals his Kingdom founded on justice, on love and on universal brotherhood.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

“I WILL HUMBLE THE DESCENDANTS OF DAVID… BUT NOT FOREVER!” (Book of Kings)

Introduction to the reading

Israel will be led to unity under the reign of David, but because, with all his heart, even after sin, David, though on a penitent pilgrimage, follows the God who had chosen him and then forgiven him. On that promise of good sworn by God to his descendants, the tribe of Judah will keep hope.

For love of David! Already at the end of Solomon’s life, the kingdom will show signs of decline. This king, in fact, although introduced and taught by his father in the government of Israel and having received from God every wisdom and enlightenment to do well… will not persevere!

Reading: 1 Kings 3:1-15

Reflection on the Word

David understands, confesses and does penance for his sin. Solomon’s attitude is different. Humble, listening, obedient at the beginning. Then, grown in fame for riches and wisdom, he ends up… going soft. Let us note some causes of the corruption of his kingdom:

– Too much luxury: certainly splendid was the Temple (built in seven years), but even more beautiful the royal palace (thirteen years to build it). 1 Kgs 6:38; 7:1-5.

– Many works, however beautiful, cost effort and… forced labor (1 Kgs 5:27; 9:15.21).

– So much splendor and so much fame attract… enemies too. Solomon will marry foreign women, accepting their idolatrous rites (1 Kgs 11:1-10).

– Compare, by contrast, the austerity and sobriety of David. His last years were lived in solitude and detachment from everything and everyone. Those of Solomon, with too many women and too many spurious ideas, will make him a megalomaniac.

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“Holy indifference governs my soul; I do what my poor strength permits in the Work of the Lord, so as to be able to consume them all for my God. It is very sweet” — “Man is a slave: he acts, he builds as long as it pleases God; but woe if he stretches out his most holy hand: the oppressed become victorious. So it will be” (L Mar. 14, 1890; May 5, 1899).

(from Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 184)

CELEBRATION 33

A PENITENT LIFE AND THE LORD’S FORGIVENESS

Introduction to the celebration

At the beginning of his reign Solomon loved the Lord and acted according to the principles of David his father. Later the biblical writer describes his conduct as unfaithful. He let himself be drawn by foreign women and their divinities, and his heart was no longer wholly the Lord’s like the heart of David his father, to whom, because of his penitent life, trusting and open to hope for forgiveness and for the fulfillment of the “Promises,” the Lord mitigated the punishment, keeping one of his descendants on the throne of Jerusalem. In Psalm 2, this One is called Son of God, chosen, consecrated, with whom he has established an eternal covenant. This heir of David was certainly awaited by the holy Anne and Joachim in prayers and supplications for the liberation and salvation of Israel.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: 1 Kings 10:14-29

Reflection on the Word

How different is Samuel’s testimony at the end of his life (1 Sam 8) from that of the “spendthrift” Solomon. If Israel must blame on its own unfaithfulness the whim of wrong choices, such as wanting a king (and how heartfelt, to the very end, was the old prophet’s disapproval!), honest, instead, is his displeasure at the political and social situation inherited from the gravest errors of Solomon, who in old age became anything but wise and a “peacemaker.” Here too, Solomon’s deviations will provoke harmful consequences: for example adversaries ready to exploit the people’s discontent; a son, Rehoboam, arrogant and evidently badly brought up by his father’s manias of grandeur and power. But above all, and Scripture seems to want to underline this for that purpose, the enormous riches accumulated by Solomon. David’s accumulating was different. First of all it had been with a view to that Temple he so desired and which he would have wished to raise as a sign of gratitude to his God. And then David’s riches had been formed, as he himself says, “in the midst of distress” (1 Chr 22:14). David’s desires were for the glory of the God of Israel. Solomon’s desires, like those of Saul, unfortunately, must be presumed to have been directed toward quite another glory.

David had prepared incalculable riches for that Temple… what was Solomon seeking in that “surpassing in riches and wisdom” all the kings of the earth? And if the wise Samuel, though seeing Israel’s obstinacy, kept pleading with God for that people, as he had kept weeping and praying for Saul, why did Solomon no longer ask God for an understanding and docile heart to guide that people entrusted to him (1 Kgs 3:9), but quite the contrary, he led it astray, letting himself be imposed upon by foreigners with blasphemous discernments?

– Certainly Scripture does not reproach this abundance of gold and silver… But Jesus, greater than Solomon (Matt 12:42), does it not seem to you that he taught, above all by his life, quite a different attitude?

– Reflect on the danger of riches: Matt 19:21-24, Luke 16:9 and on their accumulation: Matt 6:19-21.24.

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

This, which we could call the pedagogy of courage, appears in a special way in the correspondence with the Princess of Fitalia, her spiritual daughter, who was much tried by aridity and other sufferings. She repeats to her:

“Courage, for in the time of trial much is gained!” — “Oh! I can well call you by the title of gracious and strong, resolute of spirit, noble warrior, always victorious in your undertakings” —

“Courage in your undertaking! the work you do is pleasing to God…, courage!” “Courage, never be dismayed; Jesus is with you, who can be against you?” — “Courage; let us press upon the Heart of Jesus, he will console us” — (L June 26, 1885; Jan. 15, 1886; July 20, 1893; Sept. 2, 1893; Nov. 2, 1893; Feb. 27, 1895).
