CELEBRATION 34

ISRAEL’S HISTORY REVEALS HOPE

Introduction to the celebration

Underlying the history of Israel there is always the theme of Hope.

After the reign of Solomon, historical events will increasingly express unfaithfulness and depravity. But the hope that Solomon expressed in his prayer contains the strength to change God’s justice into forgiveness, with new horizons of peace, brotherhood and universal harmony.

When his vision of the future, entrusted to prayer: “We have sinned, we have done wrong, we have acted wickedly… if they return to you with their whole heart and their whole soul… hear in heaven, the place of your dwelling, their prayer and their supplication, and do them justice,” becomes reality, the Lord will answer with the promise of the messianic era, bearer of peace and cosmic harmony.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the reading

With Rehoboam, son of Solomon, the political schism will be completed. Violent, presumptuous, imprudent, he will turn the people against him. Of the twelve tribes of Israel, ten will break away and follow Jeroboam who, although he had received a most favorable prophecy and one of great responsibility from God, who invited him to lead at least a large part of the people, will betray this mission and, as his first act of government, will establish worship at Bethel and at Dan, thus bringing about the religious schism as well!

Reading: 1 Kings 11:26-40 and 12:1-30

Reflection on the Word

Amid violence, fears, political games, discontent and rebellions, God’s providential and discreet care for his people continues. Invited to make up for the errors of Solomon and Rehoboam, Jeroboam… deserts, despising the divine election. And Rehoboam, furious, who would like to reconquer by force what was lost, is again stopped by the man of God: “This situation is willed by God!” You can therefore notice how God seeks the ways of peace. And how he calls human beings to be “peacemakers.” Silently, patiently, he is leading history toward a stable, united and truly peaceful kingdom in which “the wolf will dwell with the lamb” (Isa 11:6) and the one who guides it will be a “child.” Certainly not arrogant kings with chariots and horses!

But it is not yet the time… Israel, every human being, must learn, at their own expense, that the powerful will be toppled from their thrones, that all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matt 26:52) and that whoever wants to be exalted will inevitably be humbled.

– Are you learning in this history to live with the “wolves”?

– Or do you reason like all the arrogant and the violent: “better force, better power”?

– Jesus will call the peacemakers blessed. How much do you work, even in your small way, to earn this beatitude?

– Or do you show yourself instead intolerant, impatient, a slanderer, quicker to judge than to excuse and to bear with others?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

The fear, however, of not having been completely forgiven comes back to torment her. One day she saw those sins covered by a black veil, and she wept inconsolably until the veil was lifted. Later, in confirmation of the forgiveness sealed by God, she saw over the erased sins now a palm, now a most beautiful crown; this was then replaced by the crown of thorns, to her great joy. She exclaims at the end of the account:

“Oh! poor sinner! Oh! goodness of a God and Father! Who would not wear himself out for this dear Father? Giving him all of ourselves is truly nothing compared to such immensity of greatness. Oh! boundless goodness!” (M 1.1, pp. 5-7).

The more she discovered the greatness of divine mercy, the more she saw herself, in the presence of the supreme Good and loving Father, as “a wretched sinner, a loathsome worm of the earth”; but she reacted full of gratitude and security: “It is no longer I who live, it is my Jesus who lives in me!” (cf. Gal 2:20).

(from Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 54)

CELEBRATION 35

THE FAITH AND HOPE OF ELIJAH FIND AN ANSWER

Introduction to the celebration

The Lord does not tire of raising up Prophets in every age.

The Prophet lives a profound bond with him. His whole life speaks of the presence of God in the history of humanity. The style of his speaking and acting reveals and bears witness to this presence. The divine voice guides Elijah, transforming him into the prophet who fights for the Lord. He affirms that only his Lord is a God who can give life and who can restore it. His faith and hope are not disappointed because the Lord answers his prayer. If Elijah’s contemplative spirit and his unconditional dedication edified so many devout Israelites, how much more must they have been present in the Holy Mother Anne, if she deserved from the Lord to receive in her womb the Mother of God.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

God does not abandon Israel. This is the most consoling truth of all Revelation. Jesus will confirm it, bringing this too to fulfillment: “I will be with you until the end of the ages.” God will accompany the decline of this people of his, by whom he has been rejected, continuing to be faithful to it. He leaves it, it is true, to its own choices, “to follow its own counsel”… yet he is there, present, hoping that Israel will come to its senses, will reflect, will return, will seek its God… Do you remember the father of the “prodigal son” (Luke 15:11-24)? In that parable Jesus reveals the feelings of God. God knows how to wait! God keeps in his heart, trembling, that son by whom he does not seem at all offended or betrayed. He is always his son! He does not seem, then, to be scandalized by all the miseries that the children of men show. Even that of being ungrateful toward their own parents! How much we, instead, remain disheartened, bewildered, frightened… by all the divisions, the violence, the ugliness, the scandals in the midst of which we are often forced to live. Experiencing, when we have the courage to admit it, that often we ourselves are “workers of iniquity” (Matt 7:23). Harmony, beauty, order, perfection certainly attract us. We rejoice in them, we even struggle to win them, and how embittered we become if they escape us… But how far are we capable of accepting to live with our own… disasters?

Well: the sign that God stays with Israel’s disasters is the care with which he raises up, in the midst of corruptions of various kinds, great prophets, sure guides. Let us try to reflect on two episodes that recall this divine attention.

Reading: 1 Kings 18:17-40

– Try to reflect: how much do you too “limp,” that is, often live as if God did not exist?

– Or how scandalized are you instead by God’s patience?

– Have you ever felt like a “prodigal son”?

– Have you ever experienced that, desiring to be forgiven by God for your iniquities, you were driven away or not welcomed?

– Or do you presume that, after all, you have done nothing really serious?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“I cannot fail to recall what the Lord works in me when I have to speak in conference to the Daughters of St. Anne. Just collecting myself and going to the Crucified, my Good: — The ignorant one, your slave, must speak and must treat of perfection; You, my beloved Master, prompt me, and I will repeat it —, something happens in me that, if the creatures who listen to me could see it, they would certainly be amazed; but my All does not allow it…

He seems to draw near to me; many times he dictates to me things from Sacred Scripture, he suggests to me things I never knew, other most beautiful ones he puts in my mind to say. Many times I too taste what I say. At other times not: I speak as in the third person, and I understand nothing of what I say and what I have said at the end.

What mercy! He sees the need of these creatures, he speaks through the mouth of a donkey, he does not withdraw, that is, does not draw back at the sight of my wickedness, but for the good of his dear souls he makes use of a most infamous creature to say and make heard his will to these brides of his” (M 4.2, pp. 78-80).

(in Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 104)

CELEBRATION 36

ELISHA REVEALS GOD’S COMPASSION

Introduction to the celebration

Through the person of Elisha, the Lord, endowing him with charismatic gifts, made himself present in the midst of Israel, with his kindness and compassion toward those who were waiting to be heard and with the power to work healings among the poor and the oppressed. The mission he received places him as mediator between God and his people. With his prophetic gaze he penetrates cosmic, political and historical phenomena, reading them in the light of the will of God. He suffers because of them, takes them upon himself and is ready to give his life to his God, with renewed hope of finding a hearing and compassion for Israel. He perpetuates in time the faithfulness of his ancestors and opens new horizons for future generations who will seek, like St. Anne and Most Holy Mary, to hope against hope in God alone.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: 2 Kings 5

Reflection on the Word

Elijah and Elisha are given by God to those ten tribes inherited by the traitor Jeroboam; they will form the kingdom of the North, that is, of Samaria. It is not by chance that the Lord sends the greatest prophets of that time to the most “needy.” Yet the story of Samaria remains a sad one: it will not know a single king faithful to the Covenant, and therefore capable of guiding it. It will end tragically in exile about one hundred fifty years before the other kingdom: that of Judah. Elijah has been left alone, as prophet of the Lord, and is there before the people and King Ahab to bear witness to the truth: that the people are “limping”; that they do not know how to serve, while the true God wishes to reveal himself, to call everyone to conversion, desiring to re-form on that altar of twelve stones that beloved “name”: Israel! Elisha, on the other hand, is happy to welcome a foreigner sick with leprosy so that he may come to confess, he a foreigner, “that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel.” But King Joram and the people seem to take little account that “a prophet is in their midst.” Jesus too will refer to these two great prophets when he wishes to stress that he also, sent as “Son” and therefore more than a “prophet,” to a people unfortunately blind and deaf, will not have a better lot (Luke 4:16-27).

– In your daily life, do you feel you can confess that there truly is no other Lord than Jesus?

– That is, truly, is he enough for you?

– How do you instead live the rejections, the contempt, the ingratitude or the indifference toward you, on the part of the people who live beside you or whom you meet in your surroundings?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

God confirms her through the person of St. Anne, who, on a March 1st whose year cannot be determined, places in Rosa’s hands a supernatural energy: that power of the Spirit that goes out from Christ in acts of healing and restoring; “…power came forth from him and healed them all” (Luke 6:19).

She notes down on a page of a notebook the event that concerns her:

“March 1st, from the Holy Mother Anne I received in my hands a light, in the center of the hands. And she said: — from now on all the sick whom you bless will be healed, always in the name of God you will bless them and they will be healed.”

It is evident that the Father entrusts to Rosa with special love the care of the sick and thus makes her a sharer in the very mission of the Son, who “healed them all.”

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 157)

RETREAT 7

GOD’S FAITHFULNESS DOES NOT WAVER

Introduction to the celebration

Israel has experienced the faithfulness of God, which has never wavered, even though, during the exile, his silence called into question even the hope of the just. But his renewed historical interventions are new messages that let us glimpse a better future. A time in which peace and justice will be achievable, because the Messiah will come, the Liberator and Redeemer, the Restorer of the people’s communion with its God. The one who represents the people that first welcomes the Messiah is Mary, holy ark of the Most High, splendid dwelling of God clothed in humility.

Lauds

Reading: Luke 10:25-37

Reflection on the Word

With the exile of the northern kingdom to Assyria and that of the southern kingdom to Babylon, the monarchy sets unhappily for Samaria and Jerusalem. The illusion of easy securities and the craving to resemble other peoples will be paid for dearly… If once, in Egypt, Israel had suffered “400” years of bitter slavery, more because of the violence and injustice of others, now it will have to endure another “400” years of wars, oppression and devastation, but because of its own exasperating stubbornness in not obeying the commitments undertaken with its God: commitments that, we know, would have bound it to the Living God in a covenant of love. But… here: this is where that “unspeakable” truth will be unveiled, which Joseph had already revealed prophetically to his murderous brothers: “Do not be afraid: although you intended to do harm to me, God intended it for good, in order to accomplish what is being fulfilled today: to keep a numerous people alive” (Gen 50:19-20). So the history of the monarchy as well, like that of the Exodus, of the conquest of the Land, of the Judges… although revealing a continual contempt of the human being for the will of God and a going forward by the human being on paths of death… God, mysteriously, leads it “to a good.” Joseph well understood that God would visit the children of Israel.

As he “visits” Hannah in her sterility; as he “visits” every human being in his anguish. God is the protagonist of the history of salvation, but he appears as “the one who serves”: the silent and provident “good Samaritan” of the parable. All have sinned. Not only the kings, but also the people. The guides were there, in fact: Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Micah, Isaiah, Amos and then those more obscure but who at the opportune moment intervened for the good… Why did they not listen? Why did everyone keep “limping”? So: all inexcusable. All shut up in disobedience, so that mercy may be shown to all (cf. Rom 11:32). From this tragedy too Israel will emerge purified, it will learn to call upon the faithful God with all its heart. To know one’s own misery and to know, beside you, the One who discreetly waited for you to call upon him in order to come to your aid, is the experience of the faith that saves! So: “let us hold fast to the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who made the promise is trustworthy” (Heb 10:23). And signs of this divine faithfulness are visible and numerous in these rather tormented pages of the monarchic epic as well. For example, we have seen how God works for peace (Celebration 34): tolerating divisions rather than allowing fratricidal wars. How he is ready for clemency, even with the worst kings, when signs, however insufficient, of repentance are given. With Ahab: 1 Kgs 21:25-29; with Manasseh: 2 Chr 33:11-19; when, out of that faithful kindness toward his people and sensitivity to their sufferings, he welcomes the prayer of Jehoahaz: 2 Kgs 13:3-6; of Jeroboam II: 2 Kgs 14:23-27. He will still reserve providence and help for Ahab: 1 Kgs 20:13-21; for Joram: 2 Kgs 6:24-33; 7:1-17. Attempts at conversion and return to God will be found, however, only in the kingdom of Judah, for love of David, the only king after God’s own heart; but only Hezekiah and Josiah will truly trust in God, will accept the guidance of the prophets and carry out serious religious reforms: 2 Kgs 19:1-7; 20:1-5; 23:1-27. Without wavering, then, but hoping in the divine promises, like Abraham, we can wait for God to turn into good everything that we so regularly spoil.

Looking at him, who made himself present in history through the prophets who knew how to interpret it, have you noticed their behavior?

Discreet, kind, sincere, close to the people, always ready to bear witness to or recall the commitments of the Covenant, not at all intrusive or authoritarian or seeking personal gain, but encouraging, stimulating, suggesting conversion; what Paul already said of the apostles could be said of them (cf. 2 Cor 6:3-10), everything becomes possible; truly God alone can trace paths of life “through the great waters” (Ps 77:20), because it is he who does not abandon our life in the grave. In conclusion, read Psalm 16.

– What has the failure of the monarchy taught you?

– How do you judge the work of the prophets, practically unheeded?

– What meaning does the statement of Heb 10:23 have?

– What do you mean by those “footprints of God that remain unseen” of Psalm 77:20?

– Do you agree with what Paul says to the Romans in Rom 8:28?

CELEBRATION 37

THE LORD PROMISES EMMANUEL

Introduction to the celebration

Israel experiences pain, the bitter struggle of gradual submission to the enemy. When the conflict between faithfulness and unfaithfulness to the constituent elements of the covenant reaches exasperation, the Lord speaks through the mouth of the Prophet Isaiah. He gives new vigor to what he had already promised to our first parents about the Woman and her Offspring, confirming the truthfulness of his word: “Listen, house of David! Is it not enough for you to weary human patience, that you also weary the patience of my God? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold: the Virgin will conceive a son, and shall name him Emmanuel.” Yet only a faithful “remnant” will be consoled in seeing the One awaited by the nations.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: 2 Corinthians 1:1-10

Reflection on the Word

Israel no longer exists as a people. Now divided by the schism, with two kingdoms that try to prevail over one another and that will no longer be able to come together again in unity. Not even the prophets can bring them back to the unity of faith. Now it is the end. That catastrophe seems almost necessary: first the exile of Samaria, with the land that will be abandoned to the pagans, and then that of Jerusalem; the holy city and that Temple, sign and place of the presence of the God of Israel, will be destroyed and devastated.

So, all is over.

And yet that warning of Joseph to his brothers in Egypt: “God will visit you!” becomes again the cry of hope of the prophets: “God will bring you back. God will open a road again in the desert. From exile a ‘remnant’ will return: there will be a new exodus.”

That “inexpressible” truth takes shape: God will see to it that evil serves as an instrument of good, to preserve life! From the perversions of the human mind and heart, God can create or re-create in his creature intuitions of light and unthinkable capacities for good and for life. “From death God has freed us and will free us, because of the hope we have placed in him!” This is the consolation that overflows in Paul’s heart. He too is a witness of this truth, which Israel through the centuries had to confess, in spite of everything. Paul, himself an enemy of Christ through ignorance, is now an apostle by the will of God.

How was “grace” able, in this man, a manifest persecutor, to find the way to touch his heart and mind… so as to convince him freely to become a witness of the mercy and greatness of the One he formerly abhorred?

What unexplored and mysterious ways does the divine Spirit travel in order to change the inner structure of free creatures and… win them over?

How, from falls that seem irreparable, can the human being rise again by calling upon the help of the One whom until a little earlier he wanted to ignore or even fight? To call upon him knowing and believing him to be a savior and not an enemy?

How do these changes come about?

Without being forced by divine omnipotence, indeed feeling attracted to it and yet being aware that one can decide to resist it?

How can that Crucified One who seemed an unacceptable scandal… indeed a repulsive event of death, suddenly be changed into a “boast,” into a desired way of salvation?

How can Israel, which seems to have sought every way that led to death, rebelling against that offer of covenant which God has always so earnestly proposed to it, in the end… rise again?

How can a nation that did everything to despise “grace” and therefore pays for its rebellion with destruction, finally have received mercy and returned to life and found its glory again?

How, Jerusalem, were you visited?

What hope could you nurture, if ever you listened? In what way in your death were you consoled, freed, so much so that it appears you freely sought your God?

From what depths did your cry rise up as a true, effective invocation, so as to move the heart of God?

But who taught you to call upon him, if you had turned your back on that God who now is touched by your tears?

Paul too, after the “light” of Damascus, has that… consolation: “for he is praying” (Acts 9:11). In short: how can the dead return to life?

And how can those things that today I hate be tomorrow the sole object of my desires?

God does not abandon Israel…

But how does this presence of the Spirit manage to make itself felt in the depths of the human being, to set in motion unsuspected spiritual circuits unexpectedly? Perhaps we shall never be able to grasp the meeting between these two sovereign freedoms: the divine and the human, which, though made for each other, yet the human one is always suspicious of being annulled… But this meeting is necessary so that the human being may experience that abundant consolation that manages to free him from every tribulation and death and bring him out free, loving and possessor of hope.

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“… I was assisted by my Good and by the Most Holy Virgin; never did I have her so near as to feel her love… in my soul”;

“… a joy of love because comforted… by the Most Holy Virgin” (M.2, pp. 38; 58; M.9.8, pp. 55-50).

The Mother of Jesus, then, is invoked by Rosa also with the title of Most Holy Virgin. The aspect of the mystery of Mary announced by Isaiah: “Behold: the Virgin will conceive and bear a Son and shall name him Emmanuel” (Isa 7:14), highlights and affirms God’s lordship over the world through the person of Mary, his exclusive property, land of encounter of the Eternal with the human, in the overcoming of every Law inherent in creation.

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 144)

CELEBRATION 38

THE LORD WILL ELIMINATE DEATH FOREVER

Introduction to the celebration

Despite his sin, Israel receives, with the gift of new promises, hope, which opens him to new horizons of faithfulness. The initiative is always that of his God, who through Isaiah projects him into future horizons: “On that day everyone will throw to the rats and bats the idols of silver and gold that they had made to worship… the Lord will eliminate death forever!… he will wipe away the tears from every face… and it will be said on that day… this is the Lord for whom we have hoped… let us rejoice and be glad in his salvation.” This is why St. Anne, called to contemplate the fulfillment of the Word of the Lord, could say of herself appropriately: “in me rested the sighs and groans, the tears, the prayers of all the just of the Old Testament, because from me, as from a most fruitful root of Jesse, sprang my daughter Mary Immaculate and Jesus Christ her Son” (Rule ’69, 1).

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Deuteronomy 17:14-20

Reflection on the Word

If Adam had listened to God, he would have remained in that “garden” and would have tasted the fruit of the tree of “life”: “his mouth would have been filled with immortality.” If Israel had listened, it would not have ended in this tragedy of exile. When the human being does not obey, he can experience only the “hardness of his own heart.” Which means: “following his own counsel,” that is, not wanting dialogue with God. But the revelation of Genesis has taught us that the human being is “in the image and likeness” of God. Life comes to him, that is, from his capacity for personal relationships. “It is not good that he be alone.” He needs the other. If, therefore, he refuses the original relationship with God, his first and necessary interlocutor, surely his “own counsel” can provide him only with another possible interlocutor: that “serpent” that crawls, that lives down “below,” that apparently causes no trouble, does not make its “living” weigh on anyone, with whom it is easier to converse and therefore more tempting to listen. It invites, in fact, toward an “absolute,” “self-exalting” freedom: “you will be like God, if you do not listen to God!” So deceit, loneliness, death. The human being sees himself “naked”; anything but like God! Frightened and fragile.

Always, behind every temptation, every dialogue with the “evil one,” there is an… appearance of truth. He too was in the image of God, called to fulfill himself through that one relationship that would have made him a “bearer of light,” free in fullness.

But… “he did not remain in the truth.” He did not want to continue that “relationship.” He therefore proposes to the human “counsel” that appearance of truth: a desire for… absolute freedom. For him a… “howl” that he will carry within, as eternal torment. That torment of his will be the only fruit that the human being draws from listening to him! How can the creature manage a reality that it does not possess? But which can be granted to it as a gift… solely through that relationship with the One who possesses it. Adam too, had he persevered in listening… would have become like God! If Israel had persevered in listening, from God it would have had that… king it desired! Israel, in fact, needed a guide, securities. God would have provided: “He would have filled its mouth” with this necessary food… But by following its own counsel, it was deceived, setting its gaze on the… king of other peoples! It did not know how to wait for God’s true gift: that “king” already announced in the Law of the covenant.

– Can you recognize in this description the features of the physiognomy of Jesus? Try to describe them.

– When does Jesus bear witness, and to whom, that he was born and came into the world to reveal this truth: his nature as “king”?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

In some experiences of infused contemplation, Rosa sees the Mother with the Child beside the divine Father. A presence that leads us to consider the nature of the bond that unites them in the Economy of Salvation and that is an existential message for her:

“I saw my Eternal Father with a smiling face, he pointed out to me a vacant place; and then Mary with my Child Jesus in her arms in the act of handing him to me…” (M.1, p. 39).

God’s Economy toward her shows a link between her life and that of Mary with the Child.

In the light of the History of Salvation, the Mother with the Child and the presence of the Eternal Father attest the reality of Mary in God, who from eternity thought of her and created her with the very high dignity of being Mother of the Son.

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 137)

CELEBRATION 39

THE LORD WILL REBUILD JERUSALEM

Introduction to the celebration

Israel has been purified; a “remnant” spared by the conquerors returns to Jerusalem. The Lord, through the mission of Cyrus, king of Persia, shows his kindness to his “faithful remnant.” He goes before Cyrus on his marches, levels the way for him, hands over to him treasures and riches so that he too may be the first to recognize his Omnipotence. He does all this out of love for Israel his chosen one, and so that all may know, from east to west, that there is no other God besides him. Cyrus has been compared by Isaiah to the Messiah descended from David, through whom God would save definitively the remnant and all the poor in heart who trust in him. He will rebuild the new Jerusalem, image of the Chosen One, Mother of the Messiah according to the promise: “Then the nations will see your Glory; you will be called by a new name that the mouth of the Lord will pronounce” (Isa 62:2).

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

THE PROMISES OF… RESURRECTION ARE FULFILLED (EZRA AND NEHEMIAH)

Reading: Ezra 1

Reflection on the Word

By the hand of a pagan king, Israel is getting ready to be reborn. Jerusalem will have its Temple again. As in the first “exodus,” this return to the homeland will be marked by humble and poor beginnings. Truly no… triumphalism; above all there are no lands or fictitious well-being to safeguard, there are no political borders, however modest, to defend and therefore no allies to seek anxiously. That “remnant” of Israel that now returns must know how to count solely on that “word” to which God had always sworn to be faithful: that is, Israel is his people, always loved. The guarantee of this promise (note the unforeseeable ways of God!) is that pagan king inspired to rebuild Jerusalem! And God’s people, this time too, must begin again… from zero: they are not the greatest among the peoples, nor the richest, indeed they cannot even be called a people.

In short, Israel exists only for that “God of heaven” whom Cyrus is compelled to confess as the only one who has given him “all the kingdoms of the earth,” but who commands him, a pagan, precisely, to build a temple in Judah.

Pay attention: Israel will now have to recover the sense of its mission, rediscover the reason for its existence.

Can you too begin to understand it?

Perhaps for us Christians too, in this generation, there is something to reflect on regarding the meaning of our life: were we created to seek worldly securities?

To defend earthly properties?

To devote ourselves to political or social compromises in order to survive somehow?

Or perhaps we too have forgotten the dignity of our baptism, which made us children of the “God of heaven” and therefore “heirs” of great “heavenly” properties?

Do we too not run the risk that from the new paganism there may come to us that command to rebuild, in the midst of this society, the temple to the true and only God, Lord of life and of history, Provident, Judge of the destiny of all peoples?

Is there not the danger that precisely the pagans may be inspired to feel the longing for the “infinite”?

And we, “foolish” children of light, still concerned with envying “those kingdoms of the earth,” which have not at all filled the lives of the children of darkness!

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

The Bible, and above all the psalms, are woven with the religious experience of the Power of God, of his interventions that free and protect.

This finds confirmation in Israel’s broad religious experience, sung in various psalms, in which Almighty God is acknowledged, praised, adored, thanked with terms that symbolize his Presence with the “right hand”: “… with your right hand you have been my support, multiplying your kindness toward me”; “… your right hand is full of justice…”; “… the right hand of the Lord has done wonders” (Ps 18:36; 48:11; 118:16).

Related to what is exalted in the Psalms is also the mystical experience that Rosa has on October 13, 1869:

“… I made the Holy Exercises, from the first day, the Eternal Father, … I was in my cell, in contemplation, … he stretched out his right hand to me and gave me infinite graces.”

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, pp. 42-44)

CELEBRATION 40

THE LORD GIVES COURAGE TO THE PEOPLE

Introduction to the celebration

Connected with the rebuilding of the Temple are other words of consolation from the Lord, spoken through the prophet Haggai.

He gives courage to the people according to the word of the Covenant, and assures the presence of his spirit in the midst of the people. He points out that the future glory of the Temple will be greater than that of former times and that he will give peace. Another word spoken through Isaiah is being fulfilled for Jerusalem: “No one will call you Forsaken any more, nor will your land be called Desolate, but you will be called My Delight, and your land Espoused, for the Lord will take delight in you and your land will have a husband. You will be a beautiful crown in the hand of the Lord, a royal diadem in the palm of your God” (Isa 62:3-11).

Israel, Jerusalem, the “remnant”—daughter of Zion—are personified in Mary, who stands out among the humble and the poor of the Lord, who with trust await and receive salvation from him (LG 8, 55).

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

The… “battle” begins again. Jerusalem will be rebuilt, but in “times of distress” (Dan 9:25). But one thing is judged immediately necessary: the resumption of worship.

Reading: Ezra 3

Reflection on the Word

This had also been the great insight of King Josiah (we meditated on it in 2 Kgs 23): to revive the commitments of Israel as a people of the covenant. To give back its due place to that God too often forgotten or, worse, despised. The only one who, instead, had always loved and listened, at every moment, to the cries of his people. He alone!… Now, then, the weeping, the emotion. The new foundations are a reality.

Nostalgia for the past, regret and bitterness for what had not been sufficiently appreciated and which now, with tender mercy, the “good” God grants. Joy and gratitude for this ally who wants to be once again the “gracious” God he has always been. It is no longer possible to distinguish the feelings that animate the heart of this “remnant.”

Do you know that many great saints have begun to live again precisely from here, like Israel?

From the experience of their ruin, they found strength and courage solely in the grace of God, so as to reach sublime heights of holiness.

Do you know any of them?

– And you, have you ever experienced this “goodness” of God?

– When, above all after having ignored or neglected him, perhaps for many years, you realize that he is the only one who does not abandon you, indeed that he is the only one who can help you to rebuild your life… from nothing?

– Do you understand the “charism” of the Movement?

– To give back to your life the certainty that God exists, that he is good, that you can hope in him. That in Christ you too have been forgiven and that all the graces necessary for your salvation are there, ready to be given to you, if you want?

– But it is necessary that you, like that “remnant” of Israel, no longer lean on your own plans for life.

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“… suddenly a rapture so strong and I found myself in spirit in a church where my Good had been exposed during the day. I saw the church all lit up, resplendent with light, an infinity of Angels adoring their God, my Beloved! I saw all the doors closed and I found myself alone; I approached the Tabernacle and a crowd of Angels were there, a light so bright dazzled me. I saw my Beloved of an immense beauty, a fire was burning in me…” (M 1.1, p. 66).

Carried away by ecstasy, she finds herself several times adoring him in the chapels of the Institute or in one of the many churches where he dwells among human beings and unites them with the Heavenly Church. In them, amid a splendor that transcends all natural brightness, she sees the Angels adoring and is also admitted to the vision of Paradise.

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 96)

CELEBRATION 41

ISRAEL MAKES THE CRY OF THE PROPHETS ITS OWN

Introduction to the celebration

Israel had learned from experience, and above all from the word of the prophets, the importance of faithfulness to the Lord. In moments of calamity, in order to obtain mercy, it makes its own the cry of the Prophets of its time or of those who preceded it: “… before the fierce anger of the Lord comes upon you, all you humble of the earth, who keep his commands, seek justice, seek humility, that you may be sheltered on the day of the Lord’s anger” (Zeph 2:2-3). Thus only the “poor” escape the wrath of the Lord, those who have been faithful to trust and hope in God. For the faithful “remnant” a day is announced when the Lord will be in its midst a mighty Savior. The Lord will be right in its “womb.” The restored city points to the Daughter of Zion, image of Mary who carries the Savior in her womb.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

The religious reform of Ezra and Nehemiah meant for the “remnant” of Israel recognizing that its history, like that of all the kingdoms of the earth, would have closed for good if God had not inspired Cyrus and then encouraged Darius (Ezra 6:12), and then Artaxerxes (Ezra 7:11), pagan kings, to give back a land to that people who had once served the “God of heaven.” Israel, from the manifestation of this goodness of God, is… forced to see its own misery and to confess that, because of its continual stubbornness against the plans of peace of its God, its land is now in the hands of foreigners!

Reading: Nehemiah 9

– You can notice how every penitential celebration of Israel begins with a “fast” and with a “look” at its own history. The first affirmation of this “creed” of theirs is to confess, first of all, that there is only one Lord, creator of heaven, the only one who chose Israel to be a witness, in history, of his presence.

– When you recite or, better, confess the apostolic “creed,” are you aware of witnessing to the world a history of salvation? Or do you think you are listing a “catalog” of abstract truths learned by heart?

– Are you aware that every true penitential act always begins by acknowledging that God has been “ready to forgive, gracious and merciful,” and therefore, are you truly ready, like that “remnant,” to judge your history a… “failure,” had the Lord not shown himself to you?

Personal reading of the book of Tobit

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“While I was lying face down on the ground, my forehead against the floor, my arms outstretched in the form of a cross, the Eternal Father, joy of my soul, said to me: take comfort, for you will have all that you ask of me” (M 1.1, p. 78).

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 47)

RETREAT 8

THE REMNANT FOLLOWS THE LORD

Introduction to the celebration

The experience of exile is very harsh, it crushes spirits, but it also purifies. The life of a small “remnant” is entirely directed toward following the Lord, seeking him and possessing him. The three young men, of whom the prophetic text offered for our meditation speaks, are the best sacrifice that can be offered to God. From their extreme consistency between faith and life springs the prayer that reveals a great hope in the God who cannot abandon them to the extreme consequences, but who will surely save them because he has promised the coming of a Messiah who will take on the fate of Israel. The appeal addressed to God to assert his glory and his lordship attests faith in the one Lord, God glorious over all the earth.

Lauds

Introduction to the Word

We can reflect on these beginnings of… resurrection. Israel would no longer exist. This is the reality denounced by the exile. It has nothing left. But God watches over this “nothing.” The prophets, above all Ezekiel, starting from this once again humiliating situation, will educate toward hope. Hope must now be founded solely on that “word” of God, the promise made to the descendants of David. No power, no ability, no human means… because everything is lost or destroyed: “we have no prince, no leader, no prophet, no sacrifice, no place to… find mercy.” Once again we will have to return to trusting… solely in God, we will have to open the heart to this trust: God will return… he will free… he will save! It will be necessary at this moment to reflect on the past, on the many divine interventions: was not Isaac a fruitful blessing, unhoped for, for a sterile and dead womb? And was not the exodus the liberation of a people unable to live in freedom, incapable of giving itself a history? a future?

And who brought them into that “land” inhabited by “giants,” making its conquest possible for a non-warrior people, come out of a “retreat” of forty years in the desert?

Who had prepared the gift of that king, pleasing to the heart of God, father of the Messiah, in the loins of that foreign, poor, widowed woman? Again now God is preparing his people in a poor womb without land. “Do not fear, little worm Israel!”

That small “remnant” will have trust, will hope… “against all hope.” Always so… It will have to wait. But it will see the dawn of rebirth. But how many conflicts? How much toil? “If you come forward to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for trials… do not lose heart… accept whatever happens to you: at first he will lead you through winding ways… you will have fear and dread… you will be tormented by his discipline… tested by obedience… but then you will possess the secrets of God” (Sir 2:1-9 and 4:11-18).

They begin to build again… but “harassed by fear of the local peoples” (Ezra 3:3) “who discouraged the Jews and troubled them to keep them from building” (Ezra 4:4) “stirring up imperial officials against them” (Ezra 4:5). Indeed, sending to Cyrus’ successor, Artaxerxes, a slanderous letter against the “rebellious and wicked city” (Ezra 4:12), which will bear its bitter fruit: “the work was stopped by force of arms” (Ezra 4:23). Through the encouragement of the prophets, it will be possible to foil injustice and lies (Ezra 5:1-2 and 6:7.14) and resume the building of Jerusalem.

But with what toil! The enemies grow angry: they will have to “post guards” and build holding the trowel in one hand and the sword in the other! (Neh 4:1-11). Then the scandal of usury appears among the exiles (Neh 5:6-7).

Indeed, despite the severe reforms, attempts at corruption and favoritism creep in even among the priestly classes themselves (Neh 13)!

Reading: Daniel 3:25-45

Reflection on the Word

Tribulations, then, from every side, as Paul would warn, so that it may be known that the extraordinary power of this “rebuilding” comes from God and not from presumed human abilities. So here too: “countless journeys, dangers from my own people, dangers from Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the desert… dangers from false brothers, toil and hardship… And apart from these things, there is the daily pressure on me, the anxiety”… for this “remnant” with which God wants to restore his people (2 Cor 4:7-9 and 11:23-28).

CELEBRATION 42

THE PRAYER OF TOBIT

The prophetic prayer of Tobit anticipates what will be said through the centuries, more explicitly by the Prophets, about the future of Jerusalem, designated by the name Zion: “Sing and rejoice, Daughter of Zion, for see, I am coming to dwell among you. Oracle of Yahweh” (Zech 2:14).

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

GOD PROTECTS HIS “REMNANT” (books of Tobit, Judith, Esther)

This “remnant” will no longer be the nation of Israel. The exiles belong to the tribe of Judah and will form the “community” of Jerusalem. There will be no more idolatry: God now reigns over this “remnant” as true prince of Judah. The Mosaic Law becomes the soul of the community: its civil and religious code. The government will be priestly and the high priest remains the head of a people that is distinguished from other peoples by a special and exclusive worship. In short, a small theocratic state! Once the material and religious rebuilding is finished (around 400 B.C.), the Jewish community will have two centuries of tranquility. Neither the Greek hegemony of Alexander the Great nor that of the Ptolemies of Egypt will disturb this “remnant,” which seems to be guarded by its God. (Compare what Achior will say to Holofernes: Jdt 5:21). Only under the Seleucids of Syria, who will want to meddle in the internal affairs of Jerusalem, and through the influence of Hellenism on some corrupt priests, will the fierce persecution of Antiochus Epiphanes break out. In 167 B.C., the statue of Jupiter will be set up in the Temple. The daily sacrifice will cease and idolatrous worship will be imposed on pain of death. But God will not abandon his “remnant.” The theocracy will survive, certainly purified, but giving splendid pages of heroism: it will be the era of the Maccabees.

Before these, however, which will conclude the historical books, leading us to the threshold of the coming of Jesus, there are still three small books that can help us understand the way of life of this “remnant.” They are men, or women, who have come to simplicity of heart. They have rediscovered the fear of God. They live in the “shadow of his wings.” They are certainly aware of their weakness; they know the dangers of a pagan world, often hostile, always… at the door; but they sense that Yahweh can save them from every danger. The first of these books is full of this trust in divine providence:

Tobit.

Reading: Tobit 13

Reflection on the Word

A prayer that confesses the eternal kingship of God. This is what history has taught them. The tragedies that have passed had only a medicinal purpose, because God “brings back up from the great perdition.” Their exile, that being put at the mercy and in the power of their enemies, is to make it possible to proclaim the greatness of God. From those foreign borders Israel will return, it will be gathered by the mercy of the One who alone is God, sole Lord of history.

The exultation that wells up spontaneously from the heart of this prayer is the fruit of that hope which sees in rebuilt Jerusalem, once more, the gift of peace, of God’s kindly presence in the midst of his people, of a joy that will have no end.

– What do you mean by “divine providence”?

– As you meditate on these last events of Israel: end of the monarchy, exile, return and rebuilding of the Jewish community, do you notice similarities with your own concrete life?

– Are you among the blessed: those, that is, who rebuild Jerusalem, who want it to be a “sign” of peace for all generations, who weep over its misfortunes, but who rejoice when it becomes again a place of joy and welcome for all peoples? Or are you instead indifferent to the existence of this holy city, figure of the Church, tearing it down with your sins, with your refusal of a serious conversion “with your whole heart and your whole soul”?

– In short, do you feel responsible, as St. Peter says (1 Pet 2:1-9), for this spiritual building into which you too are called to be fitted as a “living stone”?

CELEBRATION 43

JUDITH ENTRUSTS HERSELF TO GOD

Judith is presented by the Bible as the type of the Jewish woman. She represents the idealization or personification of the people of Judah; she is its type and figure. A woman in the fullness of her mature femininity, entrusted to God and victorious. Yet in the OT everything is in the lyric of expectation, everything awaits its completion in the NT, in her who will possess all the mature aspects of the Woman, personification of the faithful people, who will deserve to become, by the power of the Holy Spirit, Mother of the eternal Word.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

In the book of Judith too, God’s caring concern for this “remnant” appears. In this woman, her ardent faith and the effectiveness of her prayer are exalted. But also the witness of a chaste, reserved life, ready to serve, when God’s provident presence is called into question. These are characteristics of the post-exilic community. In the spirituality of the “remnant” the certainty is forming that God will do great things with those… “poor” and “little” ones. Will this not be the attitude in which we shall find Mary?

Reading: Judith 8:9-36

– Many times, on the journey through the desert, the people are demoralized by the lack of goods necessary for life and… immediately cry out against the authorities!

– Does this not seem to you the common attitude in our own time too?

– What are the realities in your life that demoralize you?

– When has God tested your patience?

– In what episodes of your life have you doubted the existence of God?

– How many times have you too, exasperated, let yourself be overcome by murmuring, by judgment, by criticism?

– The example of Judith, who invites us to calm and to trusting expectation of the salvation that God will surely bring, but in the times and ways that please him, does it not recall to your mind the constant attitude of Jesus, “meek and humble of heart”? Virtues that he himself wants his disciples to learn and put into practice?

– What attention do you give to this divine teaching? You can judge it by how you thank God when you are put to the test.

CELEBRATION 44

ESTHER, FIGURE OF TRUST IN GOD ALONE

God intervenes through Esther to carry forward his plan and save the people at a moment of extreme danger. She exposes herself to danger trusting in God alone. Esther too, then, is a figure or type of faith and trust in God alone, as her prayer attests, a model of humility and abandonment. As a woman, type of the people of God, she rises above history and prepares the expectation of the fulfillment of the Woman blessed among all women.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

Esther too is a figure from the period of the exile. And in this story too there is a background of suffering, of trial. Here too the spirituality of the poor will be able to sing exultation at having seen the liberating intervention of God.

On the eve of the tragedy that is about to fall upon the exiled Jews, let us listen to the prayers of Mordecai and Esther.

Reading: Esther 4:17a-17z

You will immediately notice the authentic faith of Mordecai, who confesses God’s sovereign power over all things and the knowledge that he has of the heart and the events of human beings. And you can also see how this faith is concrete, that is, how it has consequences in the daily reality of life: Mordecai cannot bow down before any human being. Even if it were the emperor Ahasuerus, at that moment lord of the world! This attitude of his, as you will have read, will lead to the edict of extermination of all the Jews. Indeed Haman, the king’s minister, in his wounded pride at not having received from this Jew the sign of absolute reverence, that is, prostration, full of anger, will want to destroy all the exiles. But read in Mordecai’s heart how much gentleness. It was not out of contempt that he refused this sign of subjection; indeed he would have humbled himself to the point of kissing the soles of his oppressor’s feet. There is no hatred. His life is illumined by this deep sense of adoration for the living God, the only Lord of the humble… of the forsaken… of the weak… of the discouraged, the savior of the desperate, as Judith had prayed. In Esther too you will have noticed this faith that is born of obedience to what she was taught: “I have heard from my birth, in the bosom of my family.”

She understands at once how suffering is a sign of a social sin, if not of Israel, then of those “enemies” who “do not know what they are doing,” blinded by pride and thirst for power, ready to do works of death. But here is the trust: God is a sure refuge for those who are alone, slaves of wickedness, oppressed by anguish.

– Compare the prayers of these figures: Tobit, Judith, Mordecai, Esther:

– Have you ever had situations similar to theirs?

– Like them, did you immediately find refuge in God?

– Like them, have you experienced divine help, liberation, his consolation?

– What do you admire most in their inner attitudes?

– What would you ask of the Lord for yourself today?

For further reflection: Psalm 3

It is true: many are our oppressors! The Jewish community, after the exile, knew this well. Only a few wanted to return. Why? Too many difficulties in rebuilding a nation practically destroyed… and many by now, perhaps well settled in temporary securities, had forgotten the divine promises and ended their lives bound only to human hopes: “I have my work, my family is well; the Chaldeans tolerate us and leave us ample room for freedom; even our prophets have recommended that we pray for the well-being of the country that receives us, that we multiply, take wives and bring children into the world… why venture on a risky journey? on projects that make no sense at all?… Can what we have already obtained not be enough for us?” (cf. Jer 29:4-7). That “remnant” which preserved quite other promises and awaited a future full of hope for plans not human but divine did not reason and hope in this way: “I have made plans of peace for you” (Jer 29:8-11).

“Salvation belongs to the Lord!”; and the exile will be the proving ground for preserving, in the midst of false gods, true worship of the living God (cf. Bar 6).

CELEBRATION 45

THE SERVANT OF YAHWEH

Introduction to the celebration

God will redeem his people to the extent that it, becoming poor and humble, places its trust in its one Savior. The one who will personify the people with the features desired by God will be the Messiah, called by Isaiah Servant of Yahweh, a mysterious figure who has precisely the characteristics of the Poor One, who expresses the tenderness of God, assures the rebirth of the people, but through an experience of suffering. Sharing with him is the faithful “remnant,” of which Anne and Joachim and their daughter Mary are part, she too glimpsed with the features of the Servant.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

With the Maccabees the theocracy that guides the Jewish community survives the terrible persecution. But with the last of the sons of the priest Mattathias, Simon, the period of enthusiastic insurrection and political independence ends. A new period will begin: that of the dynasty of the Hasmoneans, who, slowly abandoning religion, will come, through dynastic quarrels, to provoke the intervention of Rome and the accession to the throne of Judah of a ferocious Idumean: Herod. We are at the threshold of the times of Jesus. The prophecy of Isaiah (6:11-13) seems thus to come true.

Israel will be devastated; only a tenth part will remain. If it is true that the tribe of Judah had long since absorbed those of Benjamin and Simeon, Judah would be that “tenth part” of the people who, because of God’s promises made to David, to preserve a descendant for him, will manage to return from exile, re-forming that “remnant” which, though tried again by destruction and division, will see the Messiah and finally know salvation! It will be important to note in the books of the Maccabees, besides the historical events, some theological teachings:

Reading:

1) Creation out of nothing: 2 Macc 7:28.

2) The resurrection of the body: 2 Macc 7:11ff and 14:46.

3) Sacrifice for the dead: 2 Macc 12:43.

4) The efficacy of the prayer of the saints for the living: 2 Macc 15:12-16.

Edifying are the accounts that bear witness to the heroism of faith of some of the faithful, which reaches the fullness of Abraham’s: ready to lose everything in order to obey the will of God, who does not want death but assures victory over it and promises precisely the resurrection of the body and eternal life. These truths are confessed clearly by the Jewish community in this period.

CELEBRATION 46

ST. ANNE, MEMBER OF THE “REMNANT”

Introduction to the celebration

The one who realized in her life the features of the “Servant” of Yahweh prophesied by Isaiah was undoubtedly also St. Anne. As a special member of the chosen people, she was found worthy of a privileged union with Mary, and through Mary, with the history of Salvation. Therefore we contemplate her for her persevering waiting, among those who with prayers, sighs and tears prepared the coming of the Messiah.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

With the Maccabees the history of Israel ends. Begun with the call of Abraham, it ends… unfinished with that small “remnant” awaiting the “fullness of time.” But of that “remnant,” who was awaiting the “gift”? For without the gift of God all time, all history is empty! Abraham had received the promise of descendants. Yet he did not see them. Indeed, he was ready to sacrifice Isaac, the first fruit of that posterity.

How was it possible? Either God was a liar or the promised gift far surpassed a purely material posterity. Abraham therefore “saw” a different horizon… And so Moses, from the top of Mount Nebo, certainly saw other boundaries, different from those that limited the future Palestine… This faith, as we have seen in meditating on some pages of the Maccabees, found concrete expression in affirming the “resurrection” of the body and the possession of an eternal “glory”: like that of God! But judging from the history of Israel, not all had this faith of Abraham, or rather, that God revealed to him and to all those who would welcome his way. Already with Moses, and this too we have seen, how many died in the desert? They wanted to go back, rather than lean on that “word” which promised, after that tormenting journey, a land flowing with “milk and honey.” And those who reached the threshold of that land, do you remember?

How they wept because of the presence of those “seven” nations, so powerful! They were forced to wander sadly until death in that desert, again for not having had trust. But the new generation of Israelites who in the end, with Joshua, conquered that land, was no better than their “fathers.” Soon it abandoned the covenant with the living God and began those painful, illusory alliances with the gods of the conquered nations.

This drama will run through all of history… even our own!

We grow tired of waiting, of suffering the desert, of walking… on. We fix our gaze on immediate rests, on riches within reach.

We balk when we do not see clearly. We fear that tomorrow which we do not now possess. In short, Israel does not believe in that “impossible” of God which made Abraham and all his true children walk. Who saw, that is, that “day” of the resurrection which is precisely the gift promised by God: Jesus! The “remnant” in the time of Jesus, we know, has lost its ancient splendor as a theocratic “community”; it is fragmented into various groups and institutions: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, Sanhedrin, synagogues, with a narrow conception of nationalistic messianism that excludes the “nations” or pagan peoples. Who truly had kept the faith of Abraham? Who truly, like him, was ready in his heart to obey in everything the will of God, revealed in that “Law,” which became, for the steps of the just, a light in the darkness? Who had understood that “impossible” of God who constantly wanted to pour out rivers of living water on a desolately arid land? Who in his heart nourished hope in this latest “visit” of the Most High? Too great was that awaited “gift,” the conclusion of a whole “speaking” of God to the human being. Equally great attention was required in listening. This too we have seen, though briefly. The events of life… distracted Israel! Only very few understood what the Prophets taught to await: a “new heart.”

The human being, in order to become obedient to God, needed a radical change. The unheard-of, “impossible” gift… that God would become man and that deadly disease be finally stopped, which made man unable to rise from his darkness and to love the One who had loved him with an “eternal love.” That disease was stopped in the womb of Anne. In that womb, sterile but laden with expectations, with hope, turned to the impossible that came from Heaven, humanity found its original purity: Mary!

Reading: Psalm 85

Reflection on the Word

The “heaven,” then, meets the earth: mercy, that patient love which has always spoken, announcing peace for his people, for whoever wants to return to him, is the truth: those poor, sterile ones in need of salvation; those men who desired to be saved by God. Salvation is now near: “In times past, God spoke in partial and various ways to our ancestors through the prophets; in these last days, he has spoken to us through a Son, whom he made heir of all things and through whom he created the universe” (Heb 1:1-2).

“Justice and peace will kiss”

God forgives iniquity and the human being finds peace, heavenly blessing: “Peace on earth to those on whom his favor rests.” “Truth will spring from the earth…” Precisely when the human being (that… “remnant”) recognizes the poverty of his existence, the nothingness and vanity of his thoughts, of his possibilities… then from his heart will spring forth truth: that “cry” we have already known: “Remember me, Lord!” “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” “Justice will look down from heaven”: God will come down! He will bestow his good and the earth will no longer be a land of death, but will yield its fruit: the human being will again be free to love with his whole self!

RETREAT 9

GOD’S PLAN PASSES THROUGH THE LIFE OF A POOR PERSON

Introduction to the celebration

The “remnant” of Israel, rereading its own history, has discovered that God is in the last place. In Jesus, the poor one, it will understand even better God’s mysterious plan that passes through the life of a Poor One. Christ was made perfect and the source of eternal salvation precisely because he freely agreed to live as a poor man, to submit to suffering. In his earthly life, self-emptying made him last, the suffering Servant, welcomed and understood on earth only by Mary his Mother, who for this reason is the perfect model of all the poor who want to adhere totally to Christ.

Lauds

Reading: Luke 14:8-10

In search of the last place!…

Reflection on the Word

Before approaching the Prophets, the only ones who, inspired by God, know how to read history and interpret it in the light of divine revelation, in this retreat we can pause to meditate on the meaning we give to our life:

What are we looking for?

What interests us?

What are the values that truly matter to us?

How much is our relationship with God desired, wanted?

God, as we have seen, has always let himself be met there where we experience failure, nothingness or little more, in our being. The history of salvation has shown that the human being, without welcoming the divine gift, that is, the “covenant” offered from creation, does not find his true dimension, his “place,” a stable understanding of his own destiny: “our years are like a breath… seventy, eighty for the strong, yet most of them are toil and sorrow; they pass quickly and we fly away” (Ps 90:9-10) …

Where does the flow of time lead us?

Why, despite the effort to escape pain and death, does it remain true that our whole life is toil?

Where do we fly away to?

What is our future?

There is a teaching of Jesus: “When you are invited by someone to a wedding… go and take the lowest place.” This is what God did from the day he went to look for Adam in that “fear” of being “naked” (Gen 3:8-10).

Does it not seem to you that this is precisely the constant divine pedagogy? To descend to the lowest place, in order to offer the human being the gift of life?

He “came down” to Abraham, remember? A sterile old man of seventy-five!

He “came down” with Joseph… sold as a slave by his own brothers. In Egypt God waited for a family, as it grew, to find gratitude and kindly justice. But he saw that human beings oppressed and killed… he “came down” to free the oppressed who groaned in anger! And how many other times has he had to “come down” into all those “anguishes” that Israel constantly had to endure? “But he delivered them…,” Psalm 107 testifies. All the history that we have in part celebrated reminds us of this: the era of the “judges,” and then the advent of the “monarchy,” and then the tragedy: the collapse of the nation, the exile… God will return to look for the human being in that exile! Once again the last place will become a privileged place of waiting, because there God will come!

Occupying the last place seems one of the most interesting characteristics of the spirituality of the “remnant.”

Tobit is a faithful man who spends his life “walking on the paths of truth and righteousness” (Tob 1:3).

He lives as an “exile,” and yet is devoted to “many acts of almsgiving.”

For carrying out that pious duty of burying the dead, his goods will be confiscated. Having become blind through an accident, he will have to endure the humiliation of a wife who despises him.

You can sense his feelings in that prayer of lament of his (Tob 3:7-6).

Of Judith too we have admired her reserve. She comes out of her anonymity only to perform that service on behalf of her fellow citizens. She will refuse every reward, every praise… she will return to her solitude.

So it will be with Esther. Although a queen, she always considers herself a… subject. She too is ready to risk her life to rescue her people from that mortal anguish.

As for the Maccabees, perhaps we have envied their strength in faith and their readiness for sacrifice in defending that law of freedom which is the gift God made to Israel.

Therefore already present in all of these is that service which Jesus will embody in fullness in the total gift of himself and which will be the heart of his proclamation of salvation: “I have come to set the earth on fire…” (Luke 12:49-50; cf. also: Luke 22:27; Matt 20:25-28; and John 13:4-17). We are invited to a wedding, then, but of a crucified “bridegroom.” A door opens onto pastures… without end, but it is “narrow” (John 10:9 and Matt 7:13). There is a “hidden” wisdom that we do not yet know: from the “cross” comes life. One can therefore begin to sense why these “poor” risk their lives, withdraw into a discreet silence, flee the clamor, accept misery, exile, contempt… They have found again the “fear of God,” they have returned to faithfulness. And God defends them! They have sought what is no longer of the earth, but belongs to that “above” where Christ lives, riches of life. They do not flee people out of fear, therefore, but go to hide with Christ in God (Col 3:1-3).

Pay attention: of this life hidden in God, the angels too, as far as they are given to bear witness, give us confirmation. They appear in our history for as much service as they must perform on our behalf. Then they return… to God. They disappear into depths of light and life unknown to us. They are ready, that is, to enter into the presence of the majesty of God. An example is in the story of Tobit (Tob 12:15). But you can see the angels of Lot (Gen 19:12-22) with what care they bring him to safety, obeying the mercy of God. And out of mercy an angel goes to announce to Hagar (Gen 16:7-12 and 21:17). Another will go to stay the hand of Abraham (Gen 22:11-18) and to guard him in his choices (24:7). An angel will appear in the burning bush of Moses (Exod 3:2). Again an angel will speak in a dream to Jacob (Gen 31:11) and perhaps more mysteriously will wrestle with him to test him (Gen 32:25-30). Again in a dream an angel will speak to Joseph (Matt 1:20-21 and 2:13.20). There is an angel who guides Israel (Exod 14:19-20; Num 20:16; Exod 33:2 and 23:20-22). Indeed, in this last episode we can sense the… “hidden life” of the angels and the saints: “My name, says God, is in him.” The angels “possess” God, and even when the will of God that they see in themselves sends them on a mission, to human beings they appear “like God.” See the announcement to Gideon (Judg 6:11-23) and to the mother of Samson (Judg 13:3-21). So it will be also for Gabriel sent to Mary. In that announcement the angel sees and recognizes in Mary that “grace” and that “name” which he himself possesses. Life, then, is in the mystery of God, the “secret” and original source, which Christ however has revealed. Only by throwing oneself into that “mysterious last place” which he himself chose for himself and occupied is there the secret of the human being’s return to the truth of his own being.

CELEBRATION 49

THE FEAR OF GOD

Introduction to the celebration

The fear of God is not to be confused with being afraid of him, which is flight from his presence. The opponents of Christ flee from his presence. The demons too are terrified of Jesus. The divine presence is repugnant, is hated. On the contrary, for those who fear him out of love, he is “God with us,” Emmanuel, whom the Virgin conceived and bore for the salvation of the world.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Reading: Isaiah 43:1-21

Reflection on the Word

“Do not fear.” We have already spoken of the fear of God (celebration 47). It is not to be confused with being “afraid” of God, which is terror, flight from his presence. Adam goes to hide, he no longer wants to look at the face of God. On the day of judgment the damned will go away, “accursed,” from the presence of Christ the judge. They will call down upon themselves the collapse of the mountains that must hide them for good. The demons are terrified of Jesus. His presence brings them “to ruin” and they ask to disappear into the abyss, and their request is granted. An example is those swine that rush into the lake. A terror, then, that unleashes despair. The divine presence is repugnant, to be fled and hated.

Different is this “fear,” gift of the Spirit. It arises equally from the approach of God, but it is conceived as the compassionate approach of the physician to the sick person who has incurable and painful wounds.

The first impact is an impression of dismay: “Woe is me, I am doomed!” Isaiah will cry out, “for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips” (chap. 6). The prophet feels this radical “uncleanness” of his own and of the people among whom he lives as an inner tearing: the encounter with divine holiness penetrates him to the point of wounding him… but it will heal him (cf. Heb 4:12).

In the experience of Abraham too, this drama is felt: God is killing him: “Your only son, whom you love…, offer him as a holocaust!” And yet in obedience, the patriarch senses… a living: “God will provide!” A mysterious living, different, but… a living!

The prophets do not flee, do not hate this approach of God. Even if they protest, deep down they desire this presence: “Show me your glory,” Moses will cry out. Elijah will echo: “I have been zealous for the Lord of hosts…, I alone am left.” Alone in desiring that experience: the passing of the “gentleness” of God, even if through torments and… fears. It is true: of Moses too it is told that he was afraid. But it is also true that it is not he who… flees. On the contrary, he wants to draw near! God stops him, he must show him his own otherness… he commands him to… “strip himself”. Moses will have to feel his own weakness. For now he must veil his face. Later he will veil it for… the people! In revealing himself to Moses, divine holiness appears as the source and “presence” of life: “I have witnessed the affliction of my people… I have heard their cry… I have come down to rescue them!”

As later with Paul, to Moses too, because of the greatness of the revelations, a messenger of Satan will be sent to humble him: he will not enter the promised land. The leader, the guide, the intercessor cannot have a different fate from that of his people. It is God’s people, but how many times has God reminded Moses, despite the continual protests, that that people was given to him. He will have to die there, in the desert with that people, to make himself in everything one with them. The greatest of the prophets “did not receive what had been promised, since God did not want him to be made perfect alone” (Heb 11:39-40). So the letter to the Hebrews explains: because God has in view something better for all of us.

God has in view the holiness of his people: that is, of the whole of humanity! A work inconceivable and impossible for our strength.

But this “holiness” seduces the prophets! It kills… but it fascinates!

The prayer for the people will become bold…, a challenge: “This people has committed a grave sin. But now, if you would forgive… And if not, then blot me out of the book that you have written” (Exod 32:31-32).

“You seduced me,” Jeremiah will groan, but at once he adds: “and I let myself be seduced. A fire was burning within me that I could not, despite my resistance, hold in.” The creature… balks, resists, but deep down wants to be captured, seduced by this approach of God. As it was also for Jacob: he cannot let the angel of God go. He wants that “blessing” even though the angel strikes his hip: “You will be lame, you will no longer be able to walk where you wish. Now another will lead you where you do not wish to go.”

But the ways chosen by God will transfigure the human being and make him an intimate friend of God, like Abraham, like Israel which in its tormented history will remain nonetheless “strong with God,” because of that “blessing”! God will therefore always have to reassure: “Do not fear.” Because, frightened by his own misery, by his extreme creaturely fragility, the human being cannot understand how he can be “precious” in the eyes of the thrice-holy One! “My flesh shudders with dread of you, I fear your judgments!” (Ps 119:120). It is true: God appears in history to judge it… but not without compassion: “Remember no more the things of the past. See, I am doing something new.”

This fear will also be that of the apostles on Tabor (Matt 17:1-8). The sunlike brightness of Jesus overwhelms his disciples: prostrate and… terrified. But it is good to stay! They want to stay! They will again be seized with great fear after the miracle of the calming of the storm (Mark 4:35-41): “Who then is this?” “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” will instead be Peter’s lament after the miraculous catch of fish (Luke 5:11). Here too the inner dismay: before the miracle of the irruption of grace into our “weary and burdened” life, Peter’s instinct is to defend himself: not to flee, but to push away that divine “world,” too great, too luminous, too “good,” which risks awakening dormant longings, rekindling hopes held to be absurd… Sick eyes, however much they may long for the light, fear it because… it causes pain! Certainly this fear is not being afraid. Deep down Peter does not want Christ to go away, because his presence… is “ruining” his life… quite the contrary!

It is a lament that from the depths, because of that sudden light, lets show all the dismay, the powerlessness, the ugliness of a nature enslaved, accustomed to slavery, unbelieving about the possibility of being saved, more because of the age-old acceptance of a power that denies hope: “through fear of death (human beings) were subject to slavery all their life” (Heb 2:15), than because of the efficacy of divine grace that at last makes itself manifest through the work of Jesus.

Christ’s compassion for our mortal slavery makes him act… His mercy generates that wonder… See Nain (Luke 7:11-17). The fear of that crowd is the same as Peter’s: “Lord, you meet us who are in tears, because dead. We are not worthy to welcome you! Return to your ‘heaven’… but if you remain, if you truly visit us… we will exult!”

Of this fear of God the prophets have had experience. Of this fear they are masters. The experience of the Exodus is the event that illumines the history of Israel. It is in that marvelous liberation that Israel sensed it had been known. Someone gave a “name” to those who had none, a land to slaves. That God who made himself “near” became the strong ally of poor “scattered” ones. To this event the prophets will make constant reference in order to ground the trust that Israel… that every human being, is truly loved!

THE POOR KEEP THE PROMISES IN THEIR HEARTS

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

Hope in the living God, the absolute longing for his face, the soul’s yearning at his remembrance, have sufficiently enlightened us about that inner attitude which makes the prophets the guardians and witnesses of the Law of God, contemplated as a manifestation of his Word, of his inmost will; intuited as the approach of the divine being eager to lift up and give life to the human being.
