Reading: Psalm 119:1-48

Reflection on the Word

It will be good to complete the psalm with an attentive personal reading. We can notice at once how the prophets are in love with this Law (or precepts, or decrees, or words, or teachings). Blessed is the person who can walk, live, be enlightened by these promises: “the earth is full of the love of God.” “He is good and does good.” “His mercies, which are great, are a source of life and joy.” “Wonderful is the covenant with God.” “I belong to him, I can hope in his salvation.” “Let your face shine upon your servant.” His law then becomes a song, “in the land of my pilgrimage.”

Another reality worthy of attention: most scrupulous is the commitment to guard or keep the gift of the Law: “forever,” “eternally.” “I am consumed with longing for your precepts.” “I have seen that all perfection has its limit, but your Law has no bounds.” “I run the way of your commandments, for you have enlarged my heart.” “I remember your name in the night.” “I will lift up my hands to your precepts, which I love.” “I will never forget your word.” “How sweet to my palate are your words: sweeter than honey!” “I open my mouth, panting.”

These are heartfelt expressions of a… lover! Who intends to live in the presence of the beloved: “Hear me,” “I have begged you”; “teach me”; “never forsake me”; “I treasure your words in my heart so as not to offend you”; “show me your will”; “I want to consider your ways”; “lift me up”; “sustain me”; “direct me”; “do not disappoint me”; “bend my heart”; “give me life”; “I am ready and do not want to delay”; “in the middle of the night I rise to praise you”; “when will you comfort me?”; “it is time for you to act.”

For the life of the lover would indeed end dramatically: “I weep in sadness”; “You are my refuge and my shield.”

“I long for your salvation.”

“I am tired of suffering, give me life.”

“Like a lost sheep I wander.”

“I am small and despised.”

“May your hand come to my aid.”

“Grant me the gift of your Law.”

“Redeem me, defend my cause.”

“Let my supplication come before your face.”

“Your word consoles me in my misery.”

“If your Law were not my joy…”

“Great peace have those who love your Law.”

Not only does the lover have a yearning desire for the beloved because he has contemplated his beauty, his strength, his luminous wisdom, his faithfulness: “wonderful is your covenant!”, but above all because he himself is “small and despised,” “without life” and with no one to defend him.

But there is still another reason for him: it is hard to have to live as a pilgrim and a stranger in a world that dismays him: the powerful slander him, the proud insult him bitterly, the wicked lie in wait to ruin him, the insolent humiliate him. Oppressed by anguish and distress, besieged treacherously by persecutors, surrounded by lies, urged, tempted by the thirst for gain and by setting his eyes on vain things, he weeps for those who do not know and do not observe the Law of God.

Hence love for that living God who has drawn near to the poor and who, despite the power of insidious and underhanded enemies, shows his faithfulness, steadfast as the heavens, kindly to every generation. This is what the prophets testify: “before kings they will speak of his covenant, without fear of shame.” “To those who insult them, they will know how to give an answer.” “They will be, because of this love for the Law, wiser than all teachers and will have more understanding than all the elders.” “They will become light, therefore, for those who seek God: let them turn to them so as not to remain confused; on seeing them, they will rejoice!”

THE PRESENCE OF GOD IN THE PROPHETS

Introduction to the celebration

Involved with their whole lives in the mysterious initiative of God who calls them, they sense, despite all the inner tearing and the natural physical resistance that this experience provokes, that their future and that of the people to whom they are sent so urgently is projected into an “extraordinary” reality that surpasses them. Lauds

Introduction to the Word

The life that burns and shines in the inaccessible splendor of God and that comes seeking openings of welcome in the human heart truly opens the whole universe to impatience, to the desire to be freed from darkness, to that deep groaning of ours which awaits, hoping for it with certainty, redemption (Rom 8:18-25). God exists. God is creator. His is the heaven. The earth is his property. In his hands is the future of the peoples. He created Israel. And he creates the history of every human being. He alone is good and the almighty source of life.

This plan of life of his will come to fulfillment and will finally manifest his glory, loved and adored by those who will have welcomed it. For the human being can neither condition, much less hinder, the unfolding of the plan of salvation that God wills. God’s dominion is absolute.

The freedom of the human being can only be relative. Either he decides to enter docilely into the divine will and become a “good” freedom, which wills the good that God wills (and this is conversion…), or he opposes… hinders… rebels (and this is sin…), and finds death. The human being who has sinned has the possibility of correcting himself by acknowledging his own misery. “Moses calls the Lord the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. He is not God of the dead, but of the living, for to him all are alive” (Luke 20:37-38). It is Jesus’ rebuke to the Sadducees who were ironically doubting the mission of Jesus, the revealer of this event that he would accomplish in his own person: the resurrection from the dead. An event that is the foundation of Christian faith and hope. This event is historical, therefore. That is, really accomplished in a time, in a place, in a person.

An event that is the fulfillment of all those others that God, the God of the living, has accomplished in history, with concrete persons, in determined times and places. This is what the prophets announce. God exists and God reveals himself in history, manifests himself to concrete persons, involves them in a mystery of life. The prophets ground the people’s faith in the saving event of the Exodus. That too was a resurrection.

A guarantee of the nearness and kindly concern of the God of the living for the oppressed and imprisoned human being. But an event tied to promises already given to the Patriarchs. That God whom Moses will come to know is the God who knew and loved his fathers: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The prophets will constantly recall, even in the hard and dark moments, this continuity of saving events… “God’s salvation will last forever.”

“Truly the Lord has pity on Zion, on all her ruins,” as he had pity on Abraham, an old and sterile nomad. “Look to Abraham, for he was but one when I called him!” The people cannot rise again, hope, return to live unless it looks to what God accomplished with Abraham. He made of him a living man: “full of days and of good things.” God is with him and Abraham is with God!

And of Isaac, of Jacob, of Moses, of Israel… he made living ones! “Do not fear, Israel!” “Look to the rock from which you were hewn.” Abraham is a blessing. With him God created the impossible. Israel, with you too God accomplishes and will accomplish the impossible: “the ransomed will return,” “sorrow and sighing will flee.”

Why can the prophets announce all this?

Reading: Isaiah 51:1-16

Reflection on the Word

The post-exilic community, the “remnant,” will find its strength again in that “blessing” received by Abraham. It will listen once more to the “word” of the Lord and will experience his protection.

The journey of those ransomed ones, like that of Abraham, will be solitary, silent, but trusting, full of exultation. Careful to guard the “Law that went forth from the mouth of the Most High,” that justice destined to be the “light of the peoples.”

The desert will become a garden! Truly, by bringing that remnant back from exile, God will accomplish another event of resurrection in the womb of his people. The prophets will be witnesses of this faithfulness of God, promised to the fathers and in part already fulfilled with them. They know that they too share in that same blessing which one day had visited Abraham. They feel invested with that same grace which transfigured Abraham. By the same experience as the Patriarch, they are “children of the resurrection” (Luke 20:36).

The prophets, like Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, “can no longer die”: they have seen and “tasted how good the Lord is.”

– Could you set side by side, underlining the analogies, the journey of Abraham and that of the “remnant”?

– What are the fears today, and who are the adversaries, that keep you from experiencing the power of salvation that God has promised to every generation?

– What kind of insult discourages you and does not let you hope?

– The message of the prophets is founded on the faith of Abraham. What makes them sure that their experience is similar to that of the Patriarch?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“Courage on the way of Calvary, if you want to arrive at being crucified with your Beloved and to die with him on the delightful bed of the Cross”; “Every new day, a new cross! Blessed is the one whose dawn breaks amid thorns and pains!”; “In paradise there is no more cross, there are no more sufferings there: only Love, Love… Be cheerful, cheerful, for Jesus likes those who suffer: whoever does not want to suffer does not want to love” (Letter to the Sisters).

(in Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 151)

CELEBRATION 53

GOD TAKES PART IN HUMAN HISTORY

Introduction to the celebration

The God who comes to the aid of human history and takes part in it is patient, “slow to anger and abounding in love.” He does not tire of reawakening the hope of his people, consoling it through the mouth of the prophets. What he announces through Jeremiah he also confirms through Zephaniah: “On that day it will be said to Jerusalem: ‘Do not fear, Zion! Do not let your hands grow weak! Yahweh your God is in your midst, a mighty Savior! He will rejoice over you with gladness, he will renew you in his love; he will dance for you with shouts of joy as on a day of festival’” (3:16-18).

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

Witnesses of the existence of God, aware of having been “hewn” from that rock which is Abraham, happy to live in that experience of mercy which is the foundation of the Covenant, the prophets become educators and formators of hope, not only for the people, not only for that generation, but for the whole of humanity. The God they confess is precisely the God of Abraham, of Isaac, of Jacob. That living God who has always sought with “eternal love” the fallen human being. A living God, they proclaim, who is never indifferent to the slavery, to the sin, which the human being, with absurd stubbornness, again and again experiences. “A wound” that always appears “incurable.” United in the same faith, the prophets become heralds of the same hope. Like Isaiah, Jeremiah too will cry out: “Do not fear, do not be dismayed, Israel!”

Reading: Jeremiah 30:8-24; 31:1-7

Reflection on the Word

This invitation not to lose trust in divine help is, then, one of the constants of the prophetic message. Even if God is forced to correct, not to leave unpunished, he still invites us not to fear: “all the oppressions will be avenged, all the humiliations will be healed.” God will always have compassion on our ruins… This is the biblical tradition: to reveal a living God, a personal God (“the God of my father”), the God who “looks down” upon the earth to raise “the needy from the dust and make them sit with princes” (Ps 113:7). The God who makes Abraham walk “in his presence in the land of the living” (cf. Ps 116:9). A God, therefore, who makes the history of the human being, of every human being, his own. Thanks to the faith of the prophets who live and proclaim a hope founded on the oath God made to the fathers, we too can glimpse that mystery which will be revealed by the angel Gabriel to Mary: the Incarnation.

We will never fully understand this eternal love of God for the human being. “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and how unsearchable his ways!” (Rom 11:33-36). “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” (Rom 8:35-37). We must grow!…

For a long time we will have to remain… in fear, before being definitively grounded in love! Truly: “in the last days you will understand it!”

– Do you feel you have “incurable wounds”? Situations from which you cannot free yourself? Do you understand that all this happens to correct you and invite you to return to God with your whole heart?

– Who are your “lovers who have forgotten you”? Have you had, or do you have, in your life realities that you would never give up because you are too convinced that you receive life from them? Do you not suspect that what you “count on so much” will one day abandon you or disappoint you or simply come to an end? What will then become of your future? In what, then, do you seriously place your hope today? If everything truly dies, can you believe that from the “ruins” a “city” can be rebuilt? In short: do you believe, do you hope, in the resurrection?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

At other times the voice of the Supreme Good becomes a perceptible form of divine help, in the manner of a true dictation of what she must write or say to people. She writes in November 1873:

“I have letters to write. Since I am an ignorant beast, he dictates to me what I must say. I am in the presence of persons, and it concerns important matters of the Work: something happens in me, it seems that within me there is a person who speaks for me, because the words come out of me without my knowing what I say. I feel and understand that they are not mine, because I would not be capable of saying them: my God, he makes the most ignorant of creatures, such as I am, speak and work” (M 4.2, p. 15f).

(Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 103)

CELEBRATION 54

THE EXPECTATION OF THE KINGDOM IN DANIEL

Introduction to the celebration

The expectation, the hope of the Kingdom, runs through the whole book of Daniel. The Lord continues to assure its coming, but it is necessary to accept the conditions he has set.

In history the divine plan is progressively made explicit. The past, the present and the future are all a message of God, if seen in his light. Whoever does not want to learn God’s pedagogy will understand it at the appointed hour, through the evidence of the facts: “You will bear a Son and you shall name him Jesus.”

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

If the “remnant” of Israel, that post-exilic community, was able to withstand all the difficulties of a return to the homeland, of a rebuilding, of a renewed faithfulness to the covenant, and if it was able to preserve peace and humility, to set out toward a “quiet dwelling,” much is due to the prophetic word that sustained that “people of survivors.” Educated by the experience of the prophets to “hope against hope,” the “remnant” returned to the journey of the origins: “My father was a wandering Aramean”… “Abraham did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body as already dead, but gave glory to God, fully convinced that what he had promised he was also able to do” (Rom 4:19-21). This journey God had blessed and exalted.

This Israel had to learn: to be the “first of the nations” would entail remaining the smallest among the peoples. A strip of land placed at the crossroads of great empires would become the “holy mountain” to which all the nations would stream to learn the ways of the God of Jacob (cf. Isa 2).

The hope of the prophets is not tied to political alliances or to programs of social renewal, but to that oath made to an old nomad by a God who does not disappoint. A true God who exalts the obedience of a poor man who does not trust in “lovers who forget” and does not fear “the insults of human beings,” but who is “strengthened in faith” believing that God alone brings to fulfillment the desires of the human being. That old man is a rock!

And he believes in a God who is… rock and refuge for the weak!

Israel will not be permitted to “commit adultery.” God does not ask of his people human glory or success. Nor expansionist aims. But to believe, to trust in his providence, to hope in everything that he promises and has power to bring to fulfillment, despite the arrogance and contempt of the powerful, the pride and blasphemy of the wicked.

Reading: Daniel 2

Reflection on the Word

Here is what Abraham saw… from afar. Here is what the prophets point to. Here is what God unveils and wants to bring to fulfillment: “a kingdom that shall never be destroyed and shall not be passed on to another people.” A kingdom that will last forever!

– What, in your opinion, are the elements worth underlining in this prophecy of Daniel?

– What is Daniel’s attitude at the news of the decree of death for the wise men of Chaldea?

– Compare with this prophecy Luke 1:30-33 and John 18:33-40 and 19:11:

– What is the substance of the angelic announcement?

– What are the truths that Jesus reveals to Pilate, even if the latter will not want to put them into practice?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

She felt herself more and more guided by God, free from the interference of anyone who did not live the Work from within. She wrote in September 1887:

“O my Love! How well you maintain and direct your Institute!… It has no need of direction. Now I understand certain things that at times made me fear, but now that nothing is hidden from me any longer, I calmly let everything go, thinking that everything is ordered by my Good. Most Holy Mary, my Mother! What a sweet thought it is for me to know that my Good himself takes care to provide, as is needed, the persons for his Work! The work that my poor head does is because he permits his slave to put in also the material toil, in order thereby to make the work complete” (M 5.5, p. 74f).

(Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 271)

CELEBRATION 55

GOD’S SPOUSAL BOND WITH HIS PEOPLE

Introduction to the celebration

Ezekiel expresses the Covenant between God and his people with the image of marriage. The people is presented as the bride of Yahweh with all the characteristics of her infidelity to the Covenant. But the Lord, after purifying her through hard trials, will return to forgive her and to renew, in his gratuitous kindness, an eternal Covenant. Israel will find strength to live, leaning on the hope of seeing one day the fulfillment of what we contemplate as accomplished in the Book of Revelation: the Covenant of the Lamb with the Heavenly Jerusalem personified in the bride, Mary—Church.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

God exists. God loves with an eternal love. God is faithful to the human being: he creates him, raises him in mercy, exalts him. But the human being does not understand. He abuses the good he has received. He is ungrateful. He glorifies his own pride rather than confess the truth: he has received everything and has no other boast than to acknowledge the gratuitousness of the loving gaze with which God always accompanies him in existence.

Reading: Ezekiel 16

Reflection on the Word

This is our story. It is the story of the human being. The prophets know how to read it. The conclusion is in that forgiveness which we all need.

For us only the remembrance of our conduct is possible. But the true meaning of our future lies only in hoping for that divine proposal of an eternal covenant.

– Do you feel your life illumined by this prophetic word?

– Do you know your betrayals?

– Do you understand the reason for some of your humiliations? Do you accept their necessary saving pedagogy?

– Do you sense how the Christian vocation is similar to the symbolic story of Israel: to become, from nothing, the object of divine delight?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

Adherence to God, through love, opens the soul to receive a new light. In the new horizon it sees clearly the holiness of God and everything in itself and in others that is out of harmony.

From this new light a tension is born that causes a suffering all the greater in that it makes the soul perceive the intensity of its natural attachments.

Here is how Rosa describes this inner dynamism, the light that illumines her and the testimony of the mercy of her Good:

“To suffer and to rejoice. Oh! how useful these lights are to me, in a flash I see everything. Oh! what I feel, how I feel myself all aflame and I set about correcting that fault with such force because it is an offense against my Good. Be silent, heartless ones, why do you offend my dear Crucified One? What has he done to you that you (offend him) so barbarously? and I feel such pain, but Jesus is silent. Through the depths of his immense mercy, he suffers and does not punish” (M 1.1, p. 140).

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 84)

CELEBRATION 56

THE PROPHET, MAN OF DENUNCIATION AND HOPE

Introduction to the celebration

The prophetic proclamation resounds in the unfolding of history, keeping the saving events in memory and making them live again by making them present. The mission of the prophets is full of communion with God and of solidarity with the people involved in particular historical events. The Prophet is the man of denunciation, of condemnation, but also of encouragement to hope in the promises of God. He is a type or figure of the Suffering Christ, who, sharing the condition of poverty of fallen humanity, carried out his mission without splendor, with gentleness and apparently with failure. But God, with his infinite power, transformed into salvation for all the failure of Jesus the Servant, with whom he associated in a unique and exceptional way his Most Holy Mother.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

A profound reality that the prophets live is that of suffering. Truly “crucified” between God and the people to whom they are sent. Their experience of God is strong. Hard too will be the experience they must face when their life bears witness to the people of the jealous and demanding love of God. For God loves. Of this they are certain. In them, therefore, there will grow sharper the pain, not so much of being mocked or rejected or put to death, but of seeing the gift of God despised and thus of being powerless witnesses of the tragedy of those whom they would have wanted to save. We can underline some aspects of this spiritual tension. Ezekiel, for example, is called by God to be a “sentinel.” He must warn the Israelites, even if… they will not listen because they are “a rebellious house”: 2; 3:16-21; 33:1-20. To be a living sign for the exiles, moreover, the prophet will have to suffer in his own flesh what will be sorrow and trial for the people: 24:15-24.

Also Hosea will be called to a singular mission: to marry a prostitute! See chapter 1. His experience (having to love an… unfaithful and good-for-nothing woman!) will become a sign of what God wants to reveal to his people: he too feels betrayed and abandoned by his people! And yet how many proofs has the God of Israel given of his tender and faithful love? See chapter 11:1-9.

Of Jeremiah, instead, it will be asked that he not marry: 16:1-13. He will live dramatically the bitter story of a stubborn and wicked people. His protests are useless: 1:4-8; 20:7-10.14-18. Despite the contempt of his fellow citizens and the attempt to kill him, Jeremiah will continue to intercede for Jerusalem: 14:11-17; 15:1-2. After the fall of the city, even amid the tragedy, he will announce words of hope: 33:1-16. He will try to stop the remnant of the population from fleeing to Egypt: 42. In vain! But Jeremiah does not abandon them!

He will go down with those rebels: 43!

Also Amos will be sent to the northern kingdom to prophesy exile for the rebellious nation. He too, a humble shepherd, will have to endure contempt and persecution: 7:10-17. He too will have words of hope: 9:11-15.

At this point we can also recall Moses. First leader of Israel, he will have to suffer the inconstancy, the rebellions of a people that does not understand its election: Exod 14:11-14; 15:24; 16:2; 17:2; 32:1; Num 11:1-2.10-15; 17:6-13; 21:4-9. Chosen to be guide and teacher, authority and mediator between God and his people, Moses will soon have to experience the toil of this mission which, in spite of everything, will bring him closer to God.

To read: Exod 17:11-13; 32:11-12.19-27.31-32; 34:8-9; Num 14:13-19; 16:16.

He will not hide from the people the demands of the covenant. Indeed he will punish every transgression severely… but constantly he will be there, close to God, to plead; there to suffer, to die for that people. In solidarity to the very end…

Reading: Sirach 2

– After reading Sir 2, try to reflect on the mission of the Prophets: Why did they have to meet so many difficulties?

Why was their experience of God not believed?

What, in your opinion, was the virtue they exercised most?

Why did the Lord permit these sufferings in their life?

Where did they find the strength to persevere?

What does the life of these men teach you today?

Is the baptism you received not also for you a call to belong totally to God, to be sent… totally to the service of human beings?

Reflect on the true meaning you give to your life.

– Were the people’s murmurings against the prophets not prompted by pride? That is, by the desire to do their own will and not that of God, which is the only benevolent will that leads to the true salvation of the human being?

– Your own resistance too to the will of God, who calls you to come out of selfishness and laziness, is it not perhaps dictated by a desire to do or carry out your own plans?

And your plans, do you really think they are the ones that will make you fully happy?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“Take comfort, you who labor for your Jesus. Ah! you are always conversing with Jesus, because in touching those sick persons with charity, you touch Jesus… In those infirm creatures Jesus is found. Ah! what a thought, my daughters! I assure you that I feel I am dying with the desire to come to be with you, to share in your works of charity…”; “Seeing Jesus in the sick, how easy the meditation on the Passion of Jesus will be for you!” (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 23-4-1867; 7-1867).

(in Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 254)

RETREAT 11

THE PROPHETS, DOCILE INSTRUMENTS OF GOD

Introduction to the celebration

The God of life and of history was the love of the Prophets. In their existence they let themselves be seduced by him, contemplated him, made themselves docile instruments to transmit his saving “interventions.” An experience woven of searching, of struggle against the multiplying of difficulties that carved in them the features of the “Servant”—Son of God who offered himself for the salvation of all, associating with his mystery of redemption his Mother, to give her to us too as Mother.

Lauds

Reading: James 4:1-10

Reflection on the Word

We have briefly meditated on the life of the prophets. Crucified between God and the human being. Careful to be a sign of communion. Masters in guiding the people toward the truth that they themselves receive from the deep and spiritual communion they have with God and sense must be proclaimed to all. Severe, therefore, in correcting all the deviations and resistance that the people commit against the covenant. If God is manifested to Israel as the only saving God, the immediate consequence of this revelation is: the smallest, the poorest among the members of Israel is loved by God. Every human being of that people is a chosen one, precious in his eyes. Therefore the prophets become indignant with those who despise or oppress or do violence to their brothers and sisters. Woe to those who, out of thirst for power or for well-being, will exploit and put obstacles in the way, especially of the weakest or the most defenseless. Let us meditate on some of their denunciations.

Against religious hypocrisy: Isa 1:10-23 and 58.

Against greed or craving for pleasure: Isa 5:8-24; Mic 2:1-3; 3:9-12.

Against every oppression: Amos 2:6-15; 4:1-5; 8:4-7; Mic 3:1-4; Hab 1:1-4.

Against wealth: Hab 2:5-11.

One cannot love God without having mercy or compassion for one’s brothers and sisters. Rebellion against God leads inevitably to indifference, to contempt, to hatred of one’s brothers and sisters.

Reflect again on these pages of Sir 3:17; 4:10; 5:1-8

– How do you receive the word of the prophets?

– What do you think of their testimony?

– Do you take your life seriously, as a response to the gift God makes you of his covenant?

– Do you know its demands?

– Or do you believe in your heart that you can go on thinking and living as you wish, as if the law of God did not exist?

CELEBRATION 57

ISRAEL, INTERMEDIARY AMONG THE PEOPLES

Introduction to the celebration

Through the prophetic image of Ezekiel, the Lord shows us the victory of life over death, which today, after the Paschal Mystery of Jesus, is evident to us. We can see in the message of Isaiah the symbol of personal and collective resurrection. Israel becomes intermediary among all the peoples and witness of the living God present in the world and in the history of humanity.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

One can notice in the message of the prophets a great bitterness when they look at the human reality: ungrateful toward God, rebellious; quick to evil, slow and inconstant in doing good… When, however, they perceive the inspirations of the Spirit of God, they immediately gather fullness of consolation and messages of hope for the people. Driven by grace, they overcome discouragement, disappointments, weariness and become heralds of ever new promises on the part of God. In fact it is he who sets them in tension toward a future that they themselves do not grasp, but, through their message, horizons open to Israel that often transcend the real life of the people, who are immersed instead in selfish attitudes. This page of Ezekiel can help us to understand somewhat the whole history of Israel. Of a people that has always longed for a land that would be the definitive blessing of God.

Reading: Ezekiel 37

Reflection on the Word

Will humanity be able to live again after its incessant tragedies?

Will the human being be able to live again after his own negative experiences?

How can we fight those passions that stir the heart of the world and lead to death?

How, seeing this body doomed to death, can I hope for a resurrection? “Lord, you know,” the prophet will answer. The divine word, creative, can accomplish in this desolate, arid land the miracle of a new life. “Behold, I will open your graves and have you rise from them, my people. You shall know that I am the Lord! I will put my spirit in you that you may live.” This is what the prophets hoped for: this day of life and peace. And this day they announced, though seeing it from… afar!

– How many times have you too doubted divine omnipotence and exclaimed: “hope has vanished, I am lost”?

– How many times, instead, like Abraham, like the prophets, have you “not weakened in faith” and, though seeing yourself “as dead,” because of the promise of God you grew strong in faith, convinced that what God has promised you he is able to bring to fulfillment?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“Holy Saturday, from the joy that my Good was pictured risen I exulted, it was something, I know not what, stronger than myself, I could not restrain myself, I would have cried out to everyone to come with me to adore my Good who, already beautiful and sweet, was walking about Risen, and to restrain the impulse a little, I began to sing loudly, but it grew in me. Beautiful things I would have wanted to write, but I was not able to grasp them in my mind.”

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 80)

CELEBRATION 58

THE WORD OF THE PROPHETS IN THE UNFOLDING OF THE PROMISE

Introduction to the celebration

The sorrowful and joyful accents of the Prophets follow the stages in the unfolding of the Promise. Even before prophesying the figure of the Servant of Yahweh, Isaiah had already announced to the people that the Lord would do away with death forever and that on that day the people would exult, saying: “This is the Lord for whom we have waited; let us rejoice and be glad that he has saved us” (Isa 25:9).

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

Stretched between earth and heaven, immersed in the passing of time, often dramatic, between bitterness and consolation; and yet driven toward a beyond that they contemplate and long for… this is Israel. Its history is summed up in this experience of its prophets. The people was educated in the end to await a… newness.

The “singers of hope” have led Israel, but not only Israel, all humanity to frontiers that already have the taste of heaven. Through their prophecy, dry bones are already stirring and stretching toward life…

But this newness of life must be awaited from above! It is important, then, as the last message of the prophets, to grasp the features of this divine spirit that will enter the world and make it live again. The prophets will turn their eyes to those last days. Perhaps without realizing it, they sketch that face which they glimpse as promised. The true and immortal greatness of the prophets is there… in those pages that sigh in advance for the gift of God’s love. Of that “Messiah,” the beloved of the Lord, son of David, who will be the Only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus!

We will fix our attention only on the four “songs” of Isaiah.

Reading: Isaiah 42:1-9

Reflection on the Word

One alone God upholds. In one alone God delights: Jesus. The fullness of the divine spirit will be the eternal possession of Jesus. Jesus will bring justice anew to all the nations, through his apostles, his Church. Across times, places and generations… Indeed he will proclaim with firmness that rediscovered right: the dignity, once lost, of being children of God.

“Bruised reeds and dimly burning wicks” will be revived. Every human being will see the light again. The nations will no longer be “islands”… Through the proclamation of the Gospel the dead will live again. Human beings, reconciled, will again have communion. Jesus will not cry out… Patient, merciful, compassionate physician of humanity, he will bend down over every misery. He will free from every oppression, from every ignorance. Error, sin, evil will be destroyed.

For this necessary, saving mission, Jesus will not fail. He will not disappoint expectations, he will not stifle the groans. Oppositions, infidelities, betrayals will not cast him down.

– After reading Isa 61:1-4: do you truly need the “teaching” of Christ to become a person of communion? Why? From what slavery do you need to be freed? And from what affliction must you be consoled? Are you able to express your faith in Jesus with… songs of praise? Or are you still in sadness because of your unbelief?

For further reflection: Psalm 33

The eye of the Lord watches over those who hope in his grace: that year of mercy which lets us know the love of Christ. It is he who frees from death and feeds all the hungry. It is not the powers of this world that give us hope… Everything was created by the word of God and he alone brings to fulfillment all the promises of good for humanity: “God so loved the world that he gave his Son” (cf. John 3:16).

We trust in his holy name: Jesus.

The name chosen by God so that the human being may hope to find life and joy again.

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

She receives beautiful instructions on the love that Jesus bears for the human being, while the human being responds poorly:

“Oh! my Beloved! Oh! Yes, I see well how much you love your creatures and how badly they respond to you. You are all love for them! A Voice answered me: yes, I love the human being immensely, and as he said this to me he drew near to me” (M 1.1, p. 152).

New lights project her toward the future.

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 69)

CELEBRATION 59

THE GENTLE AND HUMBLE MESSIAH

Introduction to the celebration

The announced Messiah reveals in his features the Servant, gentle and humble, merciful, just and compassionate, who in the “Beatitudes” sets out the program of the poor of God. Beside him stands also the Mother in whose womb he is formed and called to his mission. She personifies the “remnant” of the poor who await the Messiah. She is the daughter of Zion who herself becomes Servant of the Lord, and after having hoped with her people for the coming of the Messiah, welcomes in herself its fulfillment.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

The “remnant” of Israel, under the guidance of the prophets, slowly became aware of being the spokesperson in humanity of this good news: the human being needs an ENVOY from God, who will free him deeply from his incapacity to give himself a path of salvation. “All the divine pedagogy with Israel served to testify to it that the human being cannot approach God without his help.” Here, then, is the prophetic message of these songs of Isaiah. The tension is toward the future. The Old Testament is without meaning if it did not open to this seed of hope: God will send his SERVANT, the only one in whom he delights. This “servant,” as we saw already in the previous celebration, will by his work enable human beings to have “communion” (they will no longer be closed off from one another like “islands”), a consequence of their inner renewal, freed from the ancient fears and ignorance, wounds of that “original sin” that shut human beings into a dark life, without meaning, prisoner in a terrible jail: death!

Let us now see another aspect of this “servant.”

Reading: Isaiah 49:1-9

Reflection on the Word

At once the invitation to listen!

And this is addressed above all to the “islands” and to the “distant nations.”

Not only to those people closed in selfishness and in the presumption of being self-sufficient, but also to all those communities, nations, peoples, entirely far from God. The pagans, in short. All those generations that do not know God, that have not yet received that good news which Israel, after all, even if unfaithful, has always kept: God exists, God has revealed himself in history, God has always loved his people. “Can a mother forget her infant?… Even if these were to forget, I will never forget you” (Isa 49:15-16). Every human being, therefore, every people, must come to know this ENVOY or PROMISED ONE of God who possesses the divine spirit and who is known by God from his mother’s womb. Protected by God, his mouth will be God’s own mouth, his own word. Upon him the divine glory will appear. Through resistance, toil, failure, he will lead not only the chosen people, but all the nations, toward light, truth, life. Precisely because of his constant trust in God, in the end he will triumph.

One cannot fail to see in this prophecy what the mission of Jesus will be: he came “to serve” (Mark 10:45); from his mother’s womb predestined to reign over Israel and over the nations as SAVIOR, a NAME pronounced by God for him: Jesus (= God saves). For this reason GREAT and… SON of the MOST HIGH! (Luke 1:31-33). A service that will CONSUME him; but it will not be lost: God will reward him, manifesting to him his own glory: that splendor of the resurrection which will raise Jesus above the heavens, revealing him to all human beings for what he was from the beginning of the world: the ONLY-BEGOTTEN SON OF GOD!

– Can you make your own that desire of Jesus to await the reward from God alone? Or do you perhaps fret too much, seeking esteem or affection or understanding from others?

– For what right do you fight? What claims are you looking for?

– What does Jesus mean by “my right is with the Lord”? And can you say the same of yourself? What do you think it means?

– How was Jesus a “light to the nations”? How are you? Or how do you think you should be?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“I found myself near the Side of my Beloved. Oh! what I felt at finding myself so near that volcano of love! Oh! how painful life seems to me! O my dear Beloved, ah! let me remain with you and not have to return to this miserable earth! O sorrowful exile! when will you end?

But at once I recovered myself and said: No! to live in order to suffer! O my dear Beloved! forgive me if I have such a thirst to be taken from this valley. But no! I repeat, to suffer! Exquisite is the honey of your sweetness: how could I not remain famished? I suffer, and I feel that this miserable creature writhes, struggles…; but no, dear Jesus! it will stay still, with your help, on the cross, suffering and languishing for you…

O my Beloved, your love consumes me; I feel burning in me a devouring flame that burns and consumes me, a continual spasm that I can no longer bear; but I do not suffer, because the joy I feel, so delightful, is without equal… Satisfy me, for pity’s sake, with your love!” (M 1.1, pp. 42-44).

(in Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 138)

CELEBRATION 60

THE SERVANT RESTORES COMMUNION BETWEEN GOD AND THE PEOPLE

Introduction to the celebration

The Servant is a faithful disciple of Yahweh, who welcomes the plan of salvation with a transparent heart and makes it his own. The Servant has no other plan than that of his God. The people shares in his very life. He exists to restore the communion of Israel with its God. The faith and hope of the “remnant” is centered on the expectation of this One who consumes himself and gives himself entirely for love of his people and of every human being. Of this privileged portion of the people, which did not want to yield to distrust, to bewilderment, to sorrow, are part Saints Anne and Joachim, parents of Mary, Mother of the Servant, Redeemer and Savior of humanity.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

The glory of Jesus, his splendor as Son of God that shines upon all the darkness of the world and upon every despair and sin of human beings, is a reason for trust on every path of redemption. How many times Jesus had to confirm the doubts, the fears, the laziness or the cowardice of the apostles, throughout his earthly journey as “servant of God,” with those truly consoling words: “Do not be afraid… Have faith in God and in me! Do not be afraid… I have conquered the world! Do not be afraid… the prince of darkness has no power over me!” Jesus was able and is able to lead back to life and will always be able to bring out of the darkness or make “the land rise again” by restoring its “ruins,” because in him alone is the Father’s delight. He alone possesses “all power in heaven and on earth” to “console his people” and “have pity on the afflicted.” He has that word sharp as a sword which commands and makes everything exist, he says to the dead: “Come out… come forth” and these… “will no longer hunger or thirst.” On this “servant,” on the victory of this “envoy,” the eyes of all humanity are turned. Let us listen to where Jesus will draw so much wisdom and that light capable of instructing, comforting, defending that right of the human being to become again the image and likeness of God.

Reading: Isaiah 50:4-11

Reflection on the Word

Jesus knows the Father. He is profoundly united with him. “For the Father loves the Son and shows him everything that he himself does, and he will show him greater works than these…” (John 5:20). He can do nothing on his own, but judges and acts according to what he hears from the Father (John 5:30), because Jesus has always sought and fulfilled the will of the one who “sent” him! For this reason he is “meek and humble of heart”: he has no need to defend himself, to use violence: God helps him! Every day, every moment, unceasingly. Jesus is enveloped in the Father’s love: he is close to him, he does him justice.

It is pleasing to Jesus to listen to, to welcome this strong, loving presence of the one who sends him so that the discouraged may find the way again. How important it is for those who seek God, for those who are without light, to hope in Jesus, who does not tire of pointing out to all the place of rest.

For personal reflection read John 5; Isa 49:1-7 and Ps 31

This third song of the “servant” also invites you to faithful listening.

“Morning by morning he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.”

– Are you aware of this necessary and vital work for every human being: listening to God? Why, in your opinion?

– Why does the “servant” not “resist”?

– Are you afraid or ashamed of humiliations? And yet in the psalm the one who prays is seriously tried: in what?

– Jesus too was severely tried: why was he not put to shame?

– Does suffering scandalize you?

– After the experience of Jesus and that of the psalmist, do you still think that you can avoid anxieties, sorrows, loneliness, marginalization, oblivion or any other trial in your life?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“It is sweet to suffer for the Beloved!” “Why do I not possess all the sufferings that there are in the world?”; “To live without suffering is to die”; “In suffering there is a sweetness so great that I do not know how to express it”; “To suffer, to suffer! you are too sweet to me for me not to burn with desire to possess you!”; “My Good, you know that suffering is my sweetness, my life is suffering, because in suffering I feel more and more your life and your strength”; “My God, to suffer with you, to die for you!”; “O my Jesus, Savior, my dear and lovable Spouse! then you alone, for you.”

(in Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 153)

CELEBRATION 61

THE HUMILIATED SERVANT HOPES IN GOD

Introduction to the celebration

With the fourth song of the Servant of Yahweh we find ourselves before the culminating moment of the revelation of the Old Testament. The Servant, presented to us with royal traits in the first song and with prophetic characteristics in the second and third, is portrayed in the fourth as despised and abandoned by human beings, immersed in sorrow and a victim of injustice. Nevertheless he continues to hope in the response of his God. Fully trusting in the Promises, he takes refuge in him, from whom he obtains a precious inheritance. In him, son of Mary of the lineage of David, the promise made to Abraham of a fruitful and perennial life will be fulfilled.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

The “servant” reveals God. “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), Jesus says to Philip. Jesus is therefore the fulfillment of the divine promises: in him ETERNAL LIFE is “heard,” “seen,” “contemplated,” “touched” (1 John 1:1-2). The source of all life, visible or invisible, the fountain of all fatherhood in heaven and on earth, “that which was from the beginning,” has become… palpable, present, near, adorable, luminous. This LIFE becomes rest after every toil, refuge from so many oppressions. But why was this LIFE not welcomed? Why did he spend “his strength” in vain? Why must Jesus be prostrated in sorrow, disfigured by the contempt and rejection of human beings? The prophecy of the fourth song can enlighten us by describing the gravity of our situation.

Reading: Isaiah 52:13-15; 53:1-12

Reflection on the Word

Truly great is the sin of the human being!

Truly thick are the shadows of ignorance. Anguishing the loneliness, dark the seductions of the “evil one,” author of death.

“We all had gone astray.” Deceived, wounded, swept away by false lights, violated by hatred, how could we understand love, peace…

How could we find the way back… how above all could we desire to see the face of God again?

It was “necessary” that the “servant” go down into the depths… into the “netherworld” of our inner torment. “My God, why have you abandoned me?” (Ps 22:2)

Jesus made his own the experience of our sin, he made himself distant from God to make himself close to us. Offering himself in atonement, he truly freed us from a horrible prison. How could we esteem such a gift?

How, for us who were dead, was it possible to recognize life?

But this is the sign of Jesus’ love: he handed himself over to death for all of us; he let himself be humiliated, silently, so that we might be freed from our iniquity.

And for us sinners he interceded and… intercedes unceasingly:

“Father, forgive them, they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).

– The suffering of the “servant” reveals the hardness of the human heart, wicked and rebellious against God. Can you see your own hardness when you are indifferent to the sufferings of the world? When you are dominated by instincts of selfishness, laziness, sensual pleasures? Do you believe that hell is spared you because Jesus offered himself for you in atonement?

– There is no greater love than that of one who offers his life in service of others, especially of the most wicked. Are you convinced that this “kind” of love, which is the truth of our being, Jesus has made known to all of us? That this is the only love capable of saving? Do you believe that eternal life lies precisely in communicating with this “kind” of love that Jesus offers us today in his word and in his sacraments?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

As in the Old Testament the Covenant between God and his people was founded on the sacrifice of animals immolated and their blood sprinkled on those defiled purified them, so the new Covenant is founded on the blood of Christ. In him, in fact, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, our consciences are cleansed from dead works to serve him in holiness and justice (cf. Heb 9:14).

Rosa lives the mystical experience of this mystery of the economy of salvation. She sees several times in vision the ransom of her sins.

“… For a long time… he made me see two books… In them were written certain names and then Saints, at the end my name was written large and then Saint, written conspicuously; in the other, which was large, were my sins, more than half was written and I saw them all canceled with the Blood of my Dear Redeemer…” (M 1.1, p. 5).

The “precious blood of Christ, as of a spotless, unblemished lamb”

(1 Pet 1:18f) is a symbol of redemption (cf. Matt 26:28). The beginning of Rosa’s conversion is marked by this symbolic presence of the Blood of Christ. She is purified by the blood to deserve to be among those who “have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb; they stand before the throne of God and worship him day and night in his temple” (Rev 7:14f).

Her life passes through the experience of the shedding of blood and remains as a precious testimony of the incommensurable value of the “blood” of Christ in his redeeming action.

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, pp. 49-50)

RETREAT 12

THE HOLY SPIRIT ANIMATES OUR HOPE

Introduction to the celebration

Our hope is a progressive penetration into the total and definitive yes of Jesus the Redeemer and of Mary the co-redemptrix. The Holy Spirit will make us live buried in his death and resurrection. We are called to live the Passover of the New and Eternal Covenant, in which the promises made to Abraham and to his descendants are fulfilled, and the Presence of the Spirit is announced, of the One who will guide us toward the full understanding of the Kingdom of God while we watchfully await the fulfillment of another promise: “… when I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back again and take you to myself, so that where I AM you also may be” (John 14:3).

Lauds

Introduction to the Word

The Old Testament concludes with these prophecies. Israel’s sun has set. Even the “remnant” has disappeared. Humanity will disappear and history will one day no longer have meaning. Everything would be in vain if the features of that divine face had not been sown in the heart of the world. The face of Jesus is the light that shines, the burning bush that is not consumed, the bright day that never sets again. The Messiah was sighed for, awaited. That Messiah has come: blessed are our eyes, which can now gaze upon him, and blessed our ears, which can hear his words. It is Jesus who announces the fulfillment of history. Time has become new, “full,” overflowing with life. The empty flow of events is now overwhelmed by an announcement: “Do not seek the living one among the dead!” The New Testament fulfills the hopes, the sighs, the desires of a whole humanity, poor, afflicted, oppressed, in darkness… That Easter morning inaugurates a new creation. Let us listen:

Reading: Luke 24

Reflection on the Word

REMEMBER!

Is it important for us too to remember these events? It was necessary that Jesus be crucified and then rise!

The prophecies had announced it. We cannot remove evil from our heart. Only a just one, truly such, could have this power: “to lay down my life in order to take it up again” (John 10:18). Those words (the Easter announcement) seemed like raving! They did not believe.

– How important do you too consider the announcement that Jesus is risen, alive, a lover of human beings, desirous of communicating his immortal life?

– How many times have you not believed, and perhaps still do not believe, the testimonies of those who have seen Jesus… alive in their own life?

Peter returned full of amazement at what had happened!

– What do you think of the resurrection? Of the immortal life inaugurated by Jesus?

– How do you welcome this event into your existence?

– For you, did it really happen?

Their eyes were prevented from recognizing him!

– Why? Why are your eyes veiled?

They stopped, looking downcast.

– Why the sadness in your life?

– Are you too “standing still”?

– Without enthusiasm?

– Do you let yourself go?

– We were hoping… but!

– How strong is your hope?

– How tenacious is your desire to seek the truth, to want to meet the one who lives?

He interpreted to them what referred to him in all the scriptures.

– How much do you know of the life, of the work of Jesus, revealed in the Sacred Scriptures?

They urged him: stay with us.

In his name, repentance for the forgiveness of sins would be preached to all the nations.

– Are you convinced that you are in sin, unable to see the light, unaware of the presence of the Spirit who wants to clothe you with vital “power,” and therefore that you too are in need of forgiveness and of a journey back to God?

Seriously:

– Do you await every day this announcement of peace, the “gospel” of Christ’s love for your life?

CELEBRATION 62

HOPE HAS BECOME CERTAINTY

Introduction to the celebration

Today we contemplate the fulfillment of the saving events that neither the righteous nor the prophets were able to see. What was promised to them is for us a certainty. Their hope has obtained for us the possibility of sharing in the fullness of revelation. God’s faithfulness toward them has become visible in Jesus, born of Mary, who is the perfect realization of Zion and the foundation of the new Jerusalem, the Church.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Commentary on the Word

What the righteous, the prophets of ancient Israel, could not see, we can.

What was promised to them is for us now reality! The hope of Israel has become certainty. God has been faithful: his Messiah has come! Here lies the difference between the New and the Old Testament… Jesus came to manifest and bring to fulfillment everything that God had already announced and begun to carry out in ancient Israel for a humanity scattered and dying because of sin and its radical incapacity to return to life. Israel was chosen, first among the nations, to begin this work.

With Jesus the new times are fulfilled. That heart of flesh promised by God, a new heart, that is, capable of loving God and neighbor, becomes reality! The gift of grace brought about by Jesus transfigures the human being. What the merciful love of God accomplished in the womb of St. Anne (the immaculate conception of Mary), a response to the faithful expectations of that “remnant” which persevered in hope, Jesus will complete in the heart of every human being who opens himself with trust to this Servant who “comes in the name of the Lord,” with the gift of his Spirit, on the day of Pentecost. Truly blessed are our eyes, which can see and taste this blessing promised to Abraham. If the queen of Sheba set out to admire the wisdom of Solomon, how much happier are we, to whom the very wisdom of God has been given! And if the inhabitants of Nineveh hoped for forgiveness, cut to the heart at the preaching of Jonah, sent lovingly by God, how much more reconciled are we by the grace granted to us by the very Word of God, who came to seek the lost sheep to carry it on his shoulders to salvation! If John the Baptist was the greatest among those born of women, how much greater are we who belong to the kingdom of grace, grafted into this blessed vine that has given back to the human being the vital sap of… the divine nature. This is the first “word” we are given to welcome, as we open the pages of the New Testament: “This is the time of fulfillment. The kingdom of God is at hand. Repent, and believe in the GOSPEL!” (Mark 1:15).

Reading: Romans 1:1-7

Reflection on the Word

Paul presents himself as an “envoy,” chosen by God to proclaim the “gospel of God.” God therefore has the “good news” for all of us: a saving message, prepared by him from the creation of the world, through the prophets he chose; unfolded in time and thus accomplished as an “event” in fullness, with the coming of Jesus, his Only-begotten. The protagonist of the “gospel” is the Most Holy Trinity itself: the one God who manifests himself and lets himself be known as Father, then as Son and finally as Spirit of love. The center of this revelation is the eternal Son of God, born in time of Mary, thus manifested by virtue of the resurrection from the dead, by the power of the Holy Spirit, who will continue through time to bear witness and to lead the human being toward this luminous and peace-giving truth: that the creature, that is, thanks to the Son and in the Spirit, can enter into communion of life with the divine being…

Note the excellent synthesis of the revealed truths that for Paul ground the “good news of God”: the Trinity (the three divine persons are manifested in history…), the Incarnation (the Son of God is born, according to his human nature, of the family of David…), the Resurrection (accomplished with power by the Holy Spirit in the lifeless body of Jesus…), the Ascension (the human nature of Jesus is glorified: the man Jesus shows himself to be the Son of God…), the Redemption (the sins of humanity are redeemed in Jesus! He is the Lord: from him every grace and therefore salvation…), the Church (foreshadowed, with the mission through the Holy Spirit, to lead all the nations to faith…).

One can, if one wishes, continue to meditate on, and celebrate, this word: GOSPEL, taking up again the worksheets: “The Gospel according to St. Paul.” It is Paul, in fact, who can introduce us to all the richness contained in this “announcement,” which is indeed of God and not of human beings.

Opening us to all the truth which, as Jesus announced, we cannot bear without the impulse, the help, the guidance of the Holy Spirit (John 16:12-14).

– Are you convinced that every time you hear the announcement of Jesus, Son of God, savior of human beings, you are invited to conversion, that is, to obey what Jesus reveals in order to obtain eternal salvation?

– Do you believe that Jesus of Nazareth rose from the dead to be the faithful “witness” of the living God? Why? How did you come to this conviction? How do you plan to bear witness to this faith of yours?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“Such was the union with my God that, as soon as I began to pray, I was at once absorbed in him; and I always saw new things… He taught me, corrected me, showed me how I must do his work…, as if I were not living but there were in me a person who acted and lived continually for me. And I saw before me a light so beautiful that, even when I was listening to someone speak, if I was not on guard, I was enchanted by it, and many times they judged me simple-minded…” (M 1.1, p. 64).

(in Spiritual Physiognomy, p. 66)

CELEBRATION 63

JESUS ATTESTS THAT HE IS THE MESSIAH

Introduction to the celebration

Jesus attests with his life and words that he is the Messiah, but not everyone understands and welcomes his person. Only those who await him sincerely and hope to know him in truth and to love him with their lives and works believe in him. The deep identity of Jesus the Messiah is unveiled by the Spirit to those who welcome him in the inner depths of their person.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

“The time is fulfilled… the kingdom of God is at hand, repent!” The human being is no longer… “god”! He must accept, if he wants to live again and not die, to be converted. To listen, to believe that God is near to him, that he is no longer alone. It becomes possible to know the truth of our existence and to come out of the lie. This is the central content of the “good news” proclaimed to the apostles: Jesus, the Son of God, has risen and has given us the power, by his victory over death, to become… children too! That existential and primordial relationship with God is given to us anew: in the only-begotten Son, we truly become children.

Reading: John 10:22-38

Reflection on the Word

“The Father is in me and I am in the Father… The Father and I are one.” The Only-begotten Son, “born of Mary of the family of David according to the flesh,” has shown us the richness of Jesus’ inner condition. Jesus insistently affirmed that God is his Father, in a way different from God’s fatherhood toward us: “My Father and your Father.” There is a profound relationship between Jesus and the Father, an intimacy and an immediate knowledge that allow him to affirm: “no one knows the Father except the Son” (Matt 11:27). That is not all: Jesus calls him “abba,” a word unusual in the Jewish tradition, which indicates a particular affectionate familiarity. The kind that exists between a father and his youngest child: a most tender bond!

This particular filial attitude of Jesus, which comes from his divine “intra-Trinitarian” life, is the gift offered to us in that announcement proclaimed to “every creature”: “I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish.” This is the newness of the “gospel”: all the divine promises converge in that “being born of God as his children” (John 1:12-13).

To all who listen to him, to all who welcome him.

For further reflection: Psalm 131

It is the prayer of the meek one: of the little one who is serene in his father’s arms. We too can hope for this calm and secure “rest”: Jesus has obtained for us “a spirit of adoption, through which we cry: Abba, Father! The Spirit itself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. And if children, then heirs” (Rom 8:15-17).

NB: also for this truth revealed by Jesus, one can, if one wishes, continue to celebrate the “word”: SON. It is important to discover, above all in the Gospel of John and then in the letters of Paul, the whole richness of this relationship between the divine persons of the Father and the Son. In this relationship, in fact, we too are called to live: heirs by adoption!

The community could be divided into small groups, entrusting to each (with celebrations at home) the reading of two or more chapters of the Gospel of John. All the passages in which Jesus is spoken of as Son of God, or in which Jesus himself reveals himself as the Only Son of God, can be gathered and heard in a community celebration. One could proceed in the same way with the letters of St. Paul.

– Do you believe that Jesus is the only-begotten Son of God? That the Son is equal in everything to the Father?

– What practical meaning does this have for you?

– What importance does listening to the preaching of Jesus and of the apostles assume?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“A Voice said to me: ‘Rosa, you know that all that you want I will give you and everything will be granted to you. If you knew what you possess and what I have given you, but no, it is not yet the hour. Only what you feel is a minimal part of what you could feel’” (M 1.1, p. 118).

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 120)

CELEBRATION 64

THE SPIRIT FULFILLS THE PROMISE IN THE SERVANT

Introduction to the celebration

The Spirit has an intimate and saving relationship with Jesus. He is the bearer of all the gifts announced by the Prophets with regard to the Servant, the Savior of the world. The origin of the Servant in the womb of Mary, new earth for a renewed creation, takes place by the power of the Holy Spirit. The new people too, represented by the Virgin Mother and the beloved disciple, is born of the Paschal Mystery of Christ Jesus and of the descent of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

Jesus, born of Mary of the family of David, was “established Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness.” The “good news” of the resurrection of Jesus reveals the fulfillment of that other great and saving truth which Jesus, already at the Last Supper, had announced to his own: the promise of the Holy Spirit. Spirit of truth and above all Spirit Consoler, because he will teach… will remind… will bear witness to the work of Jesus and will guide to the fullness of truth, declaring the things to come, “taking” them from the Son and finally “glorifying him.”

Reading: John 15:25-26 and 16:7-15

Reflection on the Word

This Spirit who will remain with us always will complete the mission of Jesus, freeing humanity from sin and death, fulfilling that promise of God revealed to the prophets: the gift of a new heart. The Holy Spirit will be the inner principle of new life that God at last pours into the human being. This presence of the divine person of the Holy Spirit characterizes the “new covenant,” in contrast to the old, because he… “dwells” in the Christian, in his spirit and in his body. He therefore makes the Christian a child of God, by making Christ dwell in his heart, and becomes a principle of resurrection, projecting him into the future. Taking the place of the evil principle of the flesh, the Spirit becomes in the human being a principle of faith, of supernatural knowledge, of love, of sanctification, of moral conduct, of apostolic courage, of hope and of prayer.

For further reflection: Psalm 62

Thanks to the gift of the Spirit, the soul truly… rests. The Spirit becomes the guarantee, the seal, the first fruits of salvation. The human being would be a “breath,” a shadow that passes fleetingly, were he not clothed with this “power” that comes “from on high” (Luke 24:49). The “time” is truly “fulfilled”: that baptism in the Spirit, announced by John the Baptist (Acts 1:5), is being accomplished: “pour out your heart before God” because God… pours out his Spirit in you! You can now trust in that “power” which belongs to God and which God gives you! “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses… to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8).

N.B.: Also of this divine reality, the presence of the Holy Spirit in our life and in the history of the world, one can continue to celebrate the “word.” Again dividing the community into small groups, one could, by a continued reading of the letters of St. Paul, gather the teachings that the apostle gives, from time to time, about the active, working, sanctifying and transfiguring presence of the divine person of the Holy Spirit.

– Do you believe in the Holy Spirit?

– What do you know concretely about this divine person?

– Have you ever invoked the action of the Holy Spirit in your daily life?

– How do you think of the presence of the Holy Spirit in your soul, in your body?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

“I was instructed about something to be done. He taught me about his love, its degree and how it is communicated to the soul… I saw everything immense, great beyond compare. I saw how the soul, in order to receive this Love, must be well purified; so one feels that one burns, is consumed, but the ardent longing grows, the ardent longing to be consumed and to burn all the more. Oh, incomprehensible mystery: to suffer and to enjoy infinitely the delights of the Beloved! One always desires only him and for him everything is little. Yes, my Love” (M 1.2, p. 45).

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, pp. 106-107)

CELEBRATION 65

THE RISEN CHRIST PRESENT IN THE CHURCH

Introduction to the celebration

The glorified Christ continues, in the Spirit, his presence in the Church.

The Spirit present at the birth of the Messiah, at the beginning of his mission and at every moment of his life, is the same who is given to the Church. The dying Jesus gives his Spirit to the Church represented by the Mother and the disciple, who knew how to share in his passion beneath the cross and to hope against all hope in his definitive triumph. The Risen Jesus transmits him to the apostles, before ascending into heaven, so that they may forgive humanity’s sins; and in the upper room, while they are gathered with Mary his Mother, awaiting his outpouring, so that they may go into all the world to proclaim his Paschal Mystery.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

The “good news” is that Jesus, the Son of God and of Mary of Nazareth, has risen from the dead. Through him, the apostles received the “grace” of being able to announce to the world a reality not only impossible, but unimaginable to us who were in darkness and suffering, in the sole experience of… having to die! On this event our faith and our hope are founded. The very presence of the apostles, sent to preach so that we may believe, is its guarantee. The “evangelists” too… write so that we may believe that “Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” and that, believing, we may have life in his name (John 20:31).

Reading: 1 Corinthians 15

Reflection on the Word

Important is that “I make known to you” with which Paul recalls to us what for him too was a… “gospel” of salvation: he the “last,” he “as one born abnormally,” the “least” among the apostles, “unfit” because “persecutor” of the Church. But… by the grace of God he is firm in this “announcement” which he not only believed but “experienced”: Paul has “seen” the Lord! He is therefore… a witness! This news now resounds from generation to generation, reaches the ends of the earth, is shouted in the squares, involves the existence of every human being. It becomes a sign of contradiction: whoever welcomes it builds his life on the cornerstone: he will withstand all the “storms” of life, he will be victorious over death. Whoever despises and rejects it will be swept away… death will destroy him! (cf. Matt 7:24-27).

A very well-known event, then, which illumines the earthly journey. Necessary in order to “be always fully devoted to the work of the Lord”: to grow in faith, to remain “steadfast” in hope, awaiting that transfiguration of our corruptible body.

For further reflection: Psalm 16

“Keep me safe, I take refuge in you.” Without this event of life: the resurrection from the dead, there is no good on earth, in our life. At least no lasting good. “I keep the Lord always before me”: the remembrance of this marvelous event makes my history, my future, “secure.” Neither death nor the tomb, in fact, will make hope waver in that “fullness of joy,” no longer fleeting, and in that “delight forever” made possible by the possession of God. It is still fitting to dwell on the reality of this event: the resurrection from the dead.

Starting from the first Easter announcement recounted by the Gospels, continue the search in the apostolic letters. With the usual method, if it has proved… good!

– Do you believe in your own resurrection?

– Do you know that the Christian faith rests entirely on this event accomplished and revealed by Jesus?

– Do you know that the victory of Jesus over death is a guarantee of the truth of what he announced?

– What practical consequences does faith in the resurrection have for you?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

Her interior reality is flooded by the lights of the Spirit who guides her with the Voice, with the gift of discernment (cf. M 1, p. 63) and other signs in the moments of growth in holiness and in the decisive steps of the mission:

“… he always teaches me, admonishes me, oh in this how severe he is. In the smallest things he warns me where I am lacking and he does not like it that I do such and such a thing not at once…”;

“Oh, how many beautiful lessons he gave me. He explained certain doubts of mine, he made me see what I had to go through…” (M 1.1, p. 109; 144).

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 106)

CELEBRATION 66

THE CHURCH IN THE SPIRIT BECOMES MARY

Introduction to the celebration

The Church, animated by the Spirit of the Risen One, is being transformed into Mary, the daughter of Anne; welcoming and pondering, like her, in her heart, the events of the Trinity, she experiences them in life. She feels saved, visited by the Lord who delights in the humble, who sooner or later brings down the pride of the arrogant, who shatters, in time, the dark and unjust designs of every powerful organization. The God of the Church is not a philosophical reality, he is the Father of Israel, of Anne and Joachim, of Mary, of Jesus, the Father of the history of every people and of every human being, he is the provident God who does not stand by and watch, but guides and sustains in the toils of life.

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

If Christ has not been raised, preaching is useless, the Easter announcement absurd and our faith also vain! If Christ has not risen, we are still in sin. Indeed “the sting of death is sin.”

Unfortunately, we do not resign ourselves to death! And death is the condemnation of the creature’s rebellion against the living God. We saw it in the book of Genesis (chap. 3). The book of Wisdom recalls it to us and confirms it: “God did not make death… but he created all things that they might exist” (Wis 1:13-14); he loves “all things that exist and loathes nothing that he has made” (Wis 11:24). Instead “through the envy of the devil, death entered the world, and they who belong to his company experience it” (Wis 2:24). And unfortunately all of us have been caught up in this bitter reality: the devil, lord of death, has held the whole of humanity subject to this terrible slavery (Heb 2:14-15).

Reading: Romans 3:9-20.23 and 5:12.18-19

Reflection on the Word

If, then, the “kindness and generous love of God our savior” (Titus 3:4) had not appeared, our living would have been in vain. Being subject to the tragedy of death would be worse, infinitely worse, than any other injustice or oppression or deceit. Without Easter Sunday, without those witnesses of an “empty tomb” and of a “risen one” who comes to meet them to flood them with light and peace, our world would be an “eternal Egypt” with no hope of “exodus.” Without the victory of Christ, humanity would already be extinguished.

It will therefore be important to reflect again on these closely connected themes: death and sin.

How present is this truth in the consciousness of the apostles: that… Christ had to die to take away the sin of the world?

If in the Scriptures of the New Testament our inner history sometimes appears dramatically dark, and the consequences of sin are underlined in gloomy colors: “Who will deliver me from this body of death?”; all the more exalting, by contrast, shines the splendor of Christ’s victory: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (cf. Rom 7:24-25).

– In your opinion, why do suffering and death exist?

– Are you convinced that Jesus had to die, in order to destroy evil?

– Are you convinced that you are a sinner? Why? Where do you most feel the state of sin, in yourself and in your family or work environment?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

The description that Rosa gives of her experience with the Spirit allows us to grasp this discreet presence in the movement that goes from the contemplation of the Face of Christ to the mysterious experience of the fire that devours and consumes her: “… I saw the face of my Redeemer. Oh! how beautiful he was! What joy, my love! He was so luminous that I would not know how to explain his light and beauty. I felt myself wholly inflamed by that object which consumed me. Ah! when will that day be when in so beautiful a moment you, my Good, will consume me?” (M 1.1, p. 13).

The Spirit draws her to Jesus: he awakens in her like a devouring fire, but what in turn arouses this power of love is the sight of the Redeemer.

The Spirit, in fact, shows her in the most splendid light the Face of her Redeemer, makes her fall in love with irresistible attraction and with a strength that is no longer her own.

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 101)

CELEBRATION 67

THE HOLY SPIRIT, SOUL AND HOPE OF THE CHURCH

Introduction to the celebration

As Mary, feeling herself visited and loved by the God of Abraham and of her fathers, sang a hymn to his faithfulness, to him who had remembered his love and had not disappointed the expectation of his people, so the Church knows how the Trinity surpasses every expectation. Living faith in the God of life and of history frees the dynamism of hope, keeps the heart awake, makes us lovers and attentive to every nuance of his presence in events and capable of making his interests and plans for the world our own. Mary, filled with the Holy Spirit, the Full of grace, the delight of the Trinity, is the one who introduces the Church, all of us, into the understanding of the life and message of Jesus: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given you besides.”

Vespers (or another hour of the Divine Office)

Introduction to the Word

If the “good news” of the victory of Jesus, the “gospel of God,” is announced to all nations, indeed to every creature, to obtain the “obedience of faith,” and if this resurrection from the dead of Jesus, the object of the preaching, is the first fruits of new life for those who were in the darkness of death and incapable of freeing themselves from it, then the “hope for the glory” (Rom 5:2) appears exalting for those who will believe. All the toils and struggles are possible because Christian hope is “set” on the living God, “the savior of all, especially of those who believe” (cf. 1 Tim 4:10). We have seen it: if there is no resurrection from the dead, the apostles would turn out to be false witnesses of God. There would be no faith in any living God! The hymn of blessing that Paul raises in gratitude for all the work accomplished by Jesus is therefore justified:

Reading: Ephesians 1:1-14

Reflection on the Word

To believers in Christ, inserted into his divine life by baptism, for whom there is no condemnation (cf. Rom 8:1): “grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ”! Already the heart can… expand. “Heaven” opens, we can lift our gaze: the Father of our Lord Jesus has blessed us! With every blessing!
