Even before the creation of the world!… We were loved with Jesus, predestined to become his dearest brothers and sisters. And all… so that we might become an explosion of gratitude, of joy, of praise for this work accomplished by him: his coming among us, his death and resurrection, the gift of his Spirit, the sending of the Church which, through the word of truth, the “gospel,” has aroused faith in the world and thus the “first installment” of our “inheritance”: that Spirit who, with inexpressible groanings, intercedes insistently for us, urging us to await, according to the designs of God, those goods that were not owed… unhoped for: resurrection… eternal life… vision of God! (Rom 8:26-27). Unsearchable the riches of Christ! How far can we still penetrate into the depth of God’s gift, in this Son who has opened in his heart inexhaustible treasures of grace, of peace, of love, of life?

– Try to pick out in Paul’s hymn the… path of salvation.

– What are the truths that Paul emphasizes and that we are invited to welcome?

– Do you believe in the “future glory”?

– And in your adoption as a “child”?

– How do you think God will accomplish all this with you?

– How did he accomplish it with Mother Rosa?

From the experience of Rosa Gattorno

The Father wished to show Rosa also the presence of Mary, Queen of heaven. Mary, Mother, Immaculate, Virgin, Queen of the Universe, associated with the glory of her Son, is contemplated also in this aspect of the fullness of her glory:

“I saw such a beautiful feast in Heaven, the Sovereign Mary sits at the Right Hand…”;

“… I saw the Sovereign of heaven and earth surrounded by Angels and Seraphim! Oh beloved Mother…” (M 1.1, p. 153);

“I had the consolation of seeing the commemoration in heaven of the Sovereign Virgin”;

“A fire was devouring me…” (M 1.1, pp. 38, 153; 12.1, p. 145).

The vision of the fullness of the mystery of Mary associated with the Mystery of the Son is for Rosa a radiance of the Trinitarian Life, present in grace and mercy, in the divine motherhood which, in Christ, with Christ and through Christ, is present in the begetting of all the children of God.

(from God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno, p. 147)

We can still celebrate, and every community will have its own path of searching which will not leave it idle, in this work of spiritual growth, both personal and communal, we can celebrate the “word”: Eternal Life. Both the evangelists and the apostolic letters overflow with this reality, which it will be good to explore more deeply.

Also interesting to celebrate, especially toward the end of the liturgical year, will be the “word”: Parousia or the final Return of Jesus the Lord. But there are many themes that the New Testament above all leaves to our desire to know the will of God. One can research, for example, the unceasing action of the Trinity in the history of the world and of every human being; the birth and growth of the Church, as Mystery and as Mystical Body; the theological virtues: Faith, Hope, Charity. All the Christian virtues that help to build up the Church and to live our spirituality, for example: Poverty, Meekness, Simplicity, Humility, Prudence, Mercy, Kindness, Patience, Hospitality, Chastity, Obedience…

But the Holy Spirit will guide you… It is he who has been given to us, precisely as Spirit of Truth, because he “searches” the depths of God and announces them to us. He will take from the inmost heart of the Son and surely, if we are on the way, willing to let ourselves be visited and to allow God to convert us, he will teach us! The one who sits at the right hand of God in Glory, Jesus our Lord, intercedes for us and the same Holy Spirit whom he poured out in our hearts will still console us because he wants us saved. Therefore he will lead us there, where it is good and healthful for us… to go! Good work, good journey! Peace and every good!

APPENDIX NO. 1

BATHSHEBA

And you, Bathsheba, were you, perhaps, weary of solitude? Did you perhaps long for the caresses of your man? Perhaps you did not know that conjugal fidelity wants to share not only joys and plans, but also pains, separations and responsibilities?

Your husband was at war, an officer of the king: a valiant fighter. Careful to be an example, a stimulus, an encouragement to so many other young soldiers, perhaps less generous than he or inexperienced or rather fearful…

Should you not have loved that duty of his which imposed renunciations and dangers on him? Perhaps they had not taught you that when the bridegroom is taken away, the faithful bride must fast? (Luke 5:35). Your body craved refreshment, but very special was the heat that afflicted it, since a single carnal union was enough to make you conceive!

Why expose it to indiscreet eyes? You knew… that your lodging could be seen from the height of the palace.

Were you perhaps aware of the king’s habits? His rest, his strolling… You were not cautious as the Hebrew Susanna was (Dan 13). She used to make sure that any curious glance was precluded.

But you, Bathsheba, how could you think that no one was looking at you… when, perhaps, you had provoked… that attention?

That body of yours bared for the bath, was it not perhaps a wink for the one who could look?

If you were entirely innocent, why did you raise no objection to the messengers whom David sent?

Did you fear, by refusing, the wrath of a king? Did you fear, perhaps, negative consequences for your husband too?

And yet one must obey God rather than human beings, and God has established a serious condemnation for adultery, even if committed with a king.

Or did you feel excused because you are not a daughter of Israel?

Too easily you yielded… so much so as to raise the hypothesis that you yourself hoped, perhaps, to be able to seduce him, the king.

Your husband far away… your beauty “wasted”… the palace there, opposite… that conception!

Did ambitious thoughts not touch your heart? Where were you when David was doing penance for that child of yours?

Your new husband… will continue afterward to want to humble himself, because of the consequences of that sin of his… you will want, instead, to be consoled at once (2 Sam 12:24).

You have already forgotten the death of a husband… of an innocent child… You do not know how to bear pain, mourning, solitude.

You are in a hurry!

You already want another son and this time the king your husband will have to swear to you that he will sit on the throne after him… (1 Kgs 1:30).

You are not named among the family of David, in voluntary exile in the face of Absalom’s threat (2 Sam 15:16-16:21).

Why? Did you refuse this humiliation?

Why did you refuse to follow David?

To guard the palace together with the other concubines, according to the king’s plan? You seem more in love with that place at the right hand of your son (1 Kgs 2:17-19).

But your weaknesses will become his…

Solomon will inherit the wisdom and the riches of David…

But you, Bathsheba, will survive and will influence your son (“he can refuse you nothing!”), who will not love the Lord as his father did. He will not obey him, as you did not obey… Because you, Bathsheba, did not love the God of Israel with all your heart! Solomon will be famous… also for his unbridled hedonistic luxury, which will lead him to the failure of his mission.

How great a part did you have, Bathsheba, in educating that king’s heart?

Different appears—in the book of the Maccabees—from yours (and… how much!) the care of that mother who yearned for quite other ambitions for the future of her dear ones! (2 Macc 7). The Holy Spirit who had inserted you, for love of David (because David loved you!), into the genealogy of the Messiah, has nevertheless kept silent about your name… But not because you were a foreigner… Ruth and Tamar were more so than you…

Because you will remain the wife of Uriah, the only title that can do you honor!

Certainly it was not David who consoled you with a son who became king, nor your ambitions, which led you far from what were your duties… The Spirit of Truth, the only one who can console you, reminds all of us of that place of yours which you loved so little!

Your name, Bathsheba, we can forget, but you remain forever the wife of a faithful soldier!

APPENDIX NO. 2

DAVID

Presentation

He is the youngest offspring of the family of Jesse (1 Sam 16:11). To anoint him, Samuel will have to wait until he returns from pasturing the flock.

Certainly no one (not even the wise Samuel) could have thought of that little shepherd as the future king of Israel… He happens (when one says “chance”!) to turn up in Saul’s camp… The victory over Goliath, the other “fortunate” exploits and, above all, the enthusiasm of the people, will unleash the jealousy of the king, who will fiercely persecute David. Full of anxiety and humiliation is his fleeing, hiding… and waiting patiently for… God to do justice!

At Saul’s death, David will promote the slow unification of all the Israelite tribes, who will finally acknowledge him as “their bone and their flesh” (2 Sam 5), proclaiming him king. The conquest of Jerusalem will definitively seal the reign of this new one chosen by God!

But another hard and dramatic exile he will have to undergo: the revolt of his son Absalom, who will want to seize his throne. Again flight, humiliation, sorrow.

Again his patient perseverance will bring him back (though prostrated by the loss of his beloved son) to the throne of Jerusalem, which he will keep until his death.

David’s Youth

Let us see in the stages of this life how God prepares the soul of his chosen ones… Let us learn what attitudes and dispositions are necessary to enter the paths of God… “paths of peace,” yes, but “his” peace.

When Samuel receives from God the order to anoint David as the new king of Israel, we notice at once that David is not present in the family… someone has to go and call him, because he is… pasturing the flock.

An easy job? Suitable for the youngest?

The older brothers are at war and someone must provide for the household economy: a necessity, then?

A job, in any case, that initiates David into a… solitary life.

How long do shepherds remain far from their families?

Perhaps they do not need, for their work, an “imposing stature” (1 Sam 16:7.12), but certainly a sense of responsibility… Indeed David defends his sheep, even if few, from the lion and the bear (1 Sam 17:34-36). Far from the battlefields, where very many young men eager to show off their vigor, their intelligence, their courage will want to try themselves… David is constrained by this humble work to stay in the… wilderness (1 Sam 17:28), in silence and solitude, with the only interruption of the service of… bringing food (1 Sam 17:17-18)! He will learn precisely there, in the wilderness, to train with courage and cunning for quite another kind of combat (suffice it to see how awkward he is in the armor furnished him by Saul, which is not at all familiar to him… 1 Sam 17:38-39). The struggle for survival is often a magnificent teacher.

It is in this youthful setting that his faith in Yahweh, Lord of the armies of Israel, matures (1 Sam 17:26.36-37.45-46). The “wilderness” is a privileged place for… listening (Hos 11:1-5; 2:16; 12:10; Amos 5:25; Isa 40:3-5; Deut 8:2-5); for learning to understand seriously the meaning of existence and the relationship of the fragile and needy creature with the absolute God…

Moreover the divine inspirations seem to prefer the… “pilgrim” more than the conqueror… who surrounds himself with walls and bulwarks…

God seems to welcome the “shepherd man”… always on the move… more than the man intent on a worldly goal. Abel is a shepherd unlike Cain… who does not seem truly oriented toward God and… his neighbor (Gen 4:4-5.9.17). After the “flood,” from the sons of Cain the “accursed” (Gen 9:25) come the powerful on earth and the valiant hunters (Gen 10:8-9), from whom then come kingdoms like those of Babel and Nineveh (Gen 10:10). Babel represents the attempt at a civilization without God; its architectural attempt will become a symbol of all human corruption (Gen 11:2.8). Nineveh is a great city, yes, but in need of a total and urgent conversion… (cf. Jonah 3:1-4).

The descendants of Shem, the “blessed” (Gen 9:26), will instead inhabit the mountains of the east (Gen 10:30), rugged places, solitary spaces, not suited to those who demand immediate usefulness (cf. Gen 13:10-12).

A shepherd again will be Abraham, wandering thousands of miles… skilled in hunting instead, Esau (Gen 25:27) who… will lose the “blessing”!

Jacob, a quiet man, will have to learn the art of the shepherd, to become, in fullness, possessor of the “divine blessing” (Gen 32:27-29).

“Shepherds” will be called the guides of Israel (cf. e.g. Ezek 34).

Precisely at the height of King David’s splendor, God himself seems not to be pleased to be “kept” in a temple, when David, satisfied with his own palace, plans a house worthy of his Lord, whose Ark is still in a “tent.”

A plan that the prophet Nathan himself at first approves…

But God’s plans are different… (2 Sam 7:1-13).

He wants… to walk, so that the human being may learn to understand that he cannot stop; God must always point out to him a… beyond! God educates the human being to the Infinite.

True is Nathan’s prophecy: it is God who builds a “house” for us… a lineage of days that will not end, a… “place” (John 14:2-4), a definitive “homeland” (cf. Heb 11:8-10.13-16.37-40), which we could never achieve, however much we might wish to!

And… “good shepherd” will be one of the titles Jesus chose for himself in his earthly pilgrimage (John 10).

In the poor and austere climate of the wilderness… in that wary and watchful solitude, in the hours of rest and silence, the other gift for which David will become famous will also be refined: he will become the “singer” of Yahweh… With these “poor” means God forms according to “his own heart” this future shepherd of his people.

David will be patient regarding marriage.

Saul first promises his daughter Merab, but with underhanded purposes (1 Sam 18:17)… only to deny her to him.

He will give him Michal (1 Sam 18:20-22), but with the intent of having him killed at the hands of the Philistines…

Unaware of these ulterior motives, David not only perseveres in faithful attachment to Saul but realistically judges his own condition inadequate to become the king’s son-in-law (1 Sam 18:18.23).

David’s successes over the Philistines will reveal Saul’s true feelings, who has decided: he himself will kill David (1 Sam 19:1)! Thus for David begins the… flight.

First he is saved by his wife Michal (1 Sam 19:17), then by Samuel (1 Sam 19:18), by Ahimelech (1 Sam 21:2)…

He even takes refuge, at first, among the Philistines, feigning madness so as not to be killed (1 Sam 21:11-14), then, for a longer time, he allies himself with mercenaries (1 Sam 27:3), and the wandering life of a band leader (1 Sam 22:1-2) will return him to the wilderness (1 Sam 23:14; 25:1).

But precisely this living in precariousness, with the constant nightmare of death lying in wait, brings him definitively to maturity.

His friends are, after all, “discontented” people, folk in “distress” (1 Sam 22:2). From them too he will suffer ingratitude: they will even want to stone him when their families become victims of a raid (1 Sam 30:6).

David will find in God, who constantly sustains him, the strength to continue to live, to hope, to… walk (1 Sam 22:5; 23:2.10-12.14; 25:26.28).

He will not hasten the times to… free himself of Saul.

After having wanted to save him once, accidentally (1 Sam 24), a second time it will be David himself who seeks an opportunity to show his king the true intentions of his faithful servant (1 Sam 26)! Thus he will protest to him his innocence, his feelings of sincere submission.

“The king pursues a flea?… If the Lord has incited you against me, may he accept the fragrance of an offering… but cursed be the men who keep me from sharing in the inheritance of the Lord!…” Unimpeachable is the reminder that those who were supposed to guard the king and who have… fallen asleep are violators of a supreme duty. David, had he truly been an enemy, could have killed him! The king is moved, but David, from now on, entrusts himself to God alone.

David Ascends the Throne

David ascends the throne… “Who may go up to the mountain of the Lord?” (Ps 24).

After Saul’s death, still difficult and long will be the road that leads David to the conquest of the Kingdom of Israel. But… he will ascend “who has clean hands.”

David does not take advantage of events that could immediately, perhaps, lead him to success, indeed… He flees easy and suspect proposals (2 Sam 1:11-16).

He quenches in blood criminal flattery. It is fate that decides for the young Amalekite who, hoping for a reward, confesses to having killed Saul at his request, bringing David the royal insignia of the latter. He will avenge the death of Saul’s son, Ishbaal (appointed, at least temporarily, king and successor of Saul…), killed in his sleep by two traitors (2 Sam 4:7) who intended to profit from the defeat of the house of Saul (2 Sam 4:8).

“Clean hands and a pure heart.” David continues to show upright intentions toward his former enemy: Saul was to be respected as “the Lord’s anointed” and a “just” man is his son Ishbaal, even without wanting to consider the investiture he had received… (2 Sam 4:9-11). David is not greedy for power. Indeed, in the last song dedicated to Saul, he extols his glorious deeds together with those of his son Jonathan (the dear friend to whom he had always been bound by most tender affection) and wants this funeral “lament” to be taught to the people of Judah. “Saul and Jonathan, beloved and lovely… swifter than eagles, stronger than lions!” (2 Sam 1:19-27). David’s heart knows how to put his sufferings into oblivion… “Let not the enemy rejoice at the death of these heroes. Let the daughters of Israel forget the ten thousand slain by David and weep instead for Saul, who clothed them in scarlet and delights!”

Not even a shadow of a resentment that might appear justified; not even a shadow of the perfidy of one who spies on another’s fall in order to prevail over him (cf. Jer 20:10).

Indeed, he shows himself grateful and tender toward those of Jabesh-gilead for having shown mercy to their king by burying his body (2 Sam 2:5-7). And for love of Jonathan, he will favor his unfortunate son Meribbaal, having him sit at his own table (2 Sam 9:1-13). A benefit of which, unfortunately, the latter will make himself unworthy… (2 Sam 16:3-4 and 19:25-31).

Truly… “he utters no lie.” David will keep the oath he promised to Saul (1 Sam 24:22). Certainly his political interests do not prevail, but rather the concern to be an instrument of the “mercy of God” toward the house of Saul!

And… “he will receive blessing.” Even his enemies will respect him. Hard and long as the civil war between Judah and Israel will be, after David takes over at Hebron the leadership of the kingdom of Judah, it will be Abner himself (the most influential and prominent man in Israel, who had—at first—brought Saul’s son Ishbaal to the succession to the throne, then breaking from him after disagreements), it will be Abner who seeks out David to negotiate with him the plan of a dual monarchy: two kingdoms with… one king: David. David trusts in Providence. Indeed, after the violent death of Abner, deprived of effective leaders, the northern tribes will spontaneously want to recognize themselves as subjects of David.

Even through violence, internal struggles, exhausting wars, political intrigues, murders and vengeance, God will lead his “chosen one” to reign over tribes so restless, continually tormented by rivalries, conflicting interests, mutual suspicions… Only under David’s reign will peace and unity be possible and… expansionist openings toward neighboring countries used as safety cushions for the missionary people.

“Such is the generation that seeks your face, O God!” Even in this so delicate stage of David’s journey, his constant listening to what the Lord inspires in him remains fundamental: he will consult the Lord… before taking initiatives (2 Sam 2:1; 5:19.23). David will have to be “king”…, but above all he will have to form that heart which, according to God’s plans, already foreshadows the features of his “descendant”: that Messiah who will make of twelve quarrelsome men a… “one heart and one mind” (Acts 4:32), that “Son of David” who will be the sign of “unity,” precisely by loving, as “flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones,” to the end (John 13:1), his own, keeping them for life.

He too, of two peoples divided by hatred (Jews and Gentiles), will form his Church, this new people, pacified and united, destroying in his own body their enmities (cf. Eph 2:14-16).

David goes on growing… because God is with him! (2 Sam 5:10). He will subdue all his enemies: Philistines (2 Sam 5:25 and 8:1), Moabites (2 Sam 8:2), Arameans (2 Sam 8:6), Edomites (2 Sam 8:14), Ammonites (2 Sam 10)… The Messiah too, called Emmanuel (God with us), will grow in wisdom and age, going about doing good and healing all those oppressed by the devil… (cf. Acts 10:38). The “Son of David” will reduce to “nothing every principality and every authority and power.” “The last enemy to be destroyed is death, for (God) has subjected everything under his feet” (1 Cor 15:24-27).

The Sins of David: Adultery

“What is evil in your eyes, I have done”

O David, how was it possible?

Truly as that wise man says: “Some who seemed to follow a sublime way of life fell to the lowest; and one who ate the bread of angels I afterward saw taking delight in the husks of swine. There is, then, no holiness if you, Lord, withdraw your hand. No wisdom avails if you cease to govern. No strength is of any use if you cease to sustain” (Imitation of Christ, Book 3, ch. 14).

But the Lord did not cease to sustain David.

Do you not remember, David, when you were fleeing from Saul? How long did you dwell in the wilderness? In rugged places in the mountains… You were hunted, to be killed…

But the Lord never put you into enemy hands. At the right moment you found help, you were consoled… Even in anguish, you were loved… awaited. Because the Lord was with you!

Why, then, did you despise your God? Rightly he complained to you: “I anointed you king… I delivered you from Saul… I gave you your master’s house… I put his wives into your arms, and if this had been too little… I would have added even more” (2 Sam 12:7-10).

But suddenly… everything seems to be forgotten! There is now only that so violent passion… that desire for possession, for pleasure…

By now you are king…

Everything is owed to you, is it not?

You do not even need to consult your God…

You are not even stopped by the fact that that woman belongs to an officer of yours who is fighting for you… so that your name may be glorious.

Once you built glory with your arm, with your vigor…

Now you take advantage of a husband at war and you clasp to yourself… not a sword, but that body… which you make your own!

“No wisdom avails if you cease to govern.”

For this you fall, David: the wisdom of God no longer guides you; or rather: you no longer allow God to govern you! When you took refuge in him because of your weakness, your fears… you could protest your innocence… and this succeeded in moving even the heart of your former enemy… because God defended you, exalted you! You could not fall, David, because your heart pleased the Lord… But now that you no longer feel weak, nor have any more fears, that you sit firmly on your throne, whom do you want to please? That woman? Perhaps yourself? Once you did not care about yourself, you had—about yourself—an objective judgment. Remember?… you were not worthy of the daughter of Saul…

Now that you are king, you dare to take what you must not want!

You have become lazy, idle, you look around, your gaze wanders complacently… and there you are, captured by a beautiful body!

You are no longer… patient, David; you worry about grabbing “everything and at once”… that is why you forgot the Lord! You no longer struggle, you no longer toil, you no longer wait, you no longer suffer, you no longer hope… Now everything is yours. But you are losing the capacity to love… and there you are stealing: you steal the woman: another man’s woman: taking advantage of the authority of your mission.

The Lord wanted you king in order to go on serving… you are king… in order to have what you no longer know how to give. Now you impose the rights of the strongest. And you will end by destroying what your “auctoritas” (authority) was meant to “augere” (increase).

You too are a human being… all of us were conceived and born in guilt.

However humble and patient… attentive and quick to call for help, this time you did not accept weakness. You grew tired of… suffering!

If you had not presumed, feeling strong in the position reached… if you had not gone on taking pleasure in looking at that body… if, as thoughts of desire were rising, you had remembered your debt to the Most High! If you had not become curious to know who that woman was… Instead you send for her… Before she comes, you reflect… But deep down you no longer want to be taught by wisdom!… Your heart grows dark… there is no longer sincerity… Sadness will now dominate it… it will have to break!

The Census

The Scriptures underline another… fall of David!

If on a late spring afternoon, strolling idly on the terrace, he had stopped to look at a woman in heat… Perhaps on an evening meeting with his ministers, anxieties and worries had arisen…

Incursions of troops by neighboring peoples… secret alliances concluded between this nation and that… new military balances in the region…

Needs will have emerged for supplies… for strengthening the royal guard… for new works to consolidate the military strongholds… for other public works… and fears of negative reactions to the decision to impose new taxes… After that agitated “cabinet,” David was perhaps walking on that terrace anything but idly. Thoughts far too grave… were churning.

Urgent decisions had to be made… What a responsibility to keep that Kingdom united… To defend it from larger nations… How many dangers!

David, where is your heart slipping? Is agitation conquering you? Is the worry arising in you of… “how many of us are there?”

And before… waiting patiently, before turning to God, your God, you do what other kings do… You decide… and hence the “census.” Even Joab dissuades you. Have you forgotten, David, who guards Israel, who is its true Shepherd? Who leads this “little flock”?

What Lord has gone to seek out this nation from among so many nations, to make it his own special possession?

Why, then, do you get agitated, why do you worry? One thing alone was necessary. That you trust! Who really fought the battles of Israel? Where were you, David, when Yahweh freed from that “fiery furnace” of Egypt what was not yet… a people? Who fed it for years in the desert? And who brought it into a happy land, defeating seven nations far more powerful than itself? The generation of your fathers too, like you… doubted.

“How could we defeat those warrior peoples? We are not prepared and our children will not survive.”

Precisely those “non-warrior” children received the land!

O David, do you want to know the strength of your people?…

It is… “sublime,” “wonderful”… “hidden”… like the “holiness” of your God… Israel will always be… a “mystery.”

Like holiness…

Of it you taste the fragrance, you sense its presence… but you cannot have it! You can desire it, but it escapes you… You are drawn to it, but it is always far away… You would like to see it, but tears hide it from you!

O David, Israel is not yours!… It is not you who defend it! The Israel of God will be, until the end of the ages… a little flock, a people not numerous… but the hostile forces of evil will not overcome it. You will have to learn to see in it the “weeds”: divisions, defeats, dispersions and death… but you will not save it… It will walk among the nations, like Cain: a wanderer, terrified of death, fearful of being killed…

But God has set upon it a sign of salvation.

Israel is that Adam who kept his God hidden… but his God keeps on searching for him!…

You cannot understand this mystery of life and death, of the interweaving of good and evil. Only the holiness of God grasps it.

For his is the earth and what it contains.

He has tenderness for all creatures… His thoughts are of peace and not of woe…

A living God and lover of life, but who sees every human being grow like the grass of the field: flourishing in the morning and withering by evening.

It is he who opens his hand and satisfies every living thing, but he sets limits to the sea and regulates the course of the day!

All peoples are his… Like the stars he calls them one by one, knows them by name… but all gathered together on the scale, they are… nothing!

As nothing are a thousand years… a day, yesterday’s, which was and is already gone!

His are the high, lofty peaks… and his the dark, unfathomable abysses… O David, the census of what forces do you want to take?

Why claim to take possession of the physiognomy of a people that you will not succeed in deciphering?

In what securities do you really want to trust? In chariots and horses? Even if riches abound, do not set your heart on them…

No, David, Israel is not possessed! Like holiness… you can see it from afar… Like pilgrims longing for rest.

We have no power to make a single hair black or white. You cannot add an hour to the time that has been fixed for you. The strength of your people lies in the “mystery” it carries, in that “Covenant” with the One who made the heavens and the earth…

Do not doubt… you are in that people, but you do not possess it. Rather, with the people you are the special possession of the One who is the only Living One!

You know the lament of Elijah, who laid before God the anguish of his solitude: “No one serves you, Lord, and I alone am left…”

And you know the answer: “Be calm! Seven thousand have not bent the knee to Baal!” Seven thousand! It is a mysterious number! Great as that 144,000 of the luminous fulfillment. It cannot be read at face value! 7 x 1000. If 7 already speaks of fullness, how much does that… x 1000 contain? Elijah welcomes that Word! Why, David, do you not look to that fullness, to that rest, given also to you as a pledge? Do you remember Jonathan? He loved you more than himself…

And Uriah? Faithful and silent… dead because of your whims, without cursing you! And Nathan? The voice of God always there to enlighten you… And Samuel, sent to support you? And Ahimelech, generous and devoted?

Ziba, Barzillai, beside you in the trial, but disinterested and ready to disappear as soon as their service as honest subjects was done…

You wanted to exalt Bathsheba so much, but how much more lovable and wise was Abigail? She kept you from being unjust… she restored to peace your heart stirred up by anger. Kindly she came to your aid, risking her life, and confirmed with prophetic wisdom your future as king.

To give herself later in marriage, in widowhood, in a hidden but attentive service.

And those valiant men… who to fulfill a wish of yours exposed their lives? Try to count them…

Of these you certainly must not take a “census”!

They are there to guarantee the Kingdom, because God gave them to you!

This is your security. Because as a gift of God, they love you! They accompany you! They are those promised 7000, who do not kneel to any divinity. The “secure” ones. The obscure “saints” who prepare the “holy one,” who defend the chosen one! It is true: God raises up saints for his people… but the people too wanted and prepared their coming. Without those tears in Egypt, God would not have willed Moses! Without the groans of Hannah, Samuel would not have been born. Without the piety of Zechariah and Elizabeth, he would not have given the greatest among those born of women…

O David, look to these “saints” of yours!

Why do you want to look at what guarantees you nothing?

Eve had… 7000 good fruits, desirable and all for gaining wisdom…

But the “seducer” bent her gaze to desire that one fruit that she was not to touch…

So you sinned, David!

So to you too “Satan” seduced the gaze… and therefore you will learn to see appear, even in your heart, in love with God, those “weeds” that you cannot pull out… You will have to walk with your weaknesses. For this too, you will have to… “suffer”!

Out of the depths I cry to you, Lord! (Psalm 130)

There is certainly an image of God in the human being, a “depth” that resists all our violence: “your law is deep within my heart” (Ps 40:9). I can violate that law… cut the roots with the absolute, deny holiness and kill the author of life (Acts 3:14-15)… but I cannot destroy that image, that depth which in me will keep on crying out despite… sin. And God keeps listening to that cry… What is the abyss into which the human being has fallen?

“The Lord God called to the man and said to him: Where are you?” (Gen 3:9).

From where did Ishmael raise his voice and weep? God heard the voice of the boy (Gen 21:15-17).

What slavery makes Israel groan? (Exod 2:23-25). God listened to its lament…

From what anguish can one call out: “My God, my God, why have you abandoned me? You have laid me in the dust of death!” (Ps 22:1.16). And yet by crying out to him one is saved!…

From what grave could the blood of one slain cry out? The Lord will say:

“Where is Abel?” (Gen 4:9-10).

Where has the human being gone, that God should seek him?…

And a cry will be lent to David too… by the mouth of the prophet. Nathan will be that faithful guardian who will know where to find… his “brother”!

And he goes to awaken him: “You are the man!”

David, you were there, in death!

And from the depths your cry will rise: “I have sinned!” Create in me, O God, a clean heart!

Adam too will be forgiven: in his heart that word of light will be sown: “The offspring of the woman will crush the head of the one who seduced and killed you.” But harsh will be the consequences of that rebellion. “The earth will be cursed because of you. In toil you will eat its yield for all the days of your life. By the sweat of your brow you will eat bread, until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken: you are dust and to dust you will return” (Gen 3:15-19).

David too will take the hard road of penance. If once he was the innocent one persecuted by external enemies… now he is the “penitent” who must suffer from… internal enemies!

His land will give him… thorns! His son Absalom will rebel! And the son of adultery… will die! Can a bad tree bear good fruit?…

But, courage, David: another Son of yours will crush the head of the typical rebel and then, yes, every curse will be canceled… every death will be conquered and the Lord will at last say to… your Lord: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps 110:1). But that “Lord of yours” too will need… to die.

Now is the time of patient waiting and patient pilgrimage…

The sword will never depart from his house, his wives will be the prey of a relative of his who will possess them in public, as an insult (2 Sam 12:11-12).

He will begin fasting, supplications, vigils (2 Sam 12:16)…

“Who knows? Perhaps the Lord will have pity on me?” (2 Sam 12:22).

But he will resign himself: he knows that God does not listen to sinners, but if one is God-fearing and does his will, he listens to him (John 9:31)… “It is true, even if I cry out and call for help, he stifles my prayer. He has barred my ways with blocks of stone. It seems useless to call upon you: you have wrapped yourself, O God, in anger, hidden in a cloud, so that my supplication cannot reach you. Lord, you have drawn away from me because I am a sinner!”

But that Son, Lord, whom he still carries in his loins, already seems to inspire him: “Do not fear, David: you will teach the erring my ways and sinners will return to me, so that I may open their lips again to my praise… Courage, I do not cast you away from my presence… All who are weary and burdened will come to me, so that I may give them the joy of feeling saved. I will pour out on them a new spirit… they will know that I am their Lord and they will live again. I will let you rest in your land. Your dried-up bones will rise again… Do not fear, David. A contrite spirit and a broken and humbled heart I do not despise… I never reject… Even if I afflict, I will again have pity, according to my immeasurable mercy. It is against my desire that I humble the children of men.

I will be “Son of Man” and your afflictions will be mine, your sorrows will bend me too, for your iniquities I will give my life… Courage, David: I have wiped out your faults: walk… My burden is light!

I will gather the tribes of Israel… into your hands. I will free them from all the rebellions by which they sinned and you will be their king, I will make with them a covenant of peace and set my sanctuary in their midst forever. Do not fear, I will show favor to Jerusalem” (Ps 51; Matt 11:28-29; Luke 5:8-10; Ezek 37; Lam 3).

Another son of his, Amnon, will die, killed by Absalom in revenge (2 Sam 13:37)… Again mourning and sorrow… for a “long time”!

And again the strength to forgive: he will bring back Absalom, who had fled in fear (2 Sam 13:39).

But David will kiss… a traitor (2 Sam 14:21.33).

Winning the affection of the Israelites (2 Sam 15:1-6), Absalom will launch an assault on his father’s throne (2 Sam 15:10-13).

Soon that people—which acclaimed and recognized David as “bone of their bones”—forgets!…

It is again collapse… dispersion!

And David does not fight… No attempt at resistance.

He already seems a defeated man. He who did not fear the bear and the lion… flees! “None of us will escape from Absalom… Depart in haste… lest disaster overtake us and strike the city with the sword” (2 Sam 15:14).

O David, is that a kind of military strategy of yours?

A political emergency? Or does your “penitent” heart truly no longer have any “claims” (Ps 131), “does not go after things too great, now beyond its strength”?

Truly, standing at a distance, you do not even dare lift your eyes to heaven and you go on only whispering: “He will rescue the poor one who cries out and the afflicted who has no one to help… He will have pity on the lowly and the poor and save the lives of his needy” (cf. Ps 72:12-14 and Luke 18).

David takes up again the way of the… wilderness!

Always a place of refuge for the weak, the scattered and the persecuted… but also a place of the unknown: “I go where I happen to go…” (2 Sam 15:20). The Ark of God does not go with him… For the Ark there will be a sanctuary, a splendid dwelling… What he had dreamed for his God, the Faithful One, the Holy One of Israel…

“Only if I find favor in the eyes of the Lord will he bring me back and let me see it again together with his dwelling. But if he says: I do not delight in you, here I am! Let him do with me what seems good to him” (2 Sam 15:25-26).

The Ark of God returns to the city! And David… climbs the ascent of the olive trees! He climbs weeping and walks with his head covered and barefoot (2 Sam 15:30).

“O hope of Israel, its savior in time of trouble, why do you want to be like a stranger in the land and like a wayfarer who stays but one night? Why do you want to be like a man dismayed, like a warrior unable to help? Yet you are in our midst, Lord, and we are called by your name. Do not abandon us!” (Jer 14:8-9).

Against You, You Alone, Have I Sinned

This David truly understood well. His sin broke, first of all, his personal relationship with God, and when, during his flight from Absalom, Shimei appears, cursing him and shouting at him: “Be gone, you scoundrel, the blood of the house of Saul falls upon you… here you are in the misfortune you deserved, because you are a… man of blood!” (2 Sam 16:7-8), David perceives, in that jealous “resentment” of the man of the family of Saul, the indignation of his God: “Let him curse, for the Lord has ordered him. If he curses it is because the Lord said to him: Curse David. And who can say: Why do you do so?” (2 Sam 16:10-11.13).

But patience, generated by self-control, generates godliness (cf. 2 Pet 1:5-6): “useful for everything, since it holds a promise of life both for the present and for the future… For this we toil and struggle, because we have set our hope on the living God, who is the savior of all, especially of those who believe” (cf. 1 Tim 4:8-10). And precisely in that weariness, in that toilsome exile, David is exercising his godliness… He believes and can hope…: “Perhaps the Lord will look upon my affliction and make it up to me with good for the cursing I am receiving today” (2 Sam 16:12).

And the Lord will turn to compassion! Hushai will foil the plans of Ahithophel, formerly David’s counselor (2 Sam 17:1-14) and will allow… a little breathing space to the fugitives.

Ziba (2 Sam 16:1-4), Shobi, Machir, Barzillai (2 Sam 17:27-29) instead, will refresh the king and his hungry people.

Yet an extreme sorrow will not be spared David.

As he had wanted to save, once, the life of the one who was persecuting him, so again now he will recommend to his commanders, before the decisive clash: “Deal gently for my sake with young Absalom” (2 Sam 18:5).

You did not dare to raise your hand against the anointed of God!

You felt your heart pound, just for having cut off a corner of Saul’s cloak (1 Sam 24)… There was in you neither wicked design nor rebellion… You did not want to be kept from sharing in the inheritance of the Lord.

For this reason too, you loved the one who was to guarantee it to you.

And if Saul was stirred up against you, you considered that trial as the fragrance of a sacred offering!

O David, you want to save your son! You are his father, but also his king, the “anointed” of God.

Did you not execute the Amalekite who had dared to stretch out his hand to kill Saul, the Lord’s anointed?

To him you cried out: your blood be on your own head!

Did you not command Solomon not to leave Shimei’s sin unpunished, since that curse, which you yourself had accepted in a spirit of penance, was directed against God’s anointed? (1 Kgs 2:8-9).

Absalom wanted your death! And if the Lord frustrated Ahithophel’s counsel, it was to bring disaster upon Absalom!

David, you know the Law: whoever mistreats his father or mother shall be put to death, his blood shall be upon him (Lev 20:9). Honoring father and mother is the first commandment, joined to a promise: that the obedient child may be happy and enjoy a long life on the earth (cf. Exod 20:12; Eph 6:2-3).

Absalom will not be able to have a long life and you will have to weep for him bitterly. It is true, you would want to die in his place. Thus far a father’s love drives you. You weep for your son and do not want to be consoled.

Truly that weeping that breaks your heart… is a sacrifice pleasing to God… “You show that you love those who hate you!” (2 Sam 19:7): in this too, Joab becomes a good prophet! “If Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, then it would be right in your eyes.”

We dared to suppose, in the case of Saul, that the patient love of a faithful subject might have helped him in the last dramatic moments of his life…

Is it perhaps still permitted to us to hope for it for this rebellious son, Absalom? The patient love of a father… that disconsolate cry: my son

Absalom!… may he have been welcomed? Before dying, pierced, there, caught among the branches of a terebinth, between heaven and earth… may that son have had the regret… the longing, the pain of a lost fatherly love?… human thought is swift…

Perhaps help can come to us from those truly invisible… traces that God often lets us glimpse (Ps 78), of his secret designs of salvation…

Another mother weeps and does not want to be consoled for the children who are no more… And God answers her: “There is a reward for your pains, they will return from the enemy’s land… there is hope for your descendants: your children will return to their own borders…” (Jer 31:16-17).

Will there be a reward for the patient and so anguished love of David?

Will Absalom return… from death?… Is there a hope for that rebellious soul to return within its borders, into that family affection, into the tenderness of that father, who would have preferred to lose everything in order to embrace that son again?

Such feelings, O David, we shall see again in another son of yours… yes, an “other” still far off… He too, tenderly moved for a mother who is carrying her only son to be buried… weeps with her. Then gives him back to her alive.

David… keep on believing, being patient, hoping… You have not yet arrived at the fullness of time… Tomorrow there will be…: the “I am the resurrection and the life!”

After so many tribulations—because you too, David, learned that to this you are called as one chosen (1 Thess 3:3) and cannot enter the Kingdom without having passed through many—after so many tribulations (Acts 14:22) you will again be a sign of unity between Judah and Israel.

In your last years, you seem to grow old alone…

Only one companionship: a young body to warm you…

For what reason that detachment of yours from everyone… that silence… it is not senile dementia: you manage to the end to govern with wisdom and authority. Why is none of those women whom you love there to share your sunset? Do you continue your penitential journey? Or do you sense the deep need of wisdom?

Are you seeking her and do you want to find rest in her? (Sir 6:16-33). Perhaps, reconciled with God, you now want to follow solely… the Lamb, wherever he goes and leads you? (Rev 14:4).

Is it from him, from that son of yours far off, that you are learning detachment… even from the dearest affections? “Woman, behold your son!”…

Is this why you will, in the end, leave the throne?

So as to be able to hand over, at last, your spirit, free, into the hands of your Lord?

Is this your last and… patient will?…

Your riches, your wisdom… accumulated in the midst of so many anguishes (1 Chr 22:14)… are entrusted to Solomon for that Temple which you cannot see… It will be the glorious presence of Yahweh in the midst of his people. And there your last thoughts are turned… there you abandon yourself…

But do not fear, faithful shepherd of Israel! Your body rests in safety. That Temple, in which you gave yourself together with your people, will be destroyed…

But God has promised it: in three days he will rebuild it!… And that Temple will be forever!

Do not fear and be at peace, King David. Shalom!
